Neither letter is cancelled and both are still binding. **Jonas Mercer says *you were right* and *there is nothing I can put next to it*, the second time that sentence has been said in this account, and nothing goes in a notebook.** Nobody gave Renn a title, a grade, a department, a chair, a seat, a form or a row on anything; his own three asks are unmoved; he went home at about ten past six. Jonas Mercer says the second system is a man of about eighty-six and five things and a sheet on a wall with his name on it, and does not say it in a shop.

**Chapter 0220 — The End of a Shift. Tuesday the second of February 2016, from about half past six in the evening, a hall off a parade of shops in Tideglass.** Lattice notice. **SHE SAID IT IN A CORNER BY THE DOOR IN PLAIN WORDS AND HE ACCEPTED IT IN ONE SENTENCE AND DID NOT ASK WHY, AND NEITHER OF THEM WAS THE REASON THE OTHER WAS IN THE ROOM, AND IT WAS NOT A REPAIR AND IT WAS NOT A RUPTURE AND IT WAS ALSO NOT NOTHING.** About nine people, a gas heater, tea the colour of a wet cigarette since five, a shoebox of photographs from a woman of about eighty-nine, and the man of about eighteen who washes up in a kitchen at the back of the parade six days a week. He has been in the room at about ten past six on a Tuesday for six weeks with no arrangement and no list. **Sanaa Iqbal, in four feet of space with a rack of leaflets in it, at about twenty to seven, with her back to the room: nine people in that building have worked out that the last ten minutes of their afternoon is a thing that happens, two of them have started saying good evening to her when he comes through the door, and she is not going to be the reason a room of nine people arrange anything.** He says *Right. I won't come at six.* and asks nothing and apologises to nobody and says nothing at all for the rest of the evening. Neither of them is the reason the other is there: he came to ask whether the room is free on a Friday in February and she came for a cup of tea. They leave at ten past eight without waiting for each other, onto the same pavement for two minutes, and then one goes north and one goes west. **He does not write it down, and it is not a thing to write down, and on the Saturday he catches himself thinking about it in a corridor and lets the thought finish and does one single thing with it.**

**Chapter 0221 — Out of the Tray. Sunday the seventh of February 2016, from about ten in the morning, a building by the water in Tideglass, and then a corridor on the first floor.** Lattice notice. **IT IS NOT IN THE TRAY ANY MORE AND NOBODY PUT IT ANYWHERE, AND A TRAY UNDER A WINDOW DOES NOT BECOME A REGISTER BY BEING EMPTY, AND NOBODY IS GOING TO BE TOLD WHAT IT IS.** A man of about ninety-two at the front door, the porter or one of the porters since before the war the notice board still advertises, gives the whole of it in about a minute and none of it was done on purpose: it came in on the Saturday, the trays went up with the water office's post on the Monday, it was still on the shelf on the Thursday before Christmas, it came off the shelf on Tuesday 26 January and went into a drawer at the end of the corridor because that is what you do with a thing you do not know, and that room is locked on a Sunday. **The borough has had it fifty-seven days, twenty-six of them in a drawer, twenty-nine on a shelf by the filing cabinets and two over Christmas in a tray under a window.** He goes up, the corridor is cold, the room is shut, and he does not try the handle. **It is a price and it is a receipt and it is a precedent and all three are still true; the only thing that has changed is that somebody in another city has read it.** A letter Iselin Krogh wrote on Friday 5 February 2016, which came on Saturday the sixth, a page and a half, read four times and not answered: she has read it, she has had her own since 18 December in a folder in a drawer, a document has travelled between two cities without anybody deciding it should, she has decided not to find out because both ways she can think of are worse than not knowing, and the water office here is not going to answer the claim and will not be told to. **It is the only thing that has come back along a document to this borough in nine months.** The man of about thirty-seven is not the man this is about; Ewen Ashgrove appears nowhere in this batch.

**Chapter 0222 — What a Room Does. Friday the twelfth of February 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, a hall off a parade of shops in Tideglass.** Lattice notice. **NINE PEOPLE CAME TO A ROOM THEY ARE NOT ON ANYTHING FOR, TWO PIECES OF PAPER IN ONE WOMAN'S HANDWRITING WENT ON THE TABLE, SOMEBODY ASKED FOR THE SHEET ON A WALL IN ANOTHER CITY, NOBODY COULD PRODUCE IT, AND THE ROOM WENT ON.** The room is let out on Sundays to a group that meets every three months, and was free on this Friday because the woman with the key was in it and does not charge for the gas. **Nell Ardent says before she puts them down that they are not the sheets: she has never had a sheet, she has a wall, an office on the other side of an estuary, a plastic bag, a fortnight, and a woman in a corridor who could not finish a sentence.** The two lines are the corridor wall sheet and the office copy, in her handwriting, copied on 4 December with a pen off her own bag and compared with a ruler. **A woman of about sixty-two asks for the one line for the noticeboard, and nobody can produce the wall sheet, and the reason given is that in about two months the only version anybody in this borough could see would be a piece of A4 in Nell Ardent's handwriting with her initials in the corner, and it would not be the sheet and it would have been the sheet, because there would not be anything else.** The room goes on. Mrs Obi, about thirty-six, takes the minutes in her own hand on a pad she takes home in a handbag; it is not in a field and she is not asked. **A young woman of about twenty is right about something small: seven keys on the board by the door and a card saying six, the sixth on a string, the unlabelled one the only one nobody uses. The woman with the key looks at it for about a minute and a half and says "well" and makes more tea, and the card still says six.**

**Chapter 0223 — He Should Not Have Said It. Wednesday the seventeenth of February 2016, from about four in the afternoon, a building by the water in Marrowgate, and then the back room of the works.** Lattice notice. **HE SAID THE TRUE THING ABOUT HIMSELF AT TWENTY PAST SIX IN THE EVENING, TO ONE PERSON, AND THEN SAID HE SHOULD NOT HAVE SAID IT, AND IT WAS NOT TAKEN BACK, AND NOTHING WAS ARRANGED FOR HIM.** The room is twelve feet by ten with a kettle, a shelf of ring binders, a stove that is off and a door that does not shut. He has been in the town a fortnight and there is nothing he has to do on the Wednesday. Walter Sallow says it in four movements: it is not that he is the only one who does it, that is the sentence in the room and everybody in it is wrong; he is the only one who can, and that is a different sentence doing the same work; he was asked once, in a room, in a spring, said yes, went outside, and there is nothing to hand it to, and everybody else in that arrangement has got a door to hand it to and he has got a gate; and the bit he cannot put anywhere is that there is nobody in that town he can be cross with, and the whole of it is better than the one he came from, and he has no complaint, and he is the complaint, and there is nobody to make it to. **He then says: *I should not have said that. To you. On a Wednesday. In a back room.*** **Jonas Mercer says nothing at all.** He thinks about a corridor in December and a woman with a folder on a window ledge, and does not tell the old man any of it, and does not say he had done it before, and does not repeat the sentence, and does not say one word of it out loud for the rest of the evening; the notebook was in his inside pocket at about ten past seven and was not opened. **Its standing is exactly the standing of the sentence said once on a pavement in September 2015 and of the one said once in a corridor in December 2015. It is the third, and the third time is not a pattern and nobody says it is a pattern.** He is not rescued, he is not asked to stop, nothing is arranged for him, no letter goes anywhere, and the sheet on the wall is not altered.

**Chapter 0224 — A Sunday in Tideglass. Sunday the twenty-first of February 2016, from about ten in the morning, a building by the water in Tideglass, and then a parade of shops.** Lattice notice. **THERE ARE TWO DOCUMENTS AND THEY DESCRIBE THE SAME ACT AND ONE OF THEM IS A THING A PERSON MAY DO AND THE OTHER IS A THING A PERSON HAS TO DO, AND ONE IS IN THIS CITY AND ONE IS IN A TOWN EIGHT MILES UP THE ESTUARY, AND NOBODY HAS PUT THEM TOGETHER.** Nina Calder is in the records room doing a water bill out of a carrier bag and says the door sticks and nothing else. He does not open the register; it is always open at the last written page. Nineteen entries, the nineteenth a yard light with a bulb in the maintenance column and the bulb out, and under it a line that stops about two inches short of the bottom. **He does the sum and it comes to four hundred and fifty-two, and the figure is on a piece of paper in his inside pocket.** The permission from Alderwick is in force and nothing in this borough has come to an end this winter that anybody was relying on and there is no season anybody has said is coming. The two documents: a sheet in a plastic wallet in his coat with one line, whose office copy has a second line in the same type and which Nell Ardent has copied out twice in her own hand; and four lines on a wall eight miles up the estuary naming a man, which he has read and has not got a copy of and which nobody in this borough could produce. **Nobody puts them side by side and no character in the chapter does.** **There is a third of them somewhere and nobody in this borough has seen it and he is not going this month, and he has no way of asking for an invitation to it that would not be an arrangement.** **The counter is in one scene and is not entered:** he stands on the pavement for about a minute with the door open and a card in the shop window carrying the shop's own telephone number and nothing else, and a woman of about sixty-five behind it with her back to the glass, and he does not go in, and the drawer under it with no key and no list is shut. **Nobody is rescued, nobody dies, nothing is minuted, the register is at nineteen and the line under it is four hundred and fifty-two days and is still blank, and it alone in that building has not moved while an instrument went out of force in it, and that is worse than a relief and is not a relief.**

## Volume 05, Batch 0004 — Chapters 225–234

**Chapter 0225 — One Line. Sunday the twenty-eighth of February 2016, from about ten in the morning, a bus, a yard gate at Penhale, and a corridor outside an office.** Lattice notice. **THE THIRD OF THE THREE REGIONAL SYSTEMS IS THE BEST OF THE THREE, ANY PERSON MAY GO IN THROUGH THE GATE ON A SUNDAY WITHOUT ARRANGING IT, THE WHOLE OF WHAT ABOUT FOUR HUNDRED PEOPLE HAVE AGREED ABOUT IS ONE SENTENCE, AND THE RULE OWNS NOTHING AT ALL.** Penhale is a bend in a road with a bus stop and about forty houses. The whole agreement is one framed line: any part of any system in this region may be used by any person. Haldane Perry, a man of about eighty-nine, explains from ten feet of concrete that the two-line version in the rack is the same rule with the bit about standing left on, because a name would make the yard a business. Everything in the yard is hired, sold, borrowed or next door. **Perry mistakes Jonas Mercer for a crew, hands him a job sheet to sign, and he signs it: £163, and a printed line underneath saying the rate for that work as agreed, 1987.** The third corridor sentence: a thing nobody owns can be used by everybody, and so can the paper that comes with it. A raven gets into the racking and the whole yard stops for a minute and a half and that is the arrangement working.

**Chapter 0226 — The Book With a Column In It. Sunday the sixth of March 2016, from about eleven in the morning, an office at Penhale, and the ten metres of concrete outside it.** **A SCHEME THAT COSTS NOTHING AND ASKS NOTHING IS PAID FOR OUT OF THE REGION, AND THE BOOK IS ON THE DESK, AND NOBODY IN THAT YARD IS ABLE TO SAY NO TO ANYBODY.** A man in his forties keeps a carbon book and a wall sheet whose heads are JOB, PLACE, DAYS, PARTS, FUEL, HIRE and CLAIM, and whose top-left box says LEVEL OF SERVICE and has been empty since it was printed. He shows it to anybody who asks and says it was never secret. **The job carries a piece of paper at the end of it and the paper is not an invoice: it is a claim form, the same form every time, and the sum on it is not what the job cost.** A Wednesday crew is booked for a job whose client will not know until the Wednesday, and nobody in the office says no to anything. A woman of about eighty-six, who let the yard be used in 1987 when it was a field, says the one sentence she has to the window: she has never charged anybody one pound, is not going to, and there is nothing anybody can do to her or for her. Nobody's required to be one of the nine yards. On the Thursday, in a car park four miles from the yard, a man adds the parts, fuel, hire and labour against the claim and gets the same answer twice: four times.

**Chapter 0227 — Out. Saturday the twelfth of March 2016, from about half past seven in the morning, a shop on a parade in Tideglass, and a van on the tarmac behind it.** Lattice notice. **A PERSON FROM THIS BOROUGH WENT OUT ON A GOOD JOB BECAUSE THE JOB WAS GOOD, AND NOBODY ASKED HER, AND THE ONE PERSON WHO WILL BE TOLD IS TOLD BY SOMEBODY WHO HAS ALREADY DECIDED SHE IS A GOOD EXAMPLE.** Abby Marlow, a woman of about twenty-three, and two men in their thirties, one of whom cannot carry, load at ten past seven for a standpipe, a gully and a soakaway at eight houses with no council and no landlord you can name. Jonas Mercer is on the pavement and does not go. **Abby Marlow says the sentence of the batch to him at a quarter to eight, with nobody within twenty feet: a person who is not counted is not a person who is helped, and that is not a punishment, that is nobody knowing — and then says she likes it here and would not have had the money or the van or the learning, and would not have it called a favour.** The man of about thirty-one is not here and has not been rung, and Jonas Mercer walks up the parade and stops at a corner and works out how he is going to put it.

**Chapter 0228 — Two Sums. Friday the eighteenth of March 2016, from about ten in the morning, a shop on a parade in Tideglass, behind the counter.** **ONE SHEET OF PAPER, THE SAME FOR EVERY JOB, NOT A BILL, SIGNED AT THE BOTTOM BY A CREW THAT WAS NEVER ASKED WHAT THE SUM WAS, BECAUSE THE SUM WAS ALREADY PRINTED ON THE TOP OF IT.** Jonas Mercer brings out the sheet he signed by mistake and Nell Ardent calls it a claim form before she says anything else, and says every part of it is correct. **The sum is not what the job cost, the sum is not what the same job costs now, the sum is correct, and the line under the sum names the year: 1987.** Tomas Renn, on the counter, is asked what the sum is and says *that's the sum*, twice, and is being helpful, and there is no way to ask the question so that a person hears it. Hanna Wray, who keeps the counter most weeks, says the sum is not what the job cost, that it is about four times bigger every time, that everybody has known for about two years, and that nobody is being cheated. She says the year doesn't seem to do anything; it sits there. The sheet goes into Nell Ardent's bag and not back into his coat.

**Chapter 0229 — As Agreed. NOBODY IS BEING CHEATED, THE SUM IS THE SUM AGREED IN 1987, THE WORK WAS DONE FOR THAT SUM THEN, AND THE RATE HAS NOT BEEN REVISED BECAUSE NOBODY WHO IS OWED THE DIFFERENCE IS STILL IN ANY OF THE BODIES THAT AGREED IT.** Jonas Mercer rings the Penhale office from a corridor because the room at the end of it is shut and is not his room. He had found nobody.

**Chapter 0230 — Four. On the Corrance counter a woman who has been there nine years says they are her biggest single account, have never been late, and that she does not know what the rate is. The Marchmont forecourt is about a tenth above the yard. **Jonas Mercer's line, out loud in a car, to himself and nobody: they did not do anything to us, they sold us what we asked for.** A node with no term in force is not a person with no address, and he almost wrote that down on the Thursday and did not write it on the Thursday. The eleven refusals stand at eleven and a twelfth did not arrive.

**Chapter 0231 — A Schedule. Friday the first of April 2016, from about eleven in the morning, that first floor room in a building by the water, and the corridor.** **A CLAIM FOR MONEY MADE CORRECTLY IN ANOTHER CITY IN DECEMBER, AND A SCHEDULE, AND THE SCHEDULE IS THE FIRST THING THAT HAS EVER COME BACK ALONG A DOCUMENT TO THIS BOROUGH THAT NAMES A PERSON BY NAME, BY DATE AND BY PLACE.** The woman of about fifty-five who has the room takes the folded sheet out of the drawer without difficulty and says out loud that she does not know what it is, and is right. **It has now been in this borough ninety-six days: twenty-eight in a drawer, thirty on a shelf by the filing cabinets, two over Christmas in a tray under a window.** On the desk there is a second sheet, from Penhale, that came up with the Friday tray and that nobody has opened: a rule across it, a column headed CLAIM, eleven ruled lines, and in each line a date, a place, a name and a sum, and the yard has got all eleven sums right. Two of the eleven names belong to people Jonas Mercer has spoken to in this borough in the last fortnight. She says the money one she can put in a drawer and the other she cannot think about. **It is a carbon, not a demand and not a bill: nothing on it that anybody can be invoiced for and nobody at the other end waiting for an answer.** The man of about thirty-one knows two of the names, has said so to nobody, and was not rung.

**Chapter 0232 — Not Counted. Wednesday the sixth of April 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, a hall off a parade of shops in Tideglass, and the corridor outside it.** **A PERSON WHO IS NOT COUNTED IS NOT A PERSON WHO IS HELPED, AND A BOROUGH THAT HAS BEEN KEPT GOING BY PEOPLE WHO WERE NEVER ASKED AND NEVER COUNTED HAS PAID NOTHING FOR ANY OF IT SINCE THE SPRING AND IS ABOUT TO BE GIVEN A BILL FOR IT BY ANOTHER CITY, AND THE SENTENCE IS CORRECT, AND SAYING IT IN A ROOM IN THIS BOROUGH IS HEARD AS MAKING AN OBJECTION.** Jonas Mercer is in the corridor with the door open four inches. **Tomas Renn stands up at ten past eight and says both halves of it without building up to it: a person who is not counted is not a person who is helped, and there is a sheet of paper with eleven names on it in a building by the water, and when it is finished somebody will work out what this borough owes, and they will not be wrong to work it out.** Mrs Obi says *that's an objection*. He says he knows. She asks what he is asking for. He opens his mouth and shuts it, and he means it, and he says no and sits down. **Then Mrs Obi says the old one, flatly, with the pad shut on her knee, having been saying it in that room for about two years: forty walls, a pump in a doorway, a shovel and a broom, a label on a shelf, a bench moved, a sign put right with a marker, a hose nobody came for, and a man of about eighty-six raking an intake by hand.** The town that owns them owns nobody, and the region that will send the bill owns nobody either, and that is the same sentence twice and it is still true. The pad went home in a handbag. A man stood in a corridor who could have put the two together and did not.

**Chapter 0233 — Six. Monday the eleventh of April 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, a Methodist hall on Carrow Lane in Tideglass, and the corridor outside it.** Lattice notice. **THE SIX QUESTIONS WERE ON A TABLE IN A ROOM AND NONE OF THEM WAS ANSWERED, AND A MAN WHO IS VERY GOOD IN THAT ROOM PUT A VERSION ON THE TABLE THAT WOULD HAVE SETTLED THREE OF THEM AT ONCE, AND IT RESTS ON A PIECE OF PAPER THAT CANNOT BE PRODUCED, AND HE SAID SO HIMSELF IN FRONT OF NINE PEOPLE AND SAT DOWN.** All six are restated in order: which dated thing will be provable first; which of eight will be decided to keep, and whether for being good or being expensive; the page or the chair; which of two opposite shapes the city must stop, the second of which is still nothing; the permission and the obligation, which is now a third document; and the claim in the drawer, which is now two claims and a schedule. The man in his sixties catches himself: the two wall sheets would settle questions four, five and half of two in a fortnight, and nobody in this borough can produce either of them, and it is not the story that settles it, it is the paper. On the wall behind him is a card, printed, there since about September, with two sentences on it that neither was argued out of the other. Somebody wrote the notes in their own hand in a book and went out of the door with it. Nobody was given a title, a grade, a department, a chair, a seat, a membership, a form or a row on a rota. At ten to ten a man stood outside the building by the water and did not go in.

**Chapter 0234 — Held. Saturday the sixteenth of April 2016, from about eleven in the morning, a building by the water in Tideglass, and a parade of shops.** **THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A PERMISSION, AN OBLIGATION AND A CLAIM IS THREE PIECES OF PAPER IN THREE PLACES, EACH IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S KEEPING, AND NONE OF THE THREE HAS BEEN ANSWERED.** Nina Calder is in the records room and says the door sticks and, in a list, that the west gate is the same as it has always been: up at seven on a Sunday morning and stopped at six on the Sunday morning after that, six days, not a week, no date on it anywhere in this city and none coming. The register is not opened: nineteen entries, a yard light, a bulb, and a blank line under the nineteenth that comes to **five hundred and seven** on a piece of paper in a coat, and nobody has put a name in the line on page two of anything and nothing has been renewed, expired or renamed. On the parade, Nell Ardent restates the three: the one-line sheet on a wall in a corridor in a city on the other side of the water, a thing a person may do; the four-line sheet on a wall in a room in a town up the estuary, a thing a person has to do, which nobody here could produce and which Jonas Mercer refused a copy of; and the folded sheet in a drawer, a thing somebody else sent. It is not a question, she says, which is worse. Nothing was minuted. In the vestibule, a man stands at a counter he does not go into, and the drawer under it with no key and no list is shut, and the woman of about sixty-five does not turn round, and a van went out of a shop on this parade five weeks and four days ago with three people in it who had not been asked.

## Volume 05, Batch 0005 — Chapters 235–244

**Chapter 0235 — The Board. Thursday the twenty-first of April 2016, from about half past eight in the morning, a boathouse off a yard in Tideglass, and the car park behind it.** **THE THING THIS BOROUGH IS CALLED FIRST FOR IS ON A BOARD IN A LOCK-UP, IN A HAND, ON CARDS, AND THE FIRST TWO LINES ARE PEOPLE AND THE THIRD IS A PLACE, AND UNDER THE THIRD ONE THERE IS A NAME THAT IS NOT THERE ANY MORE.** A brick hut with a padlock whose number four people know and none of them have written down. Three cards cut with something that was not scissors: BOAT, ENGINE, LOW PEVERELL, and a gap under the third. Nell Ardent walked up a parade and asked two men in a wet shop, who said separately that if you want to know what goes first, ask the boat, and if the boat won't tell you, ask the engine. The boat crew were in; the engine crew came at five to nine and did not open a box; nobody rang either of them. The woman with the key to the lock-up did not cut the cards and does not want to be the one somebody asks about. **The man from number forty-one came in at about ten past nine having been told by a man in a shop: his name was under the third one, somebody came round with a pen about three years ago, he said he does not do anything, he just lives there, and he took it off a fortnight later and it is in a drawer in his kitchen, because *a name on a board is a thing that gets asked about and I've been on enough lists*.** **THE MAJOR TURN: THE PRIORITY IS A PERSON AND A PLACE AND NEITHER CAN BE GIVEN TO ANYBODY, AND THE MAN UP THE ESTUARY WHO HOLDS THE FIVE THINGS WAS TOLD A YEAR AGO THAT NONE OF IT COULD BE HANDED TO ANOTHER PERSON, AND THE SAME SHAPE OF SENTENCE IS TRUE HERE AND IS A DIFFERENT SENTENCE, AND NELL ARDENT HELD BOTH AT ONCE IN FRONT OF THE BOARD** — a duty can be given to a man who is standing there, and you cannot hand a man to anybody either and you cannot hand a place to anybody, and if you put them side by side you will get both of them wrong. He is the pump Mrs Obi listed in 0232. Jonas Mercer was in the car park from nine until half past eleven, was not in the boathouse, was asked to come and did not say he would not, and did the sum: **five hundred and twelve**.

**Chapter 0236 — One at a Time. Tuesday the twenty-sixth of April 2016, from about eleven in the morning, the yard at Penhale and the office hut on the concrete, and the parade of shops in this borough.** **A COMPACT CANNOT BE AGREED WITH A YARD, AND IT CANNOT BE AGREED WITH A RULE, AND IT CANNOT BE AGREED WITH A BOOK, AND EVERY SENTENCE ANYBODY IN THAT YARD SAID ABOUT THAT WAS CORRECT.** The man at the gate said again that neither of them is on anything. Jonas Mercer stood in the doorway of the office hut and did not come in. Haldane Perry, a man of about eighty-nine, on a bench in the sun with the ledger shut on his knee, did not get up: a rule cannot be asked to agree to anything and a rule has not got a mouth. The man in his forties who keeps the book said *we can't say no* as a boast and is one of the four yards that have never sent or taken a crew, and said Haldane Perry is the boss and not a joke, and that a booking system has a manager and a manager can be asked to do something. The woman of about eighty-six said her field is not coming out of there. **THE MAJOR TURN, IN NELL ARDENT'S WORDS ON THE CONCRETE: it can't be agreed with a yard, it can't be agreed with a rule, it can't be agreed with a book; it's people, one at a time, face to face, and each one has to give something that's actually theirs, because the minute one of them gives me something a body owns then that body can have it back.** The first yes was the man in his forties agreeing in nine seconds that a line which is not a claim could go in the book, and then saying it is worth exactly nothing, because a column is a column. The second is the woman of about forty-two with the key, who gave the hall, the notebook, the gas, the door and Tuesday nights, and took no money for the gas, and set her own price: the mothers' group on a Wednesday, and the fact that a woman with a key doing a favour for nine years becomes a woman with a key running a thing. **And the one who matters most said no: Tomas Renn, because a compact agreed with people one at a time is a list, and a list is a column of lines somebody could write down, and he knows what happens to lines. He is right and nobody argues him out of it and he will not do it twice over in one afternoon.**

**Chapter 0237 — The Same Answer. Sunday the first of May 2016, from about half past ten in the morning, a shop on a parade of shops in Tideglass, a room over a shop, and a trade estate four miles out.** **THE SAME ANSWER FOUR TIMES, AND IT IS THAT THEY WOULD SELL TO SOMEBODY ELSE, AND NOT ONE OF THE FOUR HAS EVER BEEN ASKED A QUESTION AND NONE OF THEM IS WITHHOLDING ANYTHING, BECAUSE THERE IS NOTHING TO WITHHOLD.** Hanna Wray names the four and says she buys off two of them and has never asked either a question and neither of them would think it odd, and that is not a thing about them, it is a thing about a trade counter. Jonas Mercer puts the question to her first: if from the first of June the borough's crews did none of the work over the water and every job went to a crew from somewhere else, would that put your prices up, and would you sell to those crews. Tomas Renn came through with a crate of rags, said *still no* to nobody, and went out the back; Hanna Wray said that is twice now. Corrance Supply, in a room over a shop, from the woman who keeps the account book and has the yard as her biggest single account: course she would sell to whoever came, and the price on the rest of the book would go on a Tuesday instead of a Monday, and there is a rate on a board on the shelf behind her that she has never read and is not going to go and find out. Sarn Aggregates, on a weighbridge: they have never turned a job away in twenty years, and they have no book with the borough's name in it. Lowdale Hire, in a cabin, having said it all once in the February: *that's what a Tuesday is, and nobody sat down and made a Tuesday*, and if the vans go somewhere else entirely and he never finds out he still gets the fuel, and there is no blood in it anywhere and he wishes there was. Marcement, at a card on a post by a gate, about a tenth above the yard: more, they could double, to whoever walks in, nobody is coming here to be loyal to a borough. **THE MAJOR TURN: A REGION CAN BE MADE TO GO SLOW BY A SUPPLY CHAIN THAT IS BEING POLITE, AND THE ONLY THINGS IT COSTS ARE A NOTEBOOK AND A WEEK ON A TUESDAY.** Jonas Mercer wrote the Lowdale man's words down in his own hand, about a hundred and thirty of them, and none of it was a complaint.

**Chapter 0238 — Being There. Friday the sixth of May 2016, from about eleven in the morning, that first floor room in a building by the water, and a doorway at the bottom of Peverell Street.** **WHAT A RIGHT OF RETURN IS CANNOT BE FOUND OUT IN A CORRIDOR, AND EVERY VERSION OF IT THAT GOT WRITTEN ON THE BACK OF A HAND IN THAT ROOM WAS WRONG IN A DIFFERENT WAY FROM THE OTHER TWO.** The woman of about fifty-five who has that room is in on a Friday and is not in on a Sunday for anybody, and she refuses the question: *you have asked me how many ways a person is allowed to do a thing, and that is the same question about both of them, and you would take the same answer as proof they are the same and you would be right to and you would be no use whatsoever. Ask me the other half. What happens to the person who does it.* **He wrote three drafts and she read them upside down, and all three are worse than nothing: a permission with a bad end on it; a rota with no name on it yet, which is a rota waiting for somebody to fill it in, and the somebody who fills it in is the boss; and a third one she did not read out loud and called a duty and said don't.** And the other half: if you write it, it is a form, and a form has got a box on it, and the box has got a person in it; if you do not write it, anybody can pick it up and do what they like with it, and in this borough that is the same as it being true. She also says the one thing she has said to herself in that room, about a sheet on a wall up the estuary with four lines and a man's name under the second one, and that it is true and does not help her, because a man told to be somewhere has been given a place. **THE PROOF IS A DOORWAY: there is the pump, on a standpipe a man put in himself, and a hose coiled on the wall that has not been touched since the water went down, and the door is always open a hand's width, and Jonas Mercer stood in it for about two minutes and ASKED THE MAN INSIDE NOTHING AT ALL.** **THE MAJOR TURN: THE THING THAT MAKES A RETURN A RIGHT RATHER THAN A FAVOUR IS SOMEBODY BEING THERE WHEN IT IS NEEDED, AND THAT IS A THING TO BE ASKED FOR AND NOT A THING TO BE PROMISED IN ADVANCE.** Ask somebody on the day; ask them in advance and you have made a rota row, and the first person in that row would be Tomas Renn. It is not a lane anybody lives in, it is not a way of making a street findable, and nobody in the chapter says either sentence out loud.

**Chapter 0239 — Not the Man. Wednesday the eleventh of May 2016, from about eleven in the morning, the first-floor corridor in a building by the water, and a parade of shops.** **THE ASK WAS SAID OUT LOUD BY THE WRONG MAN AND COULD NOT BE TAKEN BACK, AND THE ONLY THING HE COULD DO WAS GIVE IT TO SOMEBODY WHO IS BETTER AT IT, AND THE SECOND TIME IS NOT THE SAME AS THE FIRST TIME BECAUSE HE HAS NOT RUN OUT OF ANYTHING AT ALL.** The ask, in about fifteen words: I want this borough to say out loud that if there's a regional emergency, its own crews go out of the borough before anything in the borough gets done. He did the sum against a wall: five hundred and thirty-two.**

**Chapter 0240 — Four Minutes. Sunday the fifteenth of May 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, a hall off a parade of shops in Tideglass, and the corridor outside it.** **WITHIN FOUR MINUTES OF SOMEBODY SAYING THE WORD, THE ROOM SAID OUT LOUD THAT A COMPACT IS NOT A THING A ROOM CAN AGREE TO, AND WHAT THE ROOM COULD DO INSTEAD WAS WORK OUT WHO WOULD ACTUALLY BE BOUND BY IT, AND THE ANSWER WAS A LIST OF PEOPLE NOBODY IN THAT ROOM HAD EVER ASKED, AND THE LIST WAS LONGER THAN THE ROOM, AND THE LIST WAS NOT SOMETHING THE ROOM WAS ASKED TO PRODUCE.** About nine people, the women outnumbering the men by about three to one, a pound in the meter put in before anybody came. The man in his sixties, a building estimator, in nine words: *a compact is not a thing a room can agree to* — because a room that agrees to something owns it, and a room that owns a thing has to keep it, and then you have a committee. Asked whether he would make it, he said no, and that the list is the only useful thing in this borough tonight and should be made by the people on it, one at a time, over about six months, and by then it will be a different list. He put the version on the table anyway — the two sheets would settle questions four, five and half of two — and said he made it on the eleventh of April and cannot unmake it, and cannot produce either sheet, one of them being about four hundred yards from a gate a man of eighty-six opens by hand at seven in the morning and nobody in this borough having ever asked him what time he opens it, and the other an estuary and a Tuesday away. **None of the six questions was answered and no seventh was asked.** Jonas Mercer was in the corridor from a quarter to eight until about ten, did not go in, and did the sum against the wall: **five hundred and thirty-six**. The register is at nineteen. Nobody was given a title, a grade, a department, a chair, a seat, a membership, a form or a row on a rota.

**Chapter 0241 — First Out. Friday the twentieth of May 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, a Methodist hall on Carrow Lane in Tideglass, and the corridor outside it.** **THIS BOROUGH GAVE UP ITS FIRST CALL AND SAID SO OUT LOUD IN A ROOM, AND THE ONLY REASON IT COULD BE DONE IS THAT NOBODY IN EITHER CITY CAN REQUIRE ANYBODY TO DO ANYTHING, AND THAT IS THE FIRST TIME THAT ABSENCE HAS BEEN ANY USE AND ALSO THE FIRST TIME IT HAS COST SOMEBODY SOMETHING, AND A CARD ON THE WALL IN THAT ROOM SAYS BOTH HALVES OF THAT AND NEITHER WAS ARGUIED OUT OF THE OTHER.** About nine people, a pound in the meter, and Mrs Obi with the pad shut on her knee the whole night. Asked whether it goes on paper: no. Somebody said somebody ought to write it down; the young woman of about twenty said *let it not*; **nobody wrote it down, no word of any document was altered, and no name went in any line.** The man at number forty-one said *you're not asking me* and *you're telling me you've done it*, and Mrs Obi said neither of those, and the man in his sixties read both sentences on the card aloud and said not one without the other, and the woman with the key said he could walk out and that there is nobody in that room who could stop him and nobody who could tell him he would not, and he sat down and stood up again and said *then it's worse, isn't it*, and she said yes. **And what it cost, in his own words: it isn't the crews; it's that nobody's coming down here now; there's not a body in this borough that had the low end first at eight o'clock tonight; tonight it's a street that somebody might turn up at; and I'm still going to be in it.** He declined the key to the lock-up so that nobody would have the padlock to write his name in the gap with. The man in his sixty-ties then put the right of return into words, going both ways. Jonas Mercer stood in that corridor and let all of them go past him.

**Chapter 0242 — Tuesday. Tuesday the twenty-fourth of May 2016, from about eleven in the morning, a shop on a parade of shops in Tideglass, and a kitchen in Marsh Lane.** **THE SAME MECHANISM RUNNING THE OTHER WAY, ON A BOROUGH THAT HAD JUST DONE SOMETHING GENEROUS, AND IT RAN FOR ABOUT THREE WEEKS, AND IT DID NOT LAST AND IT WAS NEVER GOING TO, AND THE ONLY PERSON WHO SAID IT WAS COMING IS A MAN WHO SAID IT IN A CAR ON THE TWENTY-SEVENTH OF MARCH AND WAS RIGHT, AND BEING RIGHT ABOUT IT DOES NOT MAKE IT BETTER.** **THE PRICE DID NOT ARRIVE ON THE TWENTIETH AND DID NOT ARRIVE BECAUSE OF THE TWENTIETH; IT HAD ARRIVED ABOUT A WEEK BEFORE THAT, THE WAY A PRICE DOES, AND NOT ONE PERSON IT REACHED HAS THE TWENTIETH ANYWHERE NEAR IT.** Hire, parts, fuel and insurance on the trade counter, twenty per cent near enough on the one that matters, and Hanna Wray's explanation: crews in the region that used to be ours and aren't ours now, and they buy where they land, and it isn't anybody, and if you go looking for somebody to be angry at you'll be looking till you're tired, because that is the trick and it isn't even a trick, it's just Tuesday. A man in his sixties who is the only good drain man in four streets, nine years in, bought four feet of wire and a length of lead and then said everybody's got a cousin and nobody's doing him wrong and it is a Tuesday and he was saying that in March. A woman in the second house in Marsh Lane had a van on a forecourt every Tuesday for six weeks, hired out of Lowdale, and there was no van: the Tuesdays had gone somewhere else, and the same van off the same forecourt went from a hundred and eighteen to a hundred and thirty-six on the same half-mile of road, and it is a market day on a Tuesday, and there is nobody in the world she can ring about it and she has looked. **And her prediction, which is the point of the chapter: it comes back to about what it was by the middle of June; it happened both ways; it went up because we gave a crew to somebody and it will go down because we gave a crew to somebody; the price is not a punishment and it is not a reward. IT'S A TUESDAY.** Jonas Mercer sat in a car park off the parade and did nothing, and had been asked nothing for six weeks, and got back into the car and shut the door.

**Chapter 0243 — A Sheet. Sunday the twenty-ninth of May 2016, from about half past ten in the morning, a bus shelter at the end of a parade of shops in Tideglass, and a shop on that parade.** **ONE SHEET, NOT ADDRESSED TO ANYBODY, ONE LINE ACROSS THE TOP WITH NO BOX UNDER IT AND NO NAME, AND UNDER THE LINE A COLUMN OF PLACES, AND THE PLACES ARE TOWNS, AND IT ANSWERS NOTHING AND ASKS FOR NOTHING.** A woman got off the bus with a plastic wallet of somebody else's papers, dealt with them on a bench in a wind rather than reading them, and about half blew away on the third go round, and one sheet was left face up at the end and she said it was not hers and got back on the bus and did not want it explained. It is A4: one line of printing across the top in about six inches of type, a column of places under it, no box, no name, no address, no reference, no date, nothing at the bottom, blank back — and the line says word for word what the framed sheet at Penhale says. **The eight places are Netherby, Tolforth, Halse Cross, Ansterwick, Kirkmoss, Ellersby, Marleby and Ockbrook.** Hanna Wray read it standing up twice and said it is the same six inches of type off a machine somebody else set, and that that is a fact about printing and not about anything else, and that it is the same sentence and not the same sheet, and that this one has eight towns under it and nobody printed a word about a single one of them, and that it could not be acted on if a committee of this borough got hold of it tomorrow and tried for a fortnight. Asked whether it can be posted: no name, no address, no reference, nothing to put on a stamp. **It is not lost, not mislaid, not stolen, and there is nobody to send it to and nobody anybody can ring, and that is four things a lost thing usually is and it is none of them.** **THE MAJOR TURN IS CARRIED BY THE EIGHT NAMES AND BY NOTHING ELSE, AND THE NARRATOR DOES NOT STATE IT: the arrangement Penhale runs on is not the first of its kind and is not the only one, and no sentence in the chapter says so.** It went into a drawer under the trade counter, face up, on top of a docket, under a lock, and Hanna Wray has the only key and has never given it to anybody.

**Chapter 0244 — First. Saturday the fourth of June 2016, from about eleven in the morning, a building by the water in Tideglass, and a Methodist hall on Carrow Lane.** **FIVE WORDS FOR THIS, AND FOUR OF THEM COULD HAVE BEEN PUT A FINGER ON IN THAT ROOM THAT AFTERNOON, AND THE FIFTH ONE CANNOT BE PUT A FINGER ON ANYWHERE AT ALL, AND THE REASON FOR THAT IS ON A PIECE OF PAPER ON A TABLE WITH EIGHT TOWNS ON IT AND NOT ONE PERSON'S NAME ON IT ANYWHERE, AND THE SHEET IS CORRECT, AND THE SHEET IS IN A DRAWER, AND NOBODY HAS OPENED IT FURTHER THAN IT WAS OPENED.** Nina Calder in the records room, the door sticks, and the register not opened: nineteen entries, a ruled column under the last one with a heading that is a number of days and nothing whatever under the heading, and a sum done standing up that comes to **five hundred and fifty-six**. The door, the yard light and the bulb are 0233's and 0234's and are not restated here. In the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane, about six people, the sheet of eight towns on the table brought by the woman who has the only key to the drawer under the trade counter, and nobody was to take it home. **The shape sits in the room and nobody puts three of the things side by side:** the man in his sixty-ties names a permission, an obligation, a claim and a right of return as the four that can be pointed at, says he has read all four, and refuses to lay them out because the last time anybody did, it produced an argument resting on a document nobody can produce. The fifth is a compact, and a compact is the one you cannot point at, and that is not a flaw in it: it is two people putting a thing down and neither keeping a copy, and a copy would be a form and a form has a manager, and then the thing is an office. **And the three things that explain nothing:** the first system did not explain the woman in the corridor, the second did not explain the man, and the shared yard did not explain the year — and the man who said that came out wrong put it the other way round, that nobody is too frightened to ask, there is simply nobody there with anything to offer him for an answer. **THE VOLUME'S OWN NEW QUESTION, ASKED ONCE, IN PLAIN WORDS, BY SOMEBODY WITH NO STANDING TO ASK IT: *Somebody had to be first. Somebody wrote the first one. Somebody set it up and put the towns under it. Where are they now? What became of the first lot?*** The woman with the key asked whether he was on anything; he said he was on the dishes, four nights and a Friday; she put her handbag on the table and kept her hand off it, and nobody else in that room had a book out. **Nobody answered him. It was not minuted. Nobody is rescued. Nobody dies.**

## Volume 05, Continuation 0006 — Chapters 245–254

**Chapter 0245 — Two Vans. Saturday the eleventh of June 2016, from about ten in the morning, a parade of shops in Tideglass, and the low end of Peverell Street.** The cold open is a fact about two crews and one arranged van: the boat left the borough on a Tuesday and was back on the Friday, the engine left on the same morning and was back on the Wednesday, neither crew was asked to go, and the only thing arranged in this borough last week was a van. Jonas Mercer is in the doorway of the shop next door to the one with the trade counter, where he has stood most mornings since the eleventh of May and where nobody has asked him anything in seven weeks. The parade is the same parade: the shutter goes up at the minute it always goes up, the window card carrying the shop's own telephone number and nothing else is where it has always been, and the woman of about sixty-five behind that counter has not been told anything. **Tomas Renn puts the chapter's finding into about a minute and names the mechanism himself, unasked: what a man gets used to is not the work, it is knowing where two vans are, and right now he knows where one is. Three men said Sunday for nine years and none of them was ever asked — his lot, the lad at Lowdale, and the man at the bottom house who had it off the Lowdale lad — and that is the whole mechanism. There is no new word for what has replaced it, and that is the whole of what has happened down here since the twentieth of May.** A white van with a scabbed corner, off Lowdale, comes round the corner at ten past ten on a Saturday morning. Nobody on the parade looks up; Renn looks up, goes inside and shuts the door. **The only new fact in the whole of the arrangement: a van that used to come back on a Sunday now comes back when it comes back.** Jonas Mercer asks one question and is told nobody can tell him that either, which is not the same answer as nobody can tell him which day, and that difference is the whole of what six weeks did. At the bottom of Peverell Street a woman comes out of a back yard for a bucket because the water is off, the man in the doorway answers her and is not asked a second question — **the low end is covered by one man who was never asked and is on nothing, and the pump and the coiled hose are where they have always been.** Nobody in either scene is thanked, nobody is measured, and the register does not move.

**Chapter 0246 — The Column. Friday the seventeenth of June 2016, from about eleven in the morning, the shared yard at Penhale, and the office hut on the concrete.** The chapter's card answer, in this file's own words and not as a quotation: the pact holds, it holds because nobody is counting it, and the proof is a gap about two inches deep in a column in a book that has been ruled since 1987, with a single line in the gap that is not a claim. The woman who has been in the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane about two years has never been to Penhale; she gets a bus and walks the last half mile because no bus goes from the end of that road. The yard owns nothing, and that is the only thing anybody there will explain to her. The framed wall sheet is A4 in a frame painted twice, hung at a height that means you have to stand up to read it, it carries the same rule as the sheet off the bench in the wind, and there is a second line under it that nobody prints. **She asks to take it down for an afternoon and Haldane Perry refuses twice; the better reason is that she is not one of the five people in the county he thinks could put a bit of paper in front of him and make him say something about it, and he would rather she stayed not one of them.** The second line is explained by nobody, and the man in his forties refuses to guess at it in front of her. The carbon book has been kept the same way since before the lanyard, and the ruling being straight and not done by hand for a very long time is the single most reassuring thing in the whole arrangement, which nobody in this borough has ever noticed. **The man in his forties refuses a figure, and that refusal is the reason the pact holds: he could total the money through that shed last year to the penny, he has never once been asked, and a figure written down about a yard is how a yard ends up having to have a good year.** Nine yards on that bend, none of which can refuse anybody, about four of which have never sent a crew out and never taken one in and pay in exactly the same, and there is no list on which those four are the four, because there is no list. The line that is not a claim is the only thing anybody has put into that book in nine years because he wanted to and not because somebody wanted it out of him, and it is worth nothing and it is in there. She writes nothing down on the bus or at home and has mentioned the visit once, to say that she has now seen the original of the thing off the bench and that the two were printed on different days by the same machine.

**Chapter 0247 — The Hose. Tuesday the twenty-first of June 2016, from about half past eight in the evening, the low end of Peverell Street in Tideglass, and a wall.** The cold open is a practical problem and not a maxim: a man on a stepladder at number thirty-eight has burst his own hose at the coupling, has a washer and not a coupling, and has no water in the house to prove a repair in, so the one question available to him is the wrong one, and it is answered from a doorway. Jonas Mercer comes down the street because there is nothing else to do with his evening, does the sum against a wall and gets **five hundred and seventy-three**, writes it on a piece of paper and puts the paper back in his coat. The man in the doorway of number forty-one, whose door is open a hand's width because it always is, has a standpipe in his yard with the stopcock open and tells him to take the hose off the wall. **It has been on that wall since the wet week in the November before last, with a grey line of dirt behind it where it has been lying in one place, and he gives it away.** The woman at number thirty-eight has been in her own yard since about seven with two washing lines full, working the length of them out of cold water off a butt behind the coal shed, and she holds the end of the man's line while he works, and neither of them asks the other anything. **A pump is not a rescue and a hose is not a rota row and a man who is there is not a man who has been set free, and none of those three sentences is said or implied in this chapter.** About ten minutes later a man from a shop on the parade comes up the low end on his way home, tells the doorway that the water is off at the top of the street and at number thirty-eight and has been since the middle of the week, and is told he will say. The man in that doorway has been at the bottom of that street for the thirty-odd years it has got houses on it, the only way anything has ever come down it in all that time is a man off the parade, neither of the two was ever asked to do it, and there is nobody down there that either of them could point at. **THE MAJOR TURN IS ONE SENTENCE, ABOUT A TUESDAY AND NOTHING ELSE, SAID TO A MAN ON A LADDER AND NOT TO JONAS MERCER, WHO WAS STANDING IN THE DARK AT THE TOP OF A WALL WITH A BIRO: *If your lot are out on a Tuesday, I'll come down and bring that hose out, and I don't want it on that board.*** The man on the ladder says *right* and goes back up the ladder and that is the end of it, and it is the only sentence anybody said down there all evening that was about anything other than water. **Nobody asked him a question. He asked nothing on any of three evenings that week, he came down the street because there was nothing else to do with his evening, and the door went to its usual width.** The chapter ends on consequence rather than on argument: the hose went up the ladder and the water came, and a second washing line went out at number thirty-eight.

**Chapter 0248 — Back Down. Sunday the twenty-sixth of June 2016, from about half past eleven in the morning, a shop on a parade of shops in Tideglass, a trade estate four miles out, and a kitchen in Marsh Lane.** The cold open says the price came back down and came back down for the same reason it went up, that nobody is a hero and nobody is a villain, and that the thing that goes up and down around here is a Tuesday. The woman in the second house of Marsh Lane is back to a hundred and eighteen on the same van off the same forecourt on the same half-mile of road, is doing her brother's materials in one trip again, and is not pleased about having been right twice. **Her two claims, in her own terms: the number came down the day the boat came back and she had nothing to do with the boat coming back, and it moved because a crew out of this borough went somewhere and came back, and not one single thing anybody in this borough has done made it move either way.** Hanna Wray at the trade counter: the Penhale account is a smaller book than it was in April, by about a sixth, the price on everything else is the same, the rate is on a board on the shelf behind her and she has not read it and is not going to, and she said in May that it would come back to about what it was by the middle of June and did not do one thing to make it. The drain man, who is given no age anywhere in the prose: **he is back to about what he had in February and he is not back.** Four streets to himself for nine years, two and a half after May, and two and three-quarter now that the lad who did the other street has gone out of town and his cousin has taken it. Back would be four, that is the part he does not get back, nobody has done him wrong, there is no arrangement in the county that gives him that street, and he is not going to be one of the two who starts saying so out loud in a hall on a Sunday, **because a man who says that is a man who has started going in.** The weighbridge man at Sarn has never turned a job away in twenty years; the forecourt card at Marchmont is about a tenth above what the shared yard pays, has been repainted twice, and nobody has asked the man in the office by the gate to read it out since the first of May; and the man in the cabin at Lowdale says the plant went out on a Friday and came back on a Sunday, that he could not tell you what he would do differently if the crews had not come back in the borough, and **that he has wanted blood in it since March, would charge more if he had it, and has a diary and not a thing.** Five people have now given the same answer in this county and nobody on that parade said anything about any of it, and Hanna Wray went back to the roll.

**Chapter 0249 — A Day. Wednesday the twenty-ninth of June 2016, from about ten in the morning, a parade of shops in Tideglass, and the top of Peverell Street.** The cold open states the shape of the chapter: the ask is put to people and not to anybody, one at a time, out loud, with nothing written down, two people say yes, and neither of the two says yes to a thing. The man of about eighteen who washes up in a kitchen four nights and a Friday asks in doorways with no preamble, knows while he is doing it that it is not a good way, and **did not make a list, and the reason is not a principle: he has nobody's names except the ones he already knew from standing in rooms.** The first man asks what day, is told there is not one yet, and answers that he would probably come if he were knocked on at half seven on the day, for about half the days between now and September, which is more than he expected to say out loud to somebody washing up in a kitchen. **THE MAJOR TURN: SOMEBODY SAYS YES WHO IS NOT THE MAN WITH THE PUMP, WHAT THEY SAY YES TO IS A DAY, AND A RIGHT OF RETURN IN THIS BOROUGH IS CURRENTLY THE SIZE OF ONE TUESDAY.** The man from the works on the far side of the river finishes at two on the twenty-eighth, will be over the bridge at about half past three, will come down, will not charge and will not tell anybody he did it, and says that is not a favour either, because you would do the same and he would want you to. He puts the size of it himself: it is one day, the day after that he is in Leeds till Wednesday, and the day after that he has no idea — one Tuesday and a man who finishes at two. He asks what is in it for him, is told nothing, and is told plainly that it is not reciprocal and is not going to be pretended to be, **because the second it is pretended to be reciprocal this stops being an ask and becomes an arrangement, an arrangement gets a name, a name gets a person under it, and then it is the other thing entirely.** A third person says no in about nine seconds and means it. A fourth asks to be asked on the day rather than now, because now is a promise and on the day it is a job, and he would rather be a man who did a job. **The only person who had ever been reliably there was not asked, and that is arithmetic and not sentiment: his own name is in a drawer in his kitchen four doors up the street, and he would have been the fourth name on anybody's list and was on nobody's.** Hanna Wray tells him at the counter that she knows three of the four, and that she could not tell him the fourth man's first name and neither could he tell her the rate. He puts the pen back where it had been and goes out. **It was a Wednesday, so there were no dishes in that kitchen for him, and he will be on the parade in the mornings until somebody stops him, and he will not have a list.**

**Chapter 0250 — Leave It. Monday the fourth of July 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, a hall off a parade of shops in Tideglass, a parade, and the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane.** The cold open: the six open questions are put in a room and handed to people who have to act on them, not one of them is answered, one of them is answered wrong on purpose by a man who says so before he says it, and the room leaves it where it is. About nine people come to a hall that is free on a Monday, with a pound already in the meter, and Mrs Obi has the pad shut on her knee. The man in his sixties does not read the six out; he changes the verb to *what would you do about it on Monday, in your actual week*, and says in advance that most of the answers will be the same answer, which is nothing, and that nothing is not the same as a failure. **THE MAJOR TURN, NOW CANON AND THE FIRST TIME ANYWHERE IN THIS ACCOUNT THAT A WRONG ANSWER HAS BEEN PUT INTO A ROOM AND LEFT THERE: he says the register is the dated thing that will be the first one somebody can prove, he says so before he puts his hand up, and then says that this is wrong.** The register is at nineteen, the last entry is a bulb in a maintenance column, the line under it goes down the page and stops about two inches short of the bottom, everything this borough has done since is not in it because it was deliberately not written down, and a book with a blank line under the last entry proves only that a room of people could see a blank line and leave it. **His reason for leaving it there: somebody will say it anyway, and if nobody in the room can take it apart then the room goes home with a wrong thing in it that everybody can repeat, four of them are in other rooms this week, and by August it is the sort of thing a man from the works repeats at a kerb. His reason for not correcting it: putting it right would oblige him to say the right one instead, he has not got the right one, and anything guessed out loud on a Monday night in that borough is in nine heads by Wednesday and in every other room in it by the end of the month.** Nobody in that hall corrects it. The young woman of about twenty names what actually happened: you are allowed to leave a wrong thing in a room if you can put the right one where it was, he cannot, none of them can, and that is not the same as the room believing it. The other five answers: kept because it was expensive, which the man from the parade owned as *that's me, not the answer*; a pad on a knee with a date on it, which two people refused to count and neither could use; **nothing, still nothing**, on the second half of the fourth, asked out loud in the plainest words anybody had used in that hall and answered in two words; the three documents not laid out on a table again, with the woman of about fifty-five saying all three of them are correct and that correct has turned out to be the least useful property a document can have; and a claim, a schedule of eleven names and a sheet of eight towns, none of them opened since the fourth of June. Mrs Obi shuts the part of the argument that would settle three of the six and says the person who raises it again will be asked to leave, in exactly the same voice as the rest of it. Jonas Mercer is under the awning at the end of the parade from about half past nine, does not go in, does the sum out of habit, gets **five hundred and eighty-six**, and has nowhere to put it. **By the Wednesday a man off the parade has said the wrong answer in a corridor on Carrow Lane to somebody who was not in the room, in the same words, and he was believed.**

**Chapter 0251 — Eight Names. Friday the eighth of July 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane in Tideglass.** The cold open: a sheet of paper comes out of a drawer under a trade counter for the second time in this borough, on a Friday night in July, in front of nine people, and not one person in that room can do one single thing with it, and that is correct. Hanna Wray brings it in her handbag, face up, and does not unfold it because it is not folded, and says in advance that she will want it back where it was by about five. The key goes into the handbag before the last of them have sat down, a woman in the front row says the gas is lovely, the man in his sixties says the boiler in the other hall would be free to anybody who wanted it, and nobody asks her one single question about the paper, which she had expected and which is the whole reason she brought it. **The key came in her handbag and goes back in her handbag, and she has never once given it to anybody in nine years; when a man from the parade asks whether it might be better in one go across two Mondays she says no, and the reason is not the paper and is not the room: if somebody wanted to look at it in March she would have said no in March.** It is A4, one line of printing across the top in about six inches of type, a column of places under it, and no box, no name, no address, no reference, no date, nothing at the bottom and a blank back — every one of those absences was said out loud in April and in June and is not said tonight. The eight places are read out twice, slowly, by the woman who has been in that hall about two years, for the third occasion in total, and it comes out the same three times. **One hand goes up out of nine, for Ockbrook, and she could not point at it and would not be able to tell you which side of the road.** The man in his sixties wants that written down in a room somewhere, says it will not be, and says that this is fine, because a thing you cannot write down is a thing you cannot be proved wrong about later, and that it is the only real property the sheet has. **THE MAJOR TURN, FROM THE MAN OF ABOUT EIGHTEEN'S OWN REASONING: the sheet is a list of eight places with a rule on top, this borough is not on it, the thing that is not a place is the one that is on the list, and if eight names were read out in that room they would be the same shape as the sheet — and neither of the two is a document, neither is anybody's job, and there is nowhere for either of them to go afterwards. NOBODY CAN ACT ON THE SHEET AND THAT IS CORRECT, AND THE ONLY THING THAT CAN BE DONE WITH IT IS NOT AN ACT.** The man in his sixties agrees with none of the reasoning and does it anyway, and is honest that doing it will not change what the paper is, will not be known in six months, and is not the point of it. The eight places are read a third time without being asked for, and eight people say their own names out loud, one after another, in no order, in whatever order they got up in; one of them works behind a counter on the parade and had never said her name in that hall, and one said his twice because he said the first one quietly. **Nothing was written down, because there was nothing on the table to write it on and nobody had brought anything, and it was not asked of anybody.** The eight did not agree on anything afterwards, two of them had to catch the bus, the man at number forty-one's name is not one of the eight and nobody suggested another name, and the sheet goes back in the drawer at ten past five with the key turned twice. **The chapter ends on two of the eight walking to the corner and to the bus stop without saying one more word about it, and neither of them could have told you what the sheet had been for.** It still carries no charter, no proxy, no root term, no hinge, no seal, no date of origin, no name of a body, no mechanism and no explanation, and this chapter gives it none.

**Chapter 0252 — What It Built. Thursday the fourteenth of July 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, a hall off a parade of shops in Tideglass, and the corridor outside it.** About six weeks pass in this chapter and what comes back out of them is a negative finding and a length of chain. The woman of about forty-two who has the key puts the booking book on the table unasked and shows a gas column that was hers before it was anybody else's and twelve pencil ticks in her own hand, and says she does not know who came, has never taken a name at the door, was asked and would not ask now, and was within her rights and that asking would have finished the thing in a fortnight. The man in his forties has carried the carbon book from Penhale up the road himself and shows the column headed with nothing at all and the one line in it that is not a claim. The young woman of about twenty calls the entire output of six weeks twelve rooms with about nine people in them at some point and one line in a book at the bottom of a hill, and is told she has not been in every one of those rooms, and says so. **Tomas Renn is in the room and has not said no a fourth time and has said yes to nothing: he has not been in one since the twentieth of May, has not said a word in a room since the week before that, came for the last hour, brought nothing, and it is a Thursday.** The question gets asked badly, which is the right way for it to be asked, because a badly put question is still one that somebody actually said. **THE MAJOR TURN: THE COMPACT IS THE THING MRS OBI SAID IT WOULD NOT BE, WHICH IS A LIST, AND NOBODY HAS MADE ONE, AND THE ONLY EVIDENCE THAT IT EXISTS IS THAT SEVERAL PEOPLE DID SOMETHING SMALL ON THE SAME DAY WITHOUT ARRANGING IT.** Her arithmetic, in her own terms: with about nine people in a room in July there is no way on God's earth to tell whether a thing happened in April or not, and a hall with a pencil tick in it and a line in a book that is not a claim would get laughed at at a magistrate and would deserve to. A compact agreed with people one at a time is a list, she said so before there was one, and the reason nobody in this borough has written down the name of a single person who has said yes to anything since April is that nobody has ever asked anybody for a name. **And then she refuses the next three sentences: she does not know what that means, she has not found out tonight, and anybody in that room who tells you they know what a compact that is not a list is, is selling you something.** The evidence is four things on Tuesday the twenty-eighth of June, not a list, not minuted, every one of it reported and not vouched for: a bath out of a second-floor landing in Marsh Lane by a man who finished at two and told nobody in advance and nobody afterwards; four feet of pipe and a fitting left on a kerb outside a shop by the boat crew and still there on the Wednesday until a woman who was tired of looking at it put it in a yard; a pound put in a meter by somebody nobody saw; and a length of chain about eight feet long bought by the man at the bottom of Peverell Street, paid for, put on a gate at the back of his house, given to nobody, and described to the woman who asked as being for a gate without saying which gate. **Nobody could connect the four of them, nobody arranged them, none of them knew about the other three, and the only thing that made them the same day is that one man said a date out loud in a street on a Wednesday morning to somebody washing up in a kitchen and did not put it in a list and went back to work.** Jonas Mercer is in the corridor, does not go in, has not been asked anything in seven weeks, and listens to a hall decide that it cannot find out what it has done, which is a sound he has not heard before in this borough and has heard a good many of. He has a biro in his coat and nothing to put it on, does not write the four things down, and on his way down the parade goes past the shop with the shutter that goes up and down and does not go in.

**Chapter 0253 — The Wrong Direction. Tuesday the nineteenth of July 2016, from about ten in the morning, the yard at Penhale, and the trade counter at the back of a shop on the parade of shops in Tideglass.** The cold open: a question goes out of this borough to the other side of the estuary inside somebody else's folder, what comes back is correct, it is not a bill and not a demand and not a claim, it is a sheet, somebody puts it in a drawer, and that is the whole of what happened. The boat goes out over the water on the Tuesday and comes back on the Friday, one of about four things that left this borough that week that nobody arranged, and the two that came back came back when they came back. The yard at Penhale is a bend in a road that owns nothing, and that is the only reason it is any use at all. The man in his forties who keeps the book under Haldane Perry says so to about four people in that yard that morning, unasked, and without appearing to enjoy it. The folder is a job wallet: brown card, a press stud, a great many dockets, it belongs to the boat, it goes out and comes back, and the man who carries it does not read it. There is nobody in this borough who could tell you what is written on any of the dockets in it at any time, and that has never once mattered. **Written on the back of the last docket, in a hand that is not a tradesman's hand, two questions about who printed the first one and whether they are still doing it. No name, no address, no company, no date, no reference. The boatman says one sentence about it — that it is a terrible way to do a thing — puts it in the wallet and does the day's work.** In the cabin at Lowdale a man watches a van come back off the bridge and a brown card wallet come out of the back of it and says nothing, because nobody in this borough has ever asked him anything and he is not going to be the one to start. Four companies supplied that yard, were not involved in any part of this, and would have supplied the same week at the same rate; the man in the cabin at Lowdale has half his turnover in this borough out of work that leaves on a Friday and comes back the Friday after. **What comes back on the Friday, on top of no docket: one sheet of A4, one line of printing across the top in about six inches of type — *Any part of any system in this region may be used by any person* — and under it, on its own, centred, one place. And the place is this borough.** The woman of about fifty-five reads it over Hanna Wray's shoulder in the shop and says one word, and Hanna Wray says the same one: *Us.* It goes up the parade to the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane, where about nine people are in by half past seven and the gas is on because somebody put a pound in and nobody saw who. The man in his sixties puts it in four parts. It is correct, and it is the same six inches of type off the same kind of machine as the sheet with eight places under the same line, so that printed a fortnight apart in a room with one window he could not tell you which was which; it is not a bill, not a demand and not a claim, and no money moves because of it and nobody owes anybody anything because of it; **and the new one — it is not about this borough at all, it is about a place, and it says a place is one of the places from which a thing may be used, and it does not say anybody is coming, does not say anything is owed, does not say anybody has to do anything, and does not say that a person who lives there has been counted or heard from or written down anywhere, and a printed place name is a fact about printing**; and the fourth: **it does not answer the question.** A lad wrote two questions about a person and somebody over there answered with a place, and that is a perfectly good answer to a question nobody asked, and it cost a boat a day of a man's time. **Nobody on either side of that water has done anything wrong or anything clever or anything hostile. Not one person has been discovered. Not one person is a perpetrator. Nothing is a fraud and nobody is a villain.** Nobody in that hall said who printed the first one, or whether they are still doing it. The man of about eighteen did not ask it again: he asked it once, on the fourth of June, and a man told him in front of nine people to say it again slower and slower, and the second half of that instruction had nothing to do with speed. The woman of about fifty-five asks whether it came off the same machine as the two pieces of A4 in a handbag in a building by the water, and is refused, because holding a document up to the light in front of people is what you do to it when you want it to be a document. It goes into the drawer under the trade counter on top of the other sheet and the lock goes round twice, so there are now two sheets in that drawer, and a boatman carried one of them across an estuary on a Friday and has never opened the wallet. **That drawer has an invoice spike in it and a lock on it, and it is not the drawer under the counter in the vestibule in the building by the water, which no chapter of this batch has mentioned at all.**

**Chapter 0254 — Ordinary. Saturday the twenty-third of July 2016, from about eleven in the morning, a building by the water in Tideglass, a parade of shops, and a hall off a parade.** The cold open: the borough has agreed to send its own crews out of itself before anything inside it gets done, about a third of the men who do that are eight miles away on this Saturday, every person in the hall that afternoon can name every one of them, not one of them can say when any of them is coming back, and that is what it looks like when it is holding. **CARD 0254 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.** Nina Calder comes in about once a month when nobody is asking her for anything, and on the twenty-third of July she is in the records room with a cup of tea on the sill, working down a list of what was left in a store. She says the door sticks. The register is not opened. Nineteen entries, the nineteenth a yard light with a bulb in a maintenance column and the bulb out, a line under it that goes down the page and stops about two inches short of the bottom, and the sum is **six hundred and five** and is still blank; he says it, she says it is the same as last month because it is on her list, agrees that it is the same as every month, and goes back to the list. The parade is the same parade: the shutter goes up at the minute it always goes up, the window card with the shop's own telephone number on it and nothing else on it is where it has always been, and the woman of about sixty-five behind that counter has not been told anything and nobody is going to today. **A man behind a till asks Jonas Mercer what a two-inch swept bend goes for in the catalogue, and he answers, and it takes about four seconds, and it is correct, and the man says cheers and writes it on the back of a receipt and asks him nothing else — and it is the first thing anybody in this borough has asked him since the eleventh of May, and it is a price, and nothing happened.** Tomas Renn has a crate of rags on his shoulder at about half past twelve and says two vans are out and that he knows where two vans are, and would like that noted, because a fortnight ago he knew where one and it was a novelty and now it is a Tuesday; nobody has asked him to be noted, he knows that, and goes inside. A white van came back off the forecourt at about eleven. The woman in the second house of Marsh Lane was not in it: she was doing her brother's materials in one trip on a Friday for the first time since April, having said in June that the hire would come back to about what it was by the middle of July, and she was right. At the bottom of Peverell Street the door of number forty-one is open a hand's width, there is a length of chain round the back of the house on a gate, the man who bought it will not say whose gate it is and nobody has asked him again, and the pump is still in the doorway with the stopcock off and nobody has asked him about the stopcock. The hall off the parade is free on a Saturday afternoon because nobody rents it, the gas is on a meter, and a pound went in before anybody came. About nine people come and every one of them is on nothing. They do not do the six questions, and the man in his sixty is the one who says why, in a sentence: they did them in April and again in July and neither time answered one, and if they do the six again in August they are a hall that meets about the six questions, which is a committee, and everybody in this borough knows what a committee is. They talk about the price of a fitting, the weather, a roof that has been off a house in Corrance Lane since April, the eight places in a drawer, the four yards at the bottom of a hill, and a boiler in the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane that anybody could have taken for nothing since about February and that nobody has taken. **The man from the parade then puts the shape of the week into the room: this is the fifth time he has not known where a van in this borough was, and it is five Tuesdays and not a fortnight, and he has stopped minding, and he wants it in the room that he has stopped minding and has not made his peace with it, and that those are two different things.** Nobody argues with him and nobody agrees with him, and the young woman of about twenty writes nothing down, because there is nothing on the table to write it on. The man from the parade puts his hand up and asks whether anybody is going to write any of it down, is told there is nothing on the table to write it on, says *you've not got a pad*, is told *I've not got a pad*, and that is the entire minute of that afternoon. **At about half past four most of it goes out into the parade and about four stay, and the new question arrives as an exchange at the side of a table: the woman of about forty-two with the key asks the man of about eighteen whether he is still after the thing he asked, and whether anybody has said anything to him about it, and he says no, and she says *right*, and puts the key in her bag, and shuts the bag, and that is the end of it.** She leaves the gas on until the last of them are out and then turns it off at the meter by the door, and the radiator in that corridor has been out since about 1998 and is still out, and she goes out and locks up, and the parade is a parade. Nobody is rescued, nobody dies, nobody renews anything, and the line under the nineteenth entry of a register in a building by the water is six hundred and five days and is still blank.
