## Volume 05, Continuation 0007 — Chapters 255–264

**Chapter 0255 — The Detail. Saturday the thirtieth of July 2016, from about ten in the morning, a parade of shops in Tideglass.** Jonas Mercer does the sum under an awning and gets **six hundred and twelve**, writes it on a piece of paper, and puts the paper back in his coat. The shutter goes up at the minute it always goes up and the window card with the shop's own telephone number on it is in the window and the woman of about sixty-five is behind her counter and is not told anything. In a queue outside the building supplies place a man off a flatbed of a firm of three lorries says the register is the thing that will be proved, and that anybody can be carried to the old one. **THE MAJOR TURN: A WOMAN BUYING POST-FIX SAYS HER MOTHER, WHO DID THE DINNERS AT A SCHOOL OVER THE ROAD, KEPT THE COPY BEFORE THAT ONE, AND THAT THERE WAS A LINE AT THE BOTTOM OF THE PAGE WHERE THEY STOPPED WRITING, AND SHE CALLS IT THE ONLY HONEST THING IN THE BUILDING. NOBODY GAVE HIM THAT DETAIL AND HE NEVER SAID IT, AND THE LINE IS REAL — IT IS THE LINE UNDER THE NINETEENTH ENTRY, AND IT IS THE MOST RELIABLE THING IN THIS BOROUGH'S RECORDS, AND IT MEANS THAT ABOUT NINE PEOPLE IN A ROOM IN APRIL DECIDED TO WRITE NOTHING DOWN AND LEFT IT SHOWING. SO A THING THAT IS TRUE IS CARRYING A THING THAT IS FALSE, AND IT CANNOT BE DENIED WITHOUT THE WHOLE BEING DENIED.** The detail travels as ordinary trade: inside three hours two of the other lorries of that firm have heard it, one of them is a different firm, and the man says *I haven't* when accused of having been in a room, and he has not been in a room and nobody in that queue knew and nobody asked. The man behind the counter asks where it came from, is told *a bloke in a hall*, and says *that's two of them, then* to a man with a trolley. **The man in his sixties is measuring a shopfront and is told the whole of it at the door. He says the line is real and that he cannot tell the shopkeeper anything else, and that the two have got joined up and he cannot get them apart. Asked which half is his, he says he could not unpick that in a fortnight because it is in three trades and a school and a queue by now, and that he is not going to start. Asked whether somebody could go and ask the woman who keeps the register, he quotes one half of the card on the wall in the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane — a body that cannot make anybody do anything cannot be told what it will do — and says the same card says it is not asked.** Nobody is a liar and nobody is a villain. Jonas Mercer wrote none of it down and was asked nothing.

**Chapter 0256 — Nine Years. Wednesday the third of August 2016, from about half past two in the afternoon, a shop on a parade, and the room behind the trade counter at the back of it.** The woman of about fifty-five brings two things to the counter: a printed sheet from the firm stripping the first-floor corridor of the building by the water between the tenth and the fourteenth of September, and a form from a county office with a reference, three boxes and a return-by date, which asks what material is held at an address, when it came, and whether the person answering intends to keep it. She has filled in one box. **HER REASON IS A GOOD ONE AND IT IS HERS: one of the two pieces of A4 in the handbag in that corridor has the name of this borough printed under a line, and she would like one piece of it somewhere a man with a stripper is not going to find.** Hanna Wray says no in four seconds, and says the no is not about the paper and not about the room, and repeats the July reason about March. **THE MAJOR TURN: the woman of about fifty-five asks whether she would ever hand the key to anybody — not today, not this year, ever — and Hanna Wray says she does not know, and says it is the first time in nine years anybody has asked her about the key instead of about the paper, and then says why she carries it: the alarm in that shop has been changed three times in nine years and each time she was the one who had to be there before the man came, and it is not on a hook behind the till and has never been on a hook behind the till.** The drawer under the trade counter is not opened; it has a lock on it and an invoice spike in it and two sheets on top of each other in it and neither has been out since 19 July. **This is the room the card requires: a form that wants a body, and there is not one. The card on the wall is referred to, both halves held together, and the word *require* is nowhere in the chapter.** A young one comes in for a barrow and the conversation happens in the back room because of it. Nobody is angry. The form goes back in the post with one of its three boxes answered and the other two left blank, which is what she said would happen when she asked. Hanna Wray puts the key in her handbag, the alarm beats twice, and she does not go up.

**Chapter 0257 — Four, Checked. Monday the eighth of August 2016, from about half past eight in the morning, a parade, Marsh Lane, a hall off the parade, and Carrow Lane.** The woman of about fifty-five goes and asks four people, in persons' fronts, what each of them had seen on the twenty-eighth of June, in the order the four things happened in her head, with four headings on the back of an envelope. **THE MAJOR TURN: THE FOUR ACCOUNTS DO NOT MATCH, AND THE ONE THAT DOES NOT MATCH IS THE ONE THAT WAS REPORTED BY SOMEBODY WHO WAS NOT THERE, AND NOBODY IN THIS BOROUGH IS A LIAR.** The bath holds: an hour, under the stairs, a man off the river gone before four, and the woman in the second house of Marsh Lane insists twice, unasked, that it was hers because she had been saying since March that she could do it and could not, and she said the date first. The pipe holds: four foot and a bit and an elbow, on the kerb outside the shop that shuts of a Sunday, Friday to Monday, gone by the Wednesday morning, never asked for, still in the yard of the house behind under a bit of roofing felt. The chain holds as an account only: the woman who has been in the Methodist hall about two years asked him on the Sunday and got *a gate*, and nobody goes and asks him. **The pound in the meter does not hold, and it was always hers. The woman of about forty-two with the key says she put it in, has put money in every week since February, nobody has ever seen her do it, nobody else has ever done it, and if somebody had she would have known because she locks up, and there is no date because she does it on a Monday or a Thursday depending what day she has remembered it.** The account that went round four rooms came from her, second-hand, out of a room she was not in, in a week she was not in; she confirms that the woman of about fifty-five said it in a gap in a hall on 2 July, and that nobody in the chain ever held it. Nobody corrects anybody. A woman says *that's what you told me* and a woman says *there's nowhere for that to go*. The three that hold are carried off by a man on the drearns in a bag, and the day itself is still the only date anybody in this borough ever agreed on. He does not put the pound back with them and he tells nobody.

**Chapter 0258 — A Sentence. Saturday the thirteenth of August 2016, from about half past nine in the morning, the first floor of a shop at the end of a parade.** An empty room over a shop is being done up for letting and four cardboard boxes in the corridor outside it have to go down two flights. The woman of about fifty-five and the young woman of about twenty cannot get the third one round the turn at the bottom of the stairs, and Renn comes along the parade with a sack barrow from a hardware shop four doors down. **THE MAJOR TURN: HE DOES A JOB AND SAYS ONE SENTENCE THAT IS NOT A REASON AND NOT A REFUSAL, AND THE SENTENCE IS ABOUT A PERSON NOBODY IN THAT CORRIDOR HAD MENTIONED.** He says yes in one word and is not asked to say it twice, carries the third box up himself, goes down with it, comes back for the fourth, and warns them about a step in the light on the half landing. **He has said no three times and has not said it a fourth time and has not said yes either; his no in April was about a compact that is a list and is not a refusal of a barrow, the chapter says so out loud, she puts it as *a barrow* and he puts it back as *it's a barrow*, and the count of his refusals in this account stays three.** The sentence is about a man who sweeps that parade at about half five in the morning, goes down the middle of it with the yellow light on and does Peverell Street afterwards, is not on anything, and whose name Renn could not tell you; Renn has never once seen anybody from this borough say one word to him, not a good morning and not a nod, and has never asked him anything and is not going to now. **It is not made into anything.** She says somebody's got to know he's there and he says he's there, and she says that is the problem and he agrees; the reason he said it on a kerb and not in a room is that in a room it becomes a thing, and then somebody comes and asks the man whether he wants the hours changed, and he has to have an answer he has not got and does not need. Nothing is arranged for that man, nobody goes down that street at half five, and the barrow goes back to its spot by the door of the hardware shop.

**Chapter 0259 — Three Gates. Friday the nineteenth of August 2016, from about ten past four in the afternoon, the lane above the low end of Peverell Street.** The college bus goes down Peverell Street and stops at the bottom of it, past the field gate. **THE MAJOR TURN: SOMEBODY FINDS OUT WHICH GATE WITHOUT ASKING HIM, AND IT IS NOT THE GATE ANYBODY WOULD HAVE GUESSED, AND IT IS NOT A RESCUE AND IT IS NOT AN ARRANGEMENT AND IT IS NOT A LIST. IT IS THE FIELD GATE AT THE BOTTOM OF THAT STREET, PAST THE LAST HOUSE, ON THE SIDE OF THE BANK.** There is a length of chain on it: bright galvanised, new, about the length of a forearm, hooked over the latch and not fastened, and the padlock on the gate itself hanging open with nothing in it. She unhooks it to get through to the stop and hooks it back exactly as she found it, which takes longer. **She eliminates the other two by looking at them, not by asking anybody: number forty-one's own back gate has a five-lever padlock on it as thick as a wrist and has had one the whole time she has been coming down there, and number thirty-eight's side gate is a wooden gate that has hung crooked since before she was born.** She goes up the street, the door of number forty-one is open a hand's width, there is a radio faintly inside it, and she does not knock and nobody speaks to her. She tells one person, in the doorway of the shop next door to the one with the trade counter. **He tells her he is not going, and his reason is in his mouth and is not a moral position: the second he stands and looks at a thing in this borough it becomes a thing somebody has been stood and looked at, then it is not a chain, it is a question, and the man at the bottom of that street would know in a week. He is not asking him about the chain, about the gate, or whether he would like somebody to stop, and he has about half an hour of his own thinking to do first, and that it is not his business.** He also puts the reason for *a gate* and not *my gate*, which is that on that wording a gate that turns out not to be his is still a gate and he has not had to own it. The chapter does not say what the chain is for. Nobody goes down there.

**Chapter 0260 — A Lamp. Thursday the twenty-fifth of August 2016, from about half past ten in the morning, the kitchen behind a parade, and the first-floor corridor of a building by the water.** The woman of about fifty-five catches the man of about eighteen on the parade and says up front that she has no favour to give back, that she does not know the rate for an hour, and that she would rather he took the money than made a thing of it. The thing is a light in the first-floor corridor where she works, out about a fortnight, which the works say is not theirs, with a three-tread kitchen step under the window and the fitting over the fire door at the other end. **THE MAJOR TURN: HE IS ASKED TO DO ONE SMALL ORDINARY THING BY SOMEBODY WHO NEEDS IT DONE AND HE DOES IT, AND NOBODY MAKES IT INTO ANYTHING, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING THAT HAPPENS, AND HE DOES NOT ASK HIS QUESTION AGAIN.** It takes twenty minutes instead of two, because the step will not reach the fitting and the box in her room has the old sort of bulb in it, so he puts the step on the top landing of the stairs, and then runs down the parade and back, and a man behind a till counts four out of a box behind the till and says they will want the money for them. She pays him, he takes it, and neither of them says anything about it. **She tells him in a corridor that she has been thinking of asking him something since the summer and has decided not to, and why — a question in a corridor would be an occasion and he would have to think about his answer in front of her, and a man in a room once told him to say it again slower and slower and the second half of that was not about speed — and he says *that was June*.** On the parade the woman he works for asks where he went and who for and says *right* and goes back to the sink. No drawer is mentioned in this chapter. He is on the dishes, on nothing, and has been given no title, grade, department, chair, seat, membership, form, rota row or way of being thanked.

**Chapter 0261 — Who Said It. Thursday the first of September 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane.** About nine people, the gas on, the six not done and one sentence about why. They talk about a roof, a quote, and whether the woman of about fifty-five can keep the two sheets, which she can. **THE MAJOR TURN: HE DOES NOT DISOWN IT AND HE DOES NOT OWN IT, AND THE THIRD THING IS SAID BY SOMEBODY ELSE.** The man from the parade puts his hand up and gives the argument of the eleventh of April as his own — a permission, an obligation, and a middle one somebody was actually handed, which would turn the other two into a pair of ends and settle three of the six at once. He heard it in a corridor on Carrow Lane in July and was not told whose it was. **Nobody in that room had heard him make it in April.** Mrs Obi does not ask anybody to leave and says why, and the reason is not mercy: she shut that argument once, off one man, on one night, in one room, and shutting it off everybody who says it would build the thing she shut it to stop. She takes nothing back from July, including the sentence about asking somebody to leave, and that sentence still stands against every mouth including hers. **What he says about it is two true halves: it is his in the sense that it came out of his head in April, it is not his in the sense that it came out of another man's mouth, and he will not take a mouth that is not his and will not say it did not come from his head; asked why he did not say that in July, he says he could have, that he said nothing in July, and that he will not manufacture a tidier reason now. He did not make the argument again and nobody is going to make him.** The third thing is said by the woman of about fifty-five, with her hands flat on the table: the argument does not need a third paper in this borough, it needs one anywhere, there is not one and there never was one and it is not lost because it was never anything to be lost, and a sheet on a wall in a corridor over that water is a sheet, and the two pieces of A4 in a bag under a chair are copies and are copies, **and a copy is not a wall**, which the young woman of about twenty puts as the difference between the argument and the proof. Nobody had this argument off a table and nobody in this account has a copy of a page anybody was ever given. Nothing is written down. The man in his sixties tells the man of about eighteen, to him and not to the room, that there is no such thing as a hall answering his question, that he has watched three people try, and that he has looked and does not know one thing to suggest. The man of about eighteen says *I know*.

**Chapter 0262 — A Day With No Use For It. Wednesday the seventh of September 2016, from about half past eight in the morning, a parade of shops.** It is raining. **THE MAJOR TURN: THE MAN WHO FINISHES AT TWO DOES NOT COME, AND NOBODY RINGS HIM, AND IT TURNS OUT THAT HE WAS NOT COMING BECAUSE OF SOMETHING TO DO WITH A WEDNESDAY AND NOT WITH THIS BOROUGH AT ALL, AND NOBODY IS HURT AND NOBODY IS DISAPPOINTED IN A WAY ANYBODY ELSE CAN HEAR.** The man of about eighteen asks five people, out loud, one at a time, in a doorway, the same sentence each time, with no floor, no water, nobody hurt, no landing and no hose, to come and stand on the parade at two. **A thing offered when nothing is wrong is not a thing asked for, and asking would be making a rota row, and nobody asked anybody for anything.** About half think it is a wind-up; the man in his sixties looks at him for slightly too long and says nothing, which from him is an answer. He had already asked the fifth of them by knocking, at half past six one evening in August, which is the only time he has ever knocked on anybody's door in this borough, and was told that a Wednesday is a Wednesday, that the man is in Leeds till Wednesday night and then back on the plant till Saturday at two, and that coming on a wet afternoon with nothing to do would not be a favour but the two of them pretending. **The boy told nobody and nobody rang him.** Five people are on that parade at two and stand in the rain for an hour and a half talking about a bus timetable, a dog, a weighbridge and a roof. At about twenty past three **the woman of about fifty-five says the thing that is actually going on in her week — she is out of that corridor on Saturday morning at eight with a room and a half of furniture and nowhere to be until the seventeenth, and she is not going to ask anybody in this borough for a floor, because she knows exactly what would happen if she asked, and she would rather sit in a corridor with a light on that she paid ten pounds for than be the woman who asked a parade for a fortnight — and nobody answers it, and it is not solved, and she is not housed.** The rain comes on properly at half past three and they go in separately, and at about eight that night the man from the works comes over the bridge with a bag of tools and walks down the parade without speaking to anybody, and nobody has asked him anything again.

**Chapter 0263 — A Statement. Monday the twelfth of September 2016, from about ten past nine in the morning, the first floor of a building by the water, and a records room on the same floor.** **THE MAJOR TURN: WHAT COMES BACK IS CORRECT, AND IT IS A STATEMENT FOR WORK DONE HERE BY A CREW THAT CAME FROM HERE AND THAT NOBODY HERE ORDERED, AND IT GOES IN A BAG WITH THE OTHERS, AND NOBODY HERE CAN ANSWER IT, AND NOTHING ELSE HAPPENED.** It has been on a sill in the corridor since the Saturday. One sheet, a heading, a reference, a date in June, one line of work — *Peverell Street — day gang, one gang, one day, gully and kerb, gang hours as booked* — eighty-eight pounds, and after the work, a four-digit job number off the yard at Penhale that belongs to work that went over the water in June and came back on the Friday. **The mechanism is in the gap between the fields and not in anybody's mouth: a day gang of this borough stood on its own street and the hours went on the ticket of a job eight miles and an estuary away, and nobody here asked and nobody here put it there, and a gang does not know a job number.** The drain is touched once, in one sentence, by Nell Ardent, and is that it is exactly the same as every other one of them, and is not elaborated on. Nina Calder gives the good news first — correct throughout, the rate has not moved since about 1987, not a bill, not a demand, not a form, no box to sign, no reply needed, it will not chase, it is paid out of a pool by people who will never know it existed — and then the one thing in it, once, and stops: there is a line that says Peverell Street and nothing that says who asked for it, and she is the person who would know, and this borough's people do not order day gangs because nobody here has ever ordered anything of anybody, so it was not ordered here and the page says it was done here and both are true, and there is nobody in that building or that town to reconcile them. It goes into the bag under the other eleven claims and **is not added up, and the reason is one sentence: the sum is a thing a person can carry, and the moment somebody adds the twelfth one in they have started a sum, and a sum wants an answer, and there is nobody in this borough to give it.** The string goes round twice. It is a bag on a shelf and not a file and has no name and no date on it. Nobody is being cheated, nothing is a fraud, no one is a villain, and no root term expires.

**Chapter 0264 — The Seventeenth. Saturday the seventeenth of September 2016, from about eleven in the morning, a building by the water, a parade, the low end of Peverell Street, and a hall off the parade.** **CARD 0264 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.** In the records room **Nina Calder tells Jonas Mercer to open the register, which he has never opened, and he opens it. It is at nineteen, the nineteenth is a yard light with a bulb in a maintenance column and the bulb is out, and under it a line goes down the page and stops about two inches short of the bottom of a book about two inches deep. The sum is six hundred and sixty-one and it is still blank.** She says it will be the same in a month, that it was the same last month, that she has said so every month since about February, and that neither of them has ever done anything about it, and that it is no longer on her list, which is the only kind of progress there has been. The parade is the same parade: the shutter, the window card, the woman of about sixty-five not told anything, a van off the bridge with a scabbed corner on the offside wing, a card read out to nobody in particular and put straight, and **a man on a ladder taking down a sign while a second man holds the ladder, neither of whom could tell you afterwards who had asked whom, which is the pact holding and is never said.** At the bottom of Peverell Street the pump is in the doorway, the stopcock is off, **and the wall beside it is bare, with a clean strip of newer paint and a grey line of dirt where a length of hose lay in one place until the twenty-first of June, and nobody in this borough has said one word about a hose to anybody since the summer came in**; a woman goes up the street with a bucket and comes back with one and does not stop at the door. **THE MAJOR TURN ARRIVES IN TWO SMALL THINGS. FIRST, IN A HALL: the wrong answer about the register is still going round and is still wrong, and the woman of about fifty-five confirms it sideways to the woman beside her and not to the room, and the woman beside her says she had it off a fellow off a lorry in July and has heard it since, and the first confirms it in the voice you use for something you were given by somebody else and have not thought about since; nobody at that table joined in, and the man in his sixties was six feet away with a cup of tea and did not look up, and the room went back to the price of glass. SECOND: the question is still a question and nobody answered it. The man from the parade asks the room, in good faith, whether anybody has ever found out who prints them, and tells the man of about eighteen to answer for himself — and he says he has no copy, no docket, no number, no name and no address, that it went out in June on the back of a docket in a boatman's brown card wallet, that it is in a box on the other side of that water, and that if the wallet went in the river in October the question would be gone. The young woman of about twenty says *there's still nothing* and he says it back.** About nine people came and every one of them was on nothing, on a meter, with the radiator in that corridor out since about 1998. The woman of about fifty-five spent the morning moving two bags and a box of books into a room over a shop and will spend five nights there, which is not a rescue and not an arrangement. **Nobody is rescued, nobody dies, nobody renews anything, nothing was minuted, and nobody is thanked and nobody refuses to be thanked. The eleven standing refusals are eleven.**

## Volume 05, Continuation 0008 — Chapters 265–274

**Chapter 0265 — A Second Day. Saturday the seventeenth of September 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, the kitchen at the back of a parade in Tideglass, and the top of that parade.** The same day as 0264 and from the evening of it. The boy is on the dishes, is not running anything, and no request was made of him; and two of them go out that same evening without having spoken to one another first, and neither mentions it to anybody. There had been a breakfast on at the shop that shuts early and the kitchen did the food and the washing-up ran past the middle of the afternoon into the evening, and the woman he works for went home at six and left him about six things in the sink and a timer on the machine that has never been reset. He is on nothing, has asked nobody for a day and offered nobody one, and nobody in that kitchen knew where he would be at half past seven. **The two are the woman of about fifty-five, who has a room over a shop until Monday and nowhere else to be, and the young woman of about twenty, off the college bus. He ties the cardboard by nine, the clock is nine minutes fast and always has been, and he locks two doors and goes down a dark parade and passes nobody. Nothing is built, nobody is hurt, nobody is thanked, and the word *thank* is at zero.

**Chapter 0266 — An Arris. Saturday the twenty-fourth of September 2016, from about half past eight in the morning, the Methodist hall on Carrow Lane in Tideglass, and a parade of shops.** There are two slabs on that hall's front step and a crack across the upper one, and two men arrive on a Saturday morning to deal with it because a third man made a remark about it in a doorway in September and was not present and was not asked to be. The man in his sixty said it, to nobody in particular and to two people who were standing there; the woman of about fifty-five was one of them and has said nothing to anybody since. A man in his thirties who does building work heard the same sentence four days later and came about it in a hardware shop and said he was not talking about it in there, and **Tomas Renn said "Then don't," and gave the reason, and it is the same one he gave about the sack barrow in August: a barrow can go out of a shop in front of anybody and a job has a name on it.** He also said the man would have asked him in about three weeks and he would have said yes and then it would have been him that did it and it would have been in the shop, and he lent him a ladder off the wall behind his own door. The key to the hall is under the third stone and has been for thirty years. **THE TWO MEN DISAGREE ONLY ABOUT THE JOB: take it all up and relay it, which needs a number, a book and a good few hundred pounds, or cut it back and re-bed the top course, which holds for thirty years and has no number on it. NEITHER WILL PUT ANYTHING IN WRITING. THE MAN IN HIS SIXTIES ASKED FOR ONE THING TO BE SAID OUT LOUD IN A ROOM SOMEBODY HEARS, WHICH WAS THAT HE WAS NOT ASKING THE OTHER MAN TO DO IT, AND THE OTHER LET HIM SAY IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE OF THE ACCOMMODATION ANYBODY MADE.** A woman in the hall says the slab cannot go up because the doors open on a Wednesday meeting, so it stands against the wall under a coat until then, and the man says that makes it a thing he is doing on a Wednesday. Then the turn, and it is the card's turn: **the front corner of the new course has gone soft at the arris; the man in his sixties says the word back twice and cannot put it to anything at all, and when a woman asks him what an arris is he says he has no idea and that the other man said it, and the man in his thirties does not explain it and is not asked to.** No duty became a place, and nobody got a reason why a crew may go.

**Chapter 0267 — A Tin. **Chapter 0268 — Bored. **Chapter 0269 — The Day. Thursday the thirteenth of October 2016, from about half past seven in the evening, a first-floor room over a shop at the end of a parade in Tideglass.** A question was put to a room which had never been given the right answer to it, the room supplied a different answer instead, that answer is the better of the two, and the room accepted it without anybody asking who had put it there. **Chapter 0270 — The Bill. Thursday the twentieth of October 2016, from about ten in the morning, the second house of Marsh Lane in Tideglass.** A figure on a sheet of paper rises, nothing done in this borough caused it, she says so out loud at her own kitchen table, and a single man hears her say it. **Chapter 0271 — A Queue. **Chapter 0272 — Nobody Owns It. **Chapter 0273 — A Knack. "No." "Somebody taught you." "No. There's nobody to teach me. I watch a thing and then I do it wrong about nine times." — and she laughs and says, "Somebody did."** It is not a thanks and not an offer and not a job and not a standing, and he says nothing more to her and she says nothing more to him. **He stays till the chairs go up, carries four of them, goes out into the rain and stands on the step because the step is the width of the hall. Nobody asks him one thing all night that was a question about him, nobody offers him one thing at all, nothing is written down, and the thing he asked in June is still the thing he asked in June.** The spanner went back in his pocket and the leg was still locked in its bracket on the Thursday, the Friday and the Monday.

**Chapter 0274 — Ordinary. Tuesday the fifteenth of November 2016, from about ten in the morning, a building by the water in Tideglass, a parade of shops, the low end of Peverell Street, and a hall off the parade.** The register stands at nineteen, the rule beneath the nineteenth entry is empty, one man on a parade asks another who had undertaken the job and is told that he had, neither of them minds, and not one question was settled anywhere in this borough at the end of the autumn. **Nell Ardent opened the register on the Tuesday for a line she wanted on a form, and opened it again because she does that, and the nineteenth is still a yard light with a bulb in a maintenance column and the bulb is still out, and the line under it goes down the page and stops about two inches short of the bottom of a book about two inches deep, and she worked it out on the corner of the form with the end of her pen, because it is a habit nobody asked her to keep, and IT CAME TO SEVEN HUNDRED AND TWENTY DAYS. and the other, unasked, gives her the day and gives it across the table the way you give somebody a thing that is better than the thing they had; and neither says where she got it; and nobody at that table joins in; and the man in his sixties is four feet away with a cup of tea and does not look up.** **AND THE QUESTION IS STILL A QUESTION: THE MAN FROM THE PARADE, WHO HAS PUT HIS HAND UP IN THAT ROOM TWICE SINCE THE SUMMER, DID NOT PUT IT UP TONIGHT, AND NOBODY NOTICED THAT EITHER, AND HE SAT THERE UNTIL TEN WITH HIS CUP IN BOTH HANDS.** Nobody is rescued, nobody dies, nobody renews anything, nothing was minuted, nobody is thanked and nobody refuses to be thanked, and the eleven standing refusals are eleven. **CARD 0274 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.**

## Volume 05, Continuation 0009 — Chapters 275–284

- **0275 — A Letterbox. Tuesday 15 November 2016, morning, the top of Marsh Lane and a parade of shops.** The same day as 0274 and a different part of the borough and a different hour. The post comes up the lane at a quarter to eight. A man with a bundle and a shoulder bag rings two, rings once at the fourth, pushes a leaflet through a letterbox standing back off the step, and posts five things through the door of the shop. **A woman at the bus shelter says that in six weeks of standing there not one of them has wanted anything off anybody, and the postman tells her that the post is the one thing in that town with somebody to sign for it, and that you could leave a bowl of water on a step and nobody would come and a postman comes, and she says you would think the post could knock, and he says post knocks and post does not get an answer.** At the top of the lane there are three bells on a small board with no names beside them, because the flat above them emptied in June. He looks at the board, puts his thumb on the top bell and does not push it, lays a white envelope down on the tiles of the recess against the jamb so the rain would go over it, writes nothing, and does not go up. **Nobody saw him. Neither woman on that lane ever heard about it. The envelope is not opened.**
- **0276 — A Job Number. Monday 21 November 2016, a back yard at the end of a street off Marsh Lane.** A stack has been leaning since the summer and a cap went on it in a hurry, and the top course came off in the last week of October. The rain going down an open flue settles the argument and the man in his thirties says nothing and then says all right. **A bill from a firm over the water has a job number printed along the top and it is a two and not a six, and the man on the estuary explains that a ticket is raised on whatever is open at the time by somebody who is not paid to write it down, and that the office will not unpick it by hand because the day it does a correction made by hand ceases to be a ticket. He names it: that is a recharge, and says it is the word they put on it, and then says he is not going to unpick it and that the day one of them did it by hand it would stop being a ticket. The man in his thirties does not know what the word means, is never given the meaning of it, and uses the word twice in the next fortnight, once in the wrong place and once in the right one.** A credit note comes on the Friday for the second of June with a line at the foot that says the same thing twice.

The third of them is the woman of about fifty-five's, she is on a month, and while he is standing there the door comes back and shuts behind her, hard enough to move the latch, and she lifts it and opens it again. **He looks at the hasp on the inside of it. Neither of them says who put it there or when.** The next door along, counting past the fire door, stands open three inches with a chair against it, and the draught under it moves a rug on the landing whenever a door opens anywhere on that floor; he knocks, says his name, asks to look at the front of the door, is told he would rather he did not. The fifth is at the end by the window that has never been painted shut, and he shuts it against the draught before he knocks, and a man in a dressing gown tells him that window has been on a list going round about a fortnight and that he will not stand in his own doorway for the sake of one, and shuts the door on it, and the draught comes the length of the landing behind him. - **0279 — The One They Keep. - **0280 — A Gate. - **0283 — Five Rooms. Tuesday 27 December 2016, five rooms.** About nine plates in a sink at half past eight and the hot water gone at nine on a timer nobody has reset. ## Volume 05, Continuation 0010 — Chapters 285–294

- **0285 — The Catch. Saturday 31 December 2016, morning, a hall off a parade.** The parade was shut and boards were going over three windows, and the woman who runs the shop that shuts early stood through all of it with her key in the lock. The door shut on its own behind people all winter, stuck fast at the top in the third week of January, and the man came back up the parade in the middle of February, looked at it and walked on.

- **0293 — One Thing. ## Volume 05, Continuation 0011 — Chapters 295–304

- **0295 — Four Steps. Tuesday 31 January 2017, afternoon, four outside steps off Marsh Lane.** A rail that came off its brackets in December is put back on the wall in a quarter of an hour, with two plugs in the four holes the sheared fixings left. Nobody asked and nobody is charged. Two people find out: a woman with a key to a hall, on her way to open it, and a man who works nights, coming down for a paper. He says out loud that somebody has had that up. The two of them stand in the doorway of that flat and ask each other for nothing. The reason the man in his thirties gives for not knocking is what a knock would cost the woman: a cup of tea, and a man on her step as a thing that can happen to her. A person who is not counted is not a person who is helped and the chapter does not pretend otherwise — he is on the days and at two in the morning, the rail was never in his wages, and the sheet in the van is for a kitchen. The rail is on the wall for the rest of the week and he never goes back.
- **0296 — The Closer. Friday 3 February 2017, early morning, a ground-floor passage in a building by the water.** A street door at the foot of that stair has a dead closer and three marks on the plaster opposite, and at twenty past two at night it comes in off the wind, goes back, and catches the woman of about fifty-five above the wrist. She uses the cold tap over that meter and a tea towel and goes back up. At twenty-five to six a man in his sixties comes in off the lane, feels the biggest mark in the dark, and in twenty minutes takes the arm off that door, fixes a plate on the jamb so the arm can be put back on, and wedges a length of timber in the corner so the door stops a hand's width short of the wall. He says the timber is the belt to the braces and nothing else, and goes out to his car. Her problem is not solved and she is not housed by anybody: still a room on a month, the hasp on her own door untouched and never raised with her.
- **0297 — A Bath. Tuesday 7 February 2017, afternoon, a first-floor landing in that building.** A steel bath that came out of a house in January has been on a signless van at the end of Marsh Lane since mid-month and has been to two car boot sales. The man who owns that van carries it up the outside stair because he has a job on a shop near the top of that lane, has to move the van at half past two, and has nobody to help with a handcart. A woman whose door stands open three inches comes out and gives him one syllable. He says right. She names two places it cannot go and then says she does not know where it goes and that it was never hers. It goes back down and stops on its side under the passage window, across from the chair put there in January. The man who works nights looks at it and goes up. Nobody asked the woman of about fifty-five whether she wanted one. He does not bring another.
- **0298 — A Hundred and Twenty-Four Pounds. Saturday 11 February 2017, evening, a hall off a parade.** A sheet of A4 comes under that door on the Wednesday with a figure on it, three lines, and two boxes at the foot. The man in his sixties finds it on the doormat at half past six, reads it in the dark and then again with the light on, and stands in the passage for about twenty minutes. That night the woman with the key writes the name over the door of the shop next door into the first box, in capitals, with a chewed pencil, and nothing into the second. The man in his forties does not stop her and she has no two-halved sentence ready. The man in his sixties says what it would do — a light on that shop's account and that room left with nothing on it — and she says she knows, and he says it is the wrong name and the right idea. Then she names the man who works nights, out loud, in the room, and he is not asked whether that is all right.
- **0299 — The First One. Tuesday 14 February 2017, morning, the top of Marsh Lane and a bus shelter.** The man from the parade asks his question out loud on a piece of hard because the radio shop's lorry has not been. The man in a fleece going to the works gives back the first answer, which is the register, and says a thing somebody did is not a thing somebody wrote down. The woman who works in a shop tells him, on the pavement, that she has heard that one off him before and has never seen it answered, and he says it will not change for being said twice in two places, and nobody argues and nobody calls him right. The man in a fleece then walks down across the ice and asks the woman with a clipboard what her course counts, and she tells him, and that is the first time anybody in this account has spoken to her. That night the hall hears where it went and the room says nothing about it. There are still four answers and not five.
- **0300 — Two Things. Sunday 19 February 2017, morning, a yard behind a shop.** The back door of that shop has a barrel in it since the summer, and the barrel will be halfway round by then, and a locksmith's card has been in her pocket since November. She goes into a shed for a tin of oddments and there is no tin. Behind the shed, under a dpm sheet the wind has taken off the wall, there is a chest of assorted hinges that the man in his thirties put there in the last week of November and nobody has ever opened. She has the lid off before she decides to. The barrel she came for is on a shelf in the office with a bit of pencil beside it in a hand not hers, and she changes the lock herself in ten minutes. The chest goes into the shed with a milk crate in front of it. Four days later the man in his thirties goes into that yard for nine feet of capping, goes round the back for batten he put there himself, and finds a swept floor and nothing else. He asks at the front, is told that shop has never had anything at the back, and brings his own batten a week later.
- **0301 — The List. Wednesday 22 February 2017, late morning, the bottom of Peverell Street.** A white van with a fridge standing in it reverses back out of that street, and a man in his thirties stands on the pavement with a shut pad and says nine things aloud: a sign at the corner, a street not on the gritting round, a pump with its stopcock off, a step under loose lino, gulls into a loft, the last bus, nobody to ring if a man falls, and two more. A man in a fleece says that is a list. A woman with a shopping bag comes back and offers him about half a bag of rock salt from her porch, says she wants nothing for it and not in writing, and he says no and says why: it would put a woman in it, and in a fortnight she would have to ask what she wanted for it, and there is nowhere he could put it. He also says salt will not do for that step. She goes on up the street and neither comes back with the sack nor mentions it again. On the Thursday he puts one of the nine into the air again beside a man in Corrance Lane, is asked which one, and cannot recall the run of them.
- **0302 — A Lamp in the Porch. Saturday 25 February 2017, early morning, a hall off a parade.** A man in a hi-vis is at the neighbouring shop at half past six with a set of keys, because that landlord never comes. There is a bulkhead over that porch dead since about 2011 and a switch inside it that has never done anything. He puts a ladder on the top step, gets the old lamp out in four minutes, finds a foot of dead stub above the switch, cuts it off, puts the flex in, presses the switch, and goes up the parade. He tells nobody, quotes no figure, leaves no card, and writes nothing down. That night the woman who works in a shop stops at the door, because that porch has had no light in it since about 2011, and says somebody has put a lamp in it. The man in his forties says aye and does not put down what is in his hand. She says right, says she is not going to find out, and says whoever it was had better have had a ladder. Nobody says whether it should be there. He comes up the parade again on the Tuesday and does not go past.
- **0303 — Five Rooms. Friday 3 March 2017, a kitchen, a shop, a corridor and a hall.** A lad of about eighteen is in five rooms on one day, on two streets and in three buildings, and the first two are not the same room and not the same doorway. There is one more chair in the shop that shuts early than there was on the Tuesday, standing by the wall and not in the row, and nobody asks him where it came from, and he stacks it the same way up as the rest, and its owner looks at the stack and says two hundred years. On a corridor the woman of about fifty-five tells him a woman coming on Wednesday would want a bag with a blanket in it and something heavy under the blanket moved off that landing, and he takes it to the foot of the stair without opening it. In the hall, the man in his forties — who had heard of him at the end of January and had never been in a room with him — asks which of the two places he does first, is told, says right, and asks nothing else. The only consequence is that the woman with the key sees that he has asked him something, and is told what the question was.
- **0304 — A Hard Frost. Friday 10 March 2017, a parade of shops and a hall off it.** A hard frost with black ice in the shade of every wall, gone by about midday. The shop that shuts early goes up an hour later than the old time. A man comes down with a shovel. A grit bin has a crust in it that was not there on Wednesday. A white van with a fridge turns round at the bottom of Peverell Street without reversing. A signless van stands at the end of Marsh Lane with an empty back. **At half past ten a man and a woman carry a box of files into the room by the desk, and a sleeve catches a book and pushes it out over the edge, and nobody opens it and nobody knows what is in it. What is written last in that book is a yard lamp with a dead bulb, and under it is only the line the paper makes for itself, and the days since that lamp went in are eight hundred and thirty-five.** A woman who was not in that room sets a binder against it at a quarter past ten not knowing what lay there. In the yard below there is a chair with a blanket over it and, some six foot off, a bath on its side with rain in the side that faces out, and a man carrying tools goes through that yard without stopping and without seeing either. At night four of them are still on that table and none has shifted since the twelfth of January, that being the twelfth of January, and the man from the parade stands up at half past nine, is looked at by three people, and after about two seconds sits down again and says the tea goes cold in four minutes every week. They both say he will ask it Thursday. That meter ran dry at ten past ten and was locked off, and the porch light was burning when the door opened.


## Volume 05, Continuation 0012 — Chapters 305–314

- **0305 — The Angle by the Fence. Saturday 11 March 2017, morning, a footpath behind the low end of Peverell Street.** A man in his thirties takes a pine door off three hinges at a house in a terrace off the Cleeve road, where a replacement goes in later in the month, and cannot get it flat into a van with a scaffold across the boards, so he stands it on its top edge in the angle where a back fence meets the end of a wall, with the letter plate facing the fence, and tells the woman who runs the shop behind that yard that it is going there, and she says it is not their yard. **A woman with a pushchair comes along that path, because the kerb is up at the front for two cars, and gets through the remaining foot and a half one wheel at a time, and the fence takes four inches off the top of the paintwork.** She comes back the same way later and it has gone on a hired van. At four in the afternoon a man in his sixties, watching from a first-floor front room on the corner, goes out, comes back and puts the light on over that door, and nobody goes under it that day except her. The man who put the door there comes back to his own van, sees it from six foot off, and does not go over to it. **On the Friday a man with a boiler on a sack barrow takes that lane instead of the parade, stops in the middle of it, looks at the door for about ten seconds, and goes back up and knocks on the side door of the shop instead of the front. The woman who runs that shop does not know her boiler came round the back, and nobody in that shop ever finds out a door stood there, and nobody goes back to look at it.**
- **0306 — Into the Kitchen. Wednesday 15 March 2017, evening, a Methodist hall on Carrow Lane and the kitchen next to it.** A man who repairs sewing machines tells that hall, without being asked, that a woman in the second house of Marsh Lane has been sent a bill that would put her landlord in a position, and explains why: the meter was swapped in November, the old one is on a different supply, and both bill her. The woman who works in a shop tells him not to say that in there, and the man in his forties tells him to leave it, and says the reason — a thing said out loud in a room leaves that room on the people in it, and that woman cannot un-say it and never said it. **She takes it into the kitchen at about half past eight and says it there as well, and the young woman of about twenty at that sink produces a figure of a hundred and ninety pounds, and nobody had given her that figure: it came from the woman who works in a shop, who had heard the post-office queue say over two hundred twice running and had said nothing to anybody for a fortnight.** They work out whose figure it is and why. The hall hears only that the conversation went into a kitchen. Nobody in that room asked where she had been. At the end of it, a length of scaffold board across the two legs of that hall's folding table is said to have come out of a skip on Cleeve Street in the summer.
- **0307 — A Fire Blanket. Saturday 18 March 2017, evening, a first-floor landing in a building by the water.** A man in his thirties opens the cupboard under that stair to look at a box for a Monday job and finds it has no lock, a key on a hook inside it that has been there since the building went up, and inside a wool fire blanket, a foot of flat steel, cable ties, wire and a bucket. The blanket goes in his bag. The steel stops four inches in. **The woman in the room next door along, whose own door stands open three inches with a chair against it, tells him the bar can go up a sleeve, and then tells him why the blanket should go and the bar should not: a cupboard with a bar and no blanket is a thing every building in the town is short of, and a cupboard with a blanket in it and nothing else in it is a thing somebody could make a noise about.** He puts the steel down. She will not ask him to take it and pretend afterwards that she had not noticed, and will not call it all right, and will not put her name to it. He does not knock on the door of the woman of about fifty-five, and says the reason, which is an earlier morning in that passage in February and about nine words and a dressing gown. He goes down the stair with the blanket. On the Monday the man in his forties finds that the bar on that fire door stops nine inches short of a door it is meant to close, and that the cupboard has never had a lock, and pushes the bar, watches it stop in the air, and says right.
- **0308 — A Hundred and Ninety. Thursday 23 March 2017, late afternoon, a parade of shops and a bus shelter.** The man who sells radios, standing outside his own half-down shutter, tells a woman with a shopping bag that a bill in the second house of Marsh Lane is over two hundred, has been twice running, is not a misread, and that the question to put to a landlord is which meter he read. **A man of about thirty at the shelter at the bottom of that parade has been holding a different figure for the same bill since February, on the authority of a man he worked with who has gone to work thirty miles off, and he kept it because it was said twice the same way.** They meet at the shelter and he says he is not going to pretend he has not got it, and she says she is not standing at a bus stop working out which of them is right, and neither of them settles it. There is no paper on any of it. The woman behind the counter of the shop that shuts early hears the first telling and says none of it. The next evening the same account goes to a man buying a battery. On the Saturday the two of them pass each other in the street and say nothing, and he does not know she exists as a person who has been quoted.
- **0309 — What the Building Did Third. Sunday 26 March 2017, a building by the water.** The stop tap in that building is off from Saturday night to Monday evening. On the Sunday morning a woman goes down the ground-floor passage for water with a jug and finds the strip light on, the tap case standing open, and the jet nozzle gone off the standpipe on the landing, with a brass cap on the outlet that is not the cap that came off the building. **That cap is kept in the cupboard under the stairs with the blanket and the steel, and the reason it is not that cap is written into the chapter and nobody in the borough ever finds out who swapped it. She stands in the passage about a minute, puts the case back, and carries the water up, and says nothing to anybody that day or the Monday.** That afternoon the woman next door along takes a wool blanket off the arm of her own chair, where it has lain eight days, knocks on the door at the end of the corridor, and gives reasons why the woman there needs it, having seen the tea towel and the cardigan from where she stands. She does not go in and is not asked and does not say where it came from. **On the Monday morning a man in his forties knocks the loose corner out of the step outside that street door, packs mortar mix under it, draws the top up flush, and stands on it, and it holds, and he tells nobody and does it before the first person down that passage has the tap open.** The brass cap is still on the outlet, the blanket is still on the bed, and the two are not connected by anybody.
- **0310 — Twice. Thursday 30 March 2017, late morning, a yard behind a shop on a parade.** A small iron bed frame came out of a back bedroom on a road off the Cleeve one and has been on the boards of a van since about the middle of the month. The man in his thirties cannot get it flat in with a door, so it goes against the gable wall of that yard on its side, head end up, and the woman who runs the shop is told it is going there. **Behind a wired glass door at that counter, the woman who works in a shop looks at it about four times a day for a fortnight, never goes out into the yard, never asks where it came from, and watches the man come down the parade about nine times without going through the gate. It goes in the skip at twenty to six on the fourth Monday with pram things, a bike wheel and a television.** Four weeks later a man of about twenty-eight with a unit off the same parade, who has had a bed frame of his own since January and been sitting on it, puts his out in the yard of a shop three doors further up because the roof over his unit drips onto the top rail of it. Nobody sees him. The landlord's men take the yard on the Monday. **He looks at the wall on the Tuesday and says nothing to anybody, ever, and does not know the first frame existed. The woman who works in a shop sees the second one from the parade, recognises it for what it is, and does not think about the first one, and goes on to the bus stop.** Both went in skips four days apart.
- **0311 — What He Said He Would Do. Wednesday 5 April 2017, morning and evening, the low end of Peverell Street, a shelter, and a hall off a parade.** A step outside a shop that has been shut since the summer before last has a two-finger lip at its outside corner under a length of blue lino whose near end has lifted. A man in his thirties kneels on it, plugs two old holes, decides it is a lip and not a hole, and says out loud that he will take it up and screed it. A man in a fleece says aye. **The next morning he says the same thing, louder, to a different man at the open end of a shelter hard, with a woman keeping a footfall tally ten foot off with her back to the road, and writes one line in pencil on a pad he has not opened since the summer.** He does not do it that week or the next, and the lino settles back onto the tarmac by itself, and the step stays two inches down. His reason is that he can invoice for a step and there is nobody here to invoice. That Thursday evening the woman with the clipboard tells the hall what she heard on the Tuesday, with her count, and the man in his thirties comes in and denies saying he would do it, and says he said he would have a look at it. She says she does not need to be right. **The man in a fleece backs her hearing and not the man's, and says he cannot say what the man was doing at that lane because their hours differ. The man puts the pad on the table face up for a second, one line on the top sheet and nothing on it, and puts it away, and says nobody has asked him to do a step and there is nothing in it.** The step is still down. The tally is given in at the back of a bank and not carried on.
- **0312 — A Saucepan for the Man Who Works Nights. Saturday 8 April 2017, afternoon and night, a hall off a parade and a kitchen behind it.** A saucepan with frozen water in it is standing by a skip in a yard behind a row. The man with the signless van empties it, turns it over, reads a stamped code and a date on the base, and carries it up a parade to a hall, because one thing is known about the man who works nights and that is that he once stood in a coal line and took nothing out of it. **He is let in, stands by the counter four minutes with it in his hand, is offered no cup, and asks who the man is and is told none of them. He says it is for him, that the code is no use to anybody, and that the year on the base is the only thing on it worth knowing, puts it on the end of the table, and goes out into the rain.** The woman who works in a shop leaves it where it is rather than put it away. The man comes in at twenty past ten in his coat, finds it at the door end, notes there is no name on it, and is told he never gave one. He turns it over, reads the stamp, and says aye, well. **He heats part of a tin on a ring at about ten to midnight, eats standing up, washes the pan, dries it on the cloth, and puts it at the back of the shelf above two lids it does not go with, because what is not his does not lie about a table in a full room.** He tells nobody he used it. Nobody asked where it went.
- **0313 — Six Days, Five Rooms, and Nobody. Thursday 13 April 2017, a kitchen at the back of a parade, a shop, a kitchen in Corrance Lane, a corridor by the water, a hall, and a bus.** A lad of about eighteen is in the same five rooms as last time, over six days rather than one, because the man whose kitchen he does is away and the woman does not want him back in there. **Nobody puts one question to him anywhere.** In the shop he stops with a chair in each hand waiting to be told where the eighth one goes, is given three words, and is told there may be more on the Saturday. A man at the end of the counter has a paper and a pen all day and says nothing. In the hall he stops deliberately in the gap by the table with a tray in his hands and the man in his forties looks up and looks back down at his cup. He moves three bottles of washing-up off a landing to a bin store because his bucket was going to hit them, and the woman he did it for says only that she will be in. **On the Thursday he tells the woman next door along that there was a blanket in the cupboard under the stairs, that there is a bar under it, that there is a key on a hook, that a man has been and taken the blanket, and that he saw it on her chair on the Saturday and not on the Monday. She says nothing at all.** That night he takes cups round that room four times and the only conversation is about a meter. **On the top deck of the bus he tells a stranger that the step outside the shut shop is still down and is nobody's to be doing and that he has not done it and is not saying he will, and the man agrees it is the one with the lino on it and goes back to his paper.** He walks down off the bus.
- **0314 — The Seventeenth of April. Monday 17 April 2017, morning and night, a parade, a building by the water, and a hall.** Rain all day off the estuary. The shop that shuts early goes up at its own time and a radio shop next door has a shutter of its own at half height with a man behind it and no sound. **The man with the shovel does not come down the parade until two and does nothing at the bank end. A gritting bin at the top of Peverell Street has a skin in the bottom and a hole through one side. A white van comes up the low end of Peverell Street, a man looks up the front of a building for a minute, and it goes back the way it came. The signless van is at the end of Marsh Lane. The step outside the shut shop is still down, with its lino lying flat where the rain put it.** A woman goes down a passage with two empty jugs because it is a Monday, and at about half past eight the register goes back onto a shelf in a room by the water, having been leaned against by a binder on a stair on the tenth of March and then carried two feet along to the next bay, with the bay door not catching. **The register is at nineteen entries, the last thing in it is a yard lamp whose bulb went out about November two years ago, the blank rule below that last entry runs about two fingers and then stops, leaving some two inches of the page itself empty, the days since that lamp went in are eight hundred and seventy-three, and nobody in the room looked at any of it. On the corridor outside is a shelf behind a door with a bag on it and a piece of string round the bag twice, and the bag has not been moved since before the winter.** That night nine people are in a hall with a meter on. **four answers have been lying on that table since the twelfth of January, that being the twelfth of January, and those still there are the ones that were there then, and no way has ever been found of putting any of them beside another.** The woman who works in a shop says nobody has added a fifth and nobody has taken one off, and that the one concerning a street concerns the same street. The man from the parade says his question again, in new words, and 0299 is the chapter that has him say it. The woman who works in a shop reports that it went round a shelter in February and that nobody has produced a fifth since. The gas runs out at ten past ten, the padlock goes on the case, the chairs go up, and a porch light cuts out when the corner lamp comes up.
