## Volume 05, Continuation 0013 — Chapters 315–324

- **0315 — A Foot of Scaffold. Tuesday 18 April 2017, morning, that corner of Peverell Street.** A van is reversed a foot off a wall to get light onto a downpipe, and the strike takes the pipe, two brackets and a length of render; the plaster behind one bracket has been wet behind the paint for years and came away the size of a closed fist. The man in his thirties can see at once that this is not a house he is going to do. The wall is brick where he would want timber, and the corner needs a tower that is already booked for the week after, so the pipe goes down into the gutter and the props are left for whoever brings the tower. What the chapter actually turns on is a length of scaffold about a foot long, cut off his own boards without being asked, stood on end where the render returns, and wired to the pipe and the render. He says, before and after, that it is a prop and not a repair, and that the wall wants opening up in the autumn. The man in a fleece is on nine houses a morning, finishes about ten past six, and nobody telephones him because he is not on anybody's list in this town. The woman who works in a shop heard all of it from the woman who runs that shop, is not going out to ask him about it, and will sell him a roll of paper like anybody else. **He came in on the Saturday, paid and left, and has not been back, and neither of those two women has any idea that he is a person who could be asked.**
- **0316 — Two Rooms. Saturday 22 April 2017, evening, a hall on Carrow Lane and the room at the back of a shop.** The man in his sixties brings in a lamp over a bank door that was burning in broad daylight on the twentieth, with a man and a woman under it working out how high it hangs before going back in, and it has been off every time he has looked since. He says himself that he ought to have had it somewhere other than where he had it. The woman who works in a shop reduces the whole of it to the fact that it has now been said in two rooms, and neither of those rooms is anywhere any of them work. She puts two questions to the man in his thirties — how long the lamp had been burning, and whose it is — and gets neither answered. The man who works nights asks whether it belongs with the four and is told it does not and that nobody is setting it beside them. The man in his forties then tells her, in front of the man in his thirties, that the same thing has already been said in another room in this town. **The man in his thirties is told in his own hearing that his sentence is already out of the room he was standing in. No fifth answer arrived and none of the four was corrected.**
- **0317 — A Length of Four Inch. Thursday 27 April 2017, morning, the first floor of a building off Cleeve Street.** A firm capped nothing, so a length of open four inch stands three foot out of a landing floor with a hopper on it. The man in his thirties cuts the old stack off and gets a new length up through the ceiling on a cord. He then has to leave it standing, because a coupling cannot be run onto a length that is in the air at the end of itself and the job wants two people. **The woman who works in a shop is the only person in that building that morning, lives in the top flat, and will not stand under a length of open pipe while somebody works a caulk iron in a joint.** Her case is a hole in her ceiling, a hopper going down four floors onto open pipe, a blockage in about six weeks, and a man who comes two days a month. His case is the same six weeks, but a stranger's fault on a step, and nobody's name on any paper because there is nothing to put it on. **He puts the length down rather than do it badly.** Separately, a man with a folded trolley and a set of steps takes a fridge out of the ground-floor flat in about four minutes, is not asked to hold anything and does not offer, and afterwards the man in his thirties observes that a man halfway up a stair with a fridge on a trolley is not an arm anybody can borrow. **Left on the landing: a capped stack, a five-inch hole, a length, a coupling, a coil of hemp, a caulk iron and a roll of carpet. Nothing was asked and nothing was arranged.**
- **0318 — What the Two of Them Said. Sunday 30 April 2017, morning, a bus stop at the end of Marsh Lane and a parade.** At a stop with no shelter, a man in a fleece tells a man with a dog that the shop which shuts early is to become a cafe, that a man from the city has been looking at it for somebody, that he wants both shops, and that the radio man has until about August — and gives his own standing in it as the fourth remove, saying it is not his and he is not having it. About a quarter of an hour later, with that shop's shutter already hooked to its top bar, the man who puts shutters up tells a young man with a rucksack a different and better-sourced version: the woman who runs the shop has bought the radio shop, the radio man is out by the end of June, and the two are to be done as one parade, two removes off a fitter and the fitter's brother-in-law. He then says the thing that matters — that both shutters came off the same bar in the same week, so whoever buys buys a parcel, and a man who sells radios is not the man who ends up running a cafe, so one of the two men has it backwards and it is not the one whose version is more interesting. He carries a ladder up the parade, knocks on the radio man's shutter and reports that the bar has dropped half an inch. **Nobody went into that shop, nobody knocked on a door, nobody telephoned anybody, not one sheet arrived, the shop went up on the Monday at its own time and shut at two, and nothing in the chapter was found.**
- **0319 — Three Days With No Water in It. Thursday 4 May 2017, covering the weekend before it, a building by the water.** That building's stop tap stays closed from the last evening of a week until one of them opens it, and this time nobody did, so there was no water in the place for three days. The tap was found across with its board lifted out and its case standing open, which nobody can account for. Three mornings, two empty jugs each time, and a cold tap that gives about two seconds and stops. **The meter on that passage wall ran for all three days and is the only thing in the building that got what it wanted, and nobody living there has ever taken a reading off it or could tell you where the figures go.** In the middle of those days the woman in the room next door along sees the two jugs and an unplugged kettle through a door she leaves open about two inches, and offers half a bucket of her own washing-up water for the kettle and for washing, on the terms that nothing is said about it and nobody fetches it, **and is refused.** Water returns on the Tuesday morning, both jugs are filled, and she never finds out who put the tap across; she heard somebody on the landing at about half past ten that night and did not open her door. **The other half of the chapter is a stair tread: the second one up from the bottom lifts half an inch and knocks once, and on the Thursday the man in his forties takes its front corner up, finds one screw sheared and one pulled out with a plug the size of a finger, drills the hole out, puts a longer screw through the bracket into sound concrete and stands on it twice. It does not move and makes no noise. He goes back down, knocks on no door at all, and a few feet below him on the stair she comes up carrying a full jug in each hand and a kettle hooked over one arm, and neither of them says a word.**
- **0320 — Twice, and About a Month Apart. Wednesday 10 May 2017, morning, a lane behind a row of shops.** A folded metal greenhouse frame in three sections, six foot by two foot out, painted steel, with a bent corner on the middle section. In the first week of April a woman leaned one against the brick of a yard at the top of that lane, having got it there on a barrow in three goes, and nobody asked her a single question about it in any direction, **and she has not walked that lane again since.** It has stood five weeks with green along its foot, and the man who works that lane with a barrow has walked past it five times. On the tenth of May the man in his thirties props another one against brick in a yard two doors above a shop and will not put it on a roof rack because of the wind coming up that lane. He tells the woman who works in a shop, from the alley, that it belongs to nobody, will be there a few days and then go, and that he knows of four in this town: two up a garden, one a bench in a garage, one against a wall further up the same lane. **She does not go and look, and would not have connected the two if she had. He has forgotten the first one. No single person saw both, and the woman who put the first one down has not been asked about it by anybody.**
- **0321 — The Gable. Monday 15 May 2017, morning, that corner, a shop off the Cleeve road, and a bay window.** Two slates on a gable above a bay have slipped about two inches and are still on rusted nails with the heads standing about half an inch proud, and one of them is the size of a door. A woman sits in that bay most days behind a table with a plant on it. On the morning of the fifth of May, at about half past eight, the man in his thirties tells a man in a fleece what the job wants — a tower, somebody to build it, somebody else to hold the boards, a day and a half of a weekend, plus his own yard for the tower — **and says in the same breath that nobody in that house has asked him.** He has not spoken to the woman in the bay and says he never intends to. Ten days later she stops him in the road, her only source being the man in a fleece, who had called at her door on the Thursday and had been unable to give her a name to go on. She puts it to him that she was told he said a fortnight; he does not deny saying a fortnight and denies only that he ever said he would do the job, and points out that he had not asked her for a telephone number at the time, which is the whole reason her street is not in his pad. **She asks for a piece of paper, not the work — a name and a date, kept in her front room, so that if a slate comes off in the autumn she can say she asked a man in that road and he wrote it down and did not come. He refuses, and gives her two reasons: there is nothing in this town to put his name on, and a paper with his name at the top would be the only one in the borough and would be about two slates; and, if he wrote her street down, then when a slate does come through that window he would be in it, whereas written nothing he is not.** He tells her plainly what is over her head and that he will not tell her twice. She goes in and leaves the sash down. **He has written nothing down anywhere.**
- **0322 — An Upright Cleaner. Thursday 18 May 2017, morning, a parade and a building by the water.** A good upright machine with a fifteen-foot lead and a cracked cuff at the machine end has been on the boards of the man with the van since the second week of April. taken from a house off the Cleeve road, emptied for a woman now living a long way off, out of a cupboard under that house's stairs, the filter holding somebody's hair, taken because the woman from the letting agency said take it in a yard with the loader running. **The whole of what he knows about the woman of about fifty-five is that in the third week of January he was in the yard behind that building late on a weekday afternoon with a torch in his hand on a pipe and a light was burning in a first-floor front room in broad daylight, and he has thought about it ever since.** The woman who works in a shop tells him there is one person on that floor, that she is not going up with him and is not telling him anything about her, and that she will open the street door and take an end of it because that stair is narrow and she is not having a woman of fifty-five do that alone — and says that the stair is the only reason. She tells him to leave it on the landing rather than in the room, that room being nine foot each way with nowhere in it to stand that. He does, comes back down, and two days later raises a hand from the cab and she raises one. **She runs it once on a Sunday, over about twenty feet of concrete, because five weeks of wind has got sand into the junctions, along the fire door and into a threshold, where a broom does not reach. The filter comes up with a bag of grit in it, the lead is fifteen foot against a landing of twenty-six so the plug had to move, and the noise brings the woman in the room next door along out of her door; she said aye, well, and went back in.** Then it went on its side in the corner where the landing widens by the fire door, its lead on top of it, against a wall that is not straight. **It has not been run again and the filter has not been emptied, and nobody in this borough has ever told him what became of it.**
- **0323 — Five Rooms, and Not One Word. Monday 22 May 2017, all day, five places, taken in the order the dateline gives them.** One day and not six, and only two of the five places are new. **The kitchen is clean before he gets there — surfaces wiped and dry, both hobs off, the rack empty, the board empty, and no third glass anywhere in it — and the man who cooks in there went home at about nine the night before and left no note.** At the greengrocer's a delivery of six boxes and a sack goes down in the middle of the shop and he is not asked to move one of them; the woman gets one sack onto her own shoulder and shoves the other two into the cold room with her foot, and wishes him a good morning at about ten past twelve. In the house at the end of Marsh Lane the man is out, the woman is not back until about eight, nobody there knows he is in the house, and he sits at a table for half an hour without going upstairs. In the corridor by the water there is nothing to mop; he goes along it with the bucket anyway and stands at the top of the outside stair for ten minutes. **What he says, to her back and not loudly, as she goes through her own door with two full jugs and a kettle, is that he is in that building at about eight on a Monday and she is on that stair at about half past seven with the two empty ones, and that he has seen her and she has not seen him, and that he was not going to make her swing round up there and have to hear it with a jug in both hands. She says nothing. The door shuts. The woman in the room next door along says nothing either.** In the hall he has not been on the tea since before Christmas, nobody has raised it with him and he has not raised it either; the urn is already on, the table is set for four and he is not one of the four, and nobody in that room says one word to him. **He leaves at a quarter to seven, walks the two miles, and had gone back for his own mop and bucket at half past four.**
- **0324 — A Saturday in May. Saturday 27 May 2017, morning and evening, out on that parade, up the water, and the Carrow Lane hall after dark.** The first dry morning since before Christmas, with about nine birds along the lip of a gutter in a row facing the same way, gone over the roof tops in about four minutes. **Two slates on a gable in the sun with their nail heads standing proud, a woman in that bay behind her own table with a plant on it, and nobody on that pavement looking up.** In the building by the water the register stands on the second shelf up in a bay off a first-floor corridor, on a door that does not shut over the catch. The last entry is a yard lamp, reported out about November two years ago under a heading reserved for that class of thing; that column has not been touched since, and below that line the sheet goes on a couple of fingers and then gives up about two inches short of the foot of the book. **The days since that lamp went in are nine hundred and thirteen, and that is the only day-count printed in the prose of these ten chapters.** Two women come in at about half past ten for a chair out of a corridor being painted, take the one at the end of the corridor and carry it out between them, more than six foot off that bay, **and neither of them knows what is on that shelf.** Up the stairs, a machine carried up on the eighteenth of May is still lying over on its side where that landing widens at the fire door, and the filter in it has not been emptied since the Sunday in May when a woman ran it once over about twenty feet of concrete. **That evening eight people are in the hall on Carrow Lane, and the four answers on that table are the same four that have been there since the twelfth of January, and nobody has managed to put one of them beside another.** The woman who works in a shop says nobody has added one and nobody has taken one off; the man in his forties says that if four are going to be anything else it will not be by one of the people at that table deciding to count; **and the man in his sixties asks what the four amount to between them, and nobody at that table says anything to it.** Then the man from the parade puts a question about whether a thing that has been written down can turn out worse than the thing that actually happened, says he is not putting it beside those four, and the man in his forties agrees that it is a question and that it therefore stays one. The man in his thirties raises the two slates and is told it is not being taken further either. The gas goes at nine, the case is locked, the chairs go up, and the porch light is still burning a quarter of an hour after the door opened.

## Volume 05, Continuation 0014 — Chapters 325–334 (added after the repair pass of this batch)

- **0325 — Across a Gate. Sunday 28 May 2017, from about ten in the morning, and again on Thursday 29 June, from about half past four in the afternoon, off a parade.** A middle-sized white van with no lettering on it stands across the gate of a yard behind the sixth of nine shops. The man in his thirties cannot get his own van out, waits about an hour and a half, moves his own small van out by inches with a bucket under a wheel, and spends the rest of that Sunday on foot, walking a mile and a quarter to a job. The parade is shut and the man who puts shutters up does not work Sundays, and nobody in that parade learns a van was in that passage. A month later the same thing happens to a different person: the van is across the back gate of the shop where the woman who works in a shop is standing, having gone in nose first and turned round, and a man with a trolley cannot get his wheels through. She will not have six boxes put down on a pavement with nine inches of it, so he carries them in on a sheet of his own in two goes while she points at the heavy ones. She then shuts a gate that goes on a latch and has not been in that yard since. A man in a fleece tells her she would not be the first. **She says she is not going to knock on anybody's door and not going to station herself in that alley watching every vehicle, because the first one she stopped she would have to stop the next.** Neither was told about the other and neither asked anything.
- **0326 — A Firm in Another Town. Saturday 3 June 2017, from about half past ten in the morning until about half past one in the afternoon, a hall on Carrow Lane and the back of a shop off a parade.** In the hall, on a meter, the man in his sixties reports that a firm down the estuary doing outsides of houses and roofs has gone over, that you cannot get anybody, that he has not got the name, and that the name was on a van and the van has gone. The man in his forties refuses to let it be counted and distinguishes a thing heard twice from a thing checked. The woman who works in a shop sat through all of that in the hall and passes the whole of it on, in her own words, to the man who works nights in the room behind her shop, where he **asks her which firm it is and gets nothing.** The same morning, independently: a man arrives with an under-counter fridge on a hand truck and it will not go through a back door with a bar on the outside. The man who works nights says take it off, the woman who works in a shop will not because of two houses behind that yard, and the man with the hand truck will not stand in a doorway with an alley behind him. The bar comes off, the fridge goes in, and then the fridge is inside the swing of a door that will not close against it, so the bar cannot go back on and its key is in a town that shut in the autumn. **The bar stays off and nobody will be able to say why.**
- **0327 — Two Hands on a Landing. Tuesday 6 June 2017, a first-floor landing in a building off a parade.** A new sash will not go up: painted shut about four times, the top rail swollen into the outer stop, and pushing it takes the top corner out of its rebate. It is a two-man job and the man in his thirties says so twice. **The man in the ground floor flat, who has held the head of a sash for him three times, comes out in his socks and says, before anything is asked, that it is a two-man job, that he is on at four, and that the trestle is across his own front door — and adds the point that is conceded: By saying nothing you have enrolled me in it.** Later the same morning, a woman in the middle flat cannot get her own front door back on its hinges because a corner of that frame has dropped half an inch, and the job wants somebody to hold the door square while the slack is taken out of the hinge. He can do the packing alone and cannot do the holding alone. Both stand. The woman who works in a shop is the only person told any of it, **and she asks how many, and is told that nobody has ever counted anything in this town and no one has ever been given a pencil on a landing and asked to write.**
- **0328 — The Bin Day. Sunday 11 June 2017, from about a quarter past nine until about a quarter past eleven, the bottom of the Cleeve road, a parade off it and a shop on it.** The man in a fleece tells a stranger at a bus stop that the Thursday collection is moving and that it is the road works. The man who puts shutters up tells a woman outside a closed shop that it is the Tuesday, and that it is not one parade but two hundred yard of the top of the road. **One claims a parade and one claims a stretch of road and only one of the two men was in the road.** The woman who works in a shop has both, and works out that a thing that is a change and a thing that is a date are not the same statement. **The notice that would settle it went on about sixty doors from the Thursday off a lorry carrying no lettering at all, in about three quarters of an hour, and nobody in the shop and nobody at the stop saw a man get out of it.** Both men who touched a copy put it in a bin without reading it. Nobody in that parade has read one. The woman who works in a shop says this is not noise and is not two things either — it is the weather, and the only thing that could settle it is on sixty doors nobody has read.
- **0329 — The Fifth Thing. Thursday 15 June 2017, and the week of the twelfth, a building by the water and a passage three streets off it.** A glazed lantern on a flat roof over a first-floor corridor has nothing sealing round the exposed edge of its curb, and in the second week of June water comes down the stairwell wall, along the underside of the ceiling, past both door heads on that side, and down a wall in a crescent, taking the paper off a skirting board in one strip. **The woman of about fifty-five found the water herself on the Tuesday of that week and put a bowl of her own under it, has carried it out several times a day every day since, and there is a wet mark on the ceiling the size of a tea tray that has not got bigger at all since.** Nobody has been on that roof. The woman in the room next door along comes out on the Wednesday, sees the bowl, mentions a smell in the morning, and shuts her door. Three streets off, the man in his forties finds a wheelie bin on its side in a passage, hooks it back over two studs, takes a quarter of an inch of play out of the lower stud with a key, **pulls on it and the whole thing comes off the wall in one piece, and he does knock on neither of the two front doors.** The two repairs are four hundred yard apart and nobody connects them.
- **0330 — Three White Things. Wednesday 21 June 2017, a lane behind a row of shops off a parade.** A painted timber gate, four foot by three, white, shipped in a polythene sleeve with brown tape at its waist and its clear wrapper, and nothing in the wrapper that could say whose it is. One was left in a yard in the third week of May, one in the first week of June, one on Monday the nineteenth of June. **The man in his thirties counted them on the Wednesday morning by walking the lane, said the number out loud to himself for the first time in his life, and found that two of the three were already gone.** **AND THE CHAPTER SAYS WHY THAT IS NOT 0327, WHICH HE ALSO WALKED OUT OF: on that lane, before he goes to the shop, he puts the two halves of his own sentence from 0327 side by side, where the refusing half and the counting half are not the same half, and says that what he has lost it on is saying a number out loud where a person is standing in the room with him. A reader who does not have that paragraph will read this chapter as a contradiction of the last one, and the change is the point of it.** He got the pad out in the van and shut it again. **The only person in this borough who watched one of them go is the woman who works in a shop, from her own window, at about six in the morning on the Tuesday, and she told nobody and does not know the man with the barrow's name, and he found out only after he had counted three.** He did not ask her to say she had told him, because then she would be a woman watching a lane.
- **0331 — Three Lengths and a Gap. Sunday 25 June 2017, the low end of Cleeve Street.** Three lengths of close-board are lying against the brick of a yard, out of a job, not put up, and the opening measures about four foot across shoulder height, and about nine people went through it that morning. On the Friday before, at a door, to a man in a fleece on the step, the man in his thirties said he would have them in before the end of the month. **Nine days later he works out in about four seconds what was wrong with that sentence: the mistake was made off the doorstep rather than in the yard, and a promise made about another person's ground is a promise about their ground.** A woman with a clipboard has that gate on her sheet twice with two different numbers against it; a man in a fleece told her a man had said he would close it. She does not say he did it. **He gives it to her straight, at that door, nine days ago, and refuses to be let off it.** She asks whether he will do it and he says no, rules out the two easy reasons, gives the real one, and then says the thing that ends it: no third party exists who could have heard it, him and a man in a fleece, and that man is not here. **She wrote about a quarter of an inch on the edge of her sheet, looked at it, rubbed it out with a thumb, and said nothing about having done it.** He opened the pad in the road and shut it again. On the second of July the three lengths are still against that wall.
- **0332 — A Carpet and a Chest. Friday 30 June 2017, a building by the water.** A wool carpet about nine foot by six with the underlay still pinned to it in staples went up that outside stair in the second week of June, led by the woman of about fifty-five, and she had said, before it came up, that no carpet was going in that room. **She laid it herself two days later, kept it down three weeks, got a corner up off the skirting with her nails wanting to reach the dust beneath, and it came away in a shape and would not go back, and on the thirtieth she stood it edgeways where the wall takes the light, and it is there now.** On that same morning the same man carried a chest up that stair, put it on the step outside her door, knocked twice, and said the whole of what he had come to say and then that she could say no. **She said no. He said right you are, went down with it, shut the street door, and put it under a folding stool and two trestles in the back of his van.** Four seconds passed and nothing was said in them and he did not ask. He did not carry the vacuum cleaner down that stair and nothing in that chapter says he did; the machine is still on its side in the corner of that landing, which is what 0322, 0324 and 0329 say. The woman who works in a shop was told about none of it from him and asked for none of it.
- **0333 — Nobody Asked Him Anything. Monday 3 July 2017, from half past seven in the morning until about seven in the evening, and in that order, a kitchen at the back of a parade, a greengrocer's off it, a house at the end of Marsh Lane, a first-floor corridor, and a hall off the parade.** One day, five places, no task put to him in any of them, and four of the five rooms with a person in them, which is the difference from 0323 and is on the page rather than in a file. In the kitchen the man who cooks in it is sitting there and the lad washes a plate and two things and no destination is given to him. In the greengrocer's a man leaves a sack of leeks on the counter for two hours and nobody asks anybody to shift it. In the house at the end of Marsh Lane two people say good morning and that is all of it. In the corridor by the water there has been nothing to mop since before Christmas and he goes the length of his mop regardless, and **he does not speak to the woman of about fifty-five this time, because he put a remark to her back in May and got no reply.** In the hall off the parade, at ten to seven, he says out loud across the table, to the woman of about forty-two who holds that key and to two other men who can hear, that the woman next door along in that building has not been seen on that corridor since a Wednesday nineteen days back, that she goes past the bowl twice a day, and that in seven months the two women have not spoken and he cannot tell whether they are not speaking or never were. **Nobody answers him.** He walks two miles home with nothing in his hands.
- **0334 — A Saturday in July. Saturday 8 July 2017, a hall on Carrow Lane.** the warmest day of that year to date, and the chapter stays inside the room and lets the street come past the window: a shutter going up on a man's own, a van that stood and went, a man toward the foot of that street carrying something and back down it without it while nine people in that hall did not go to the window, and a shower that goes through. There are nine in the room and the roster names nine, eight of them having been there at the end of May, and the one who is new is a man in a fleece who has never been in that hall. **Halfway through, the woman of about fifty-five gives the day-count of the register unprompted, both hands about her cup, saying she counted it herself off a calendar and counted it twice, and the man in his forties says nobody's going to check that and the man in his sixties says it is a lamp.** Four answers are still going round that table, four of them since the twelfth of January, none of them addable, none of them added to or taken off, and the woman who works in a shop gives the count for the third time in three different weeks. The question is a question for a third time in a third wording, put by the newcomer: whether anybody in that room has ever been asked to do a thing for nothing and turned it down. **It goes nowhere: the man in his forties lays his hands flat on the boards and says the thing is a question and is going to remain one, and the man in a fleece accepts that, and nobody at that table carries it further.** Near the end the man in his thirties raises a gutter on that parade that has come away from the kerb outside the fish shop, and the woman who works in a shop puts a puddle and a bin of hers into it, and the room does not take either up, and the room empties later than it did in May, the case is locked at about twenty past nine, the chairs go up one at a time by whoever is nearest, and a light on the door side was on throughout and nobody in that hall can say which of the two lamps he turned on. **Nobody answered anything.** Nine people went out at ten o'clock into a street that had gone hard, and the case behind them was locked.

## Volume 05, Continuation 0015 — Chapters 335–344

- **0335 — A Warm Wall. Sunday 9 July 2017, morning into afternoon, a block of four storeys off a parade, and a street three streets off it.** The sixth thing the building did was heat and it was not water: since about the first of July the wall behind the room at the end of that corridor on the first floor has been warm to the back of the hand, standing about as broad as she is and running up past where she can reach, there through the daylight and gone by four in the morning, and it is the wall she shares with a house behind that has a kitchen at the back of it. **Nobody has set foot on that roof since the middle of June, nobody means to in July, and nobody has put a question to her about any of it.** Her own answers were to shove the bed two foot along that wall, which carried the bulb on its flex off the middle of the mattress and over the edge of it, to have the window open from about eight until about nine with a plastic chair under it for her feet, and to stand a bowl of cold water on the floor on each of three days over twenty-eight degrees. The damp strip at the end wall has not got bigger and the mark on that ceiling is exactly the size it was. The neighbour came out once, put an observation about the back of that wall to her, was told she was right, and set it on the kitchen at number thirty-one; **she got two words back and gave nothing further, and her own door went back where it always stands.** Three streets off, on the Thursday of the same week, the man in his forties lifted a bollard out of a road that a woman with a bag had caught her ankle on the day before, dug a foot deeper than the hole that came out of the tarmac, bedded it on rubble and dry fixings, set it plumb off the kerb, filled and trowelled, in about an hour, and none of the four houses within thirty yards is told. A man who is not on anything watched him for about four minutes, asked whether the job was for somebody, was told no, and went on. **The two are four hundred yard apart with a parade between them and no living person knows about both.**
- **0336 — A Set Taken Off a Wall. Thursday 13 July 2017, morning into afternoon, a yard behind a shop on a parade, a lane two streets off it, and that shop.** A wireless in a brown bakelite case the size of a tea tray, with a fabric speaker cloth, a dial glass that is not scratched and a crack in the top left corner under tape gone the colour of weak tea, stood against a store wall in a yard about twelve foot across behind the third of nine shops from the last week of May, and it works. **The man in his thirties saw it on the fifth of July, over about six minutes spent on a cold feed bracket that wanted nothing, and did not touch it. He came back for it a week later with a bag, told nobody, and carried it about two mile on foot, on the ground that anything sitting in a van looks like a man who has stopped for a reason and will be asked for it.** He slowed outside the shop where the woman works, stood on the step about a minute, and said four sentences, **three of which were about the crack and not one of them was about where the set had been standing.** She put it on a back-room shelf on a bit of newspaper and said it is not for sale, not in the window, not going to the shop and not going to the man, and that anybody who comes for it is welcome to it, and that she is not going to be the woman with somebody's wireless in a shop. **She went into that yard nine times in seven weeks, saw the set properly once, said nothing to a living soul, and was not in that yard on the day it came out of it — and she is the only person in this borough who knows both places, and nobody puts those two things together.** The aerial is not on it, the old set inside it is for a bin at the back of that shop, and nobody there keeps a note of that either.
- **0337 — Two Questions About a Clock. Sunday 16 July 2017, morning into afternoon, a hall on Carrow Lane, a shop off a parade, and a hardware shop at the top of the Cleeve road.** The man in his sixties says in the hall on a meter that a clock has come off the bracket it stood on over a shop that shut in March, that he looked at both clocks on that stretch and this is the one that is off, that he saw nobody take it and was not there on the Friday morning, that the man now in that shop is not the man the clock was fitted for, and that nobody ever told that man what was over his door. The man in his forties does not write it down. **He carries the sentence into the shop where the woman works in six sentences of his own, and when she will not have it on the end of the others he gives her the reason: that room has four things in front of it and not two of them sit beside one another, he cannot say in an afternoon what those four come to, and he has done nothing with any of them and would do nothing with this one even if it stood by itself — and that is not a rule, because there is nothing to have a rule about.** At about half past three, in a hardware shop at the top of the Cleeve road, the woman tells the man who works nights, because the man in his forties is buying screws at the front of that building and has heard none of it. **He puts two questions and neither is answered: which clock, of which there are two and about which nobody was asked a second time; and whether it had been right while it hung there — which could not be answered by anybody who wanted it answered, because a clock taken off a bracket by nobody on a day when nobody was working leaves behind no record of its own accuracy, the man who set it has been dead thirty years, the man who sold it is dead before that, and the bracket is on a building that has never been anybody's job.** She starts to ask what she is meant to tell him and is told to tell him nothing and go home. **No fifth of anything is produced, the third answer is not corrected, the fourth is not called a fifth, and nobody is told which day any collection comes on.**
- **0338 — A Shutter Down, and a Gate Hung Wrong. Friday 21 July 2017, morning into afternoon, a parade, a yard at the top of a street, and that parade.** The fish shop, second from the top of that parade, is shut with the bar across and the padlock on and no light inside it at about a quarter past nine on a Friday morning. **The man in a fleece goes past with a paper and does not stop, gets a bus, and does not think about it again until ten to twelve, when it is open, the bar is back on its brackets, and the man behind the counter says good morning the way a man says it to somebody who goes past every morning of his life.** The man who puts shutters up carries his ladder past it and does not stop, and nobody asks the man in the fish shop anything and he has not said. At about one, in a yard off the second house on the left as you go up a street off the top of Marsh Lane, the man in his thirties cannot get to his sink for four minutes, because the side gate has been hung on the wrong side and shuts against the brick about a foot above the ground, with a piece of card and a bright screw in the top hanger and the ground under the hinge post dug and filled in again inside a fortnight and not settled. **A woman at the fourth house on that side has been parking in that yard through the whole of the first week of July, and he has not asked her and will not.** He does his job, has to pull the gate to get out, says nothing to anybody and has not been up that street since. **The only person told both is the woman who works in a shop, and she is in neither place: the man with the ladder told her at about ten, the man in his thirties told her at about half past four, and she put the two of them nowhere, and it is not a thing anybody has tried, because a shopkeeper closing for a morning is a thing that happens to a shopkeeper and a gate hung on the wrong side is a thing that happens to a gate; what joins the two reports is a person who heard both.**
- **0339 — Three Letters Off a Sign. Monday 24 July 2017, morning into midday, the low end of Cleeve Street.** A shop that shuts at about half past three carries its name in cut letters about four inches high on fourteen foot of pressed aluminium, **and three of those letters came out of their fixings in the second week of June. Two were found — one on a flat roof and one in a gutter — and the third has never been found. There are three holes the size of a pencil, and the rings the fixings sat in are still round them, and rain comes in by them and reaches the counter a little way back from the front of it, and a plastic bucket has been standing on that counter under the middle of the three since that same week, going into the sink several times a day, and it is not kept on the floor because of what happens to a bucket on that floor.** In the second week of June, at that door, the man in his thirties said he would have those three letters made and put back before the end of that month. Four people heard him. **It is the twenty-fourth of July. On the Monday morning he says it a third time at half past nine, unasked, before anybody has asked him anything, and hears himself do it, and the woman who runs that shop tells him the bucket has been standing there since the week he said it, and he says that was the third time and she can count them; then at a quarter to twelve he says it a fourth time to a woman with a clipboard.** The woman with a clipboard stops under that sign because three letters out of a run of fourteen is what she stops under, and a run where nine of the fourteen are complete is what she is looking at, **and he says it to her before she has said anything.** She has heard it from two other men and not from him — a man in a fleece at the shelter at the top end about three weeks ago, and the man who does that hall on Carrow Lane, who put the same of it to a man in his forties back in June, and neither of them gave a name. **What has gone round that borough is that a sign is going to get done, and what he said is that three letters are going to be made, and those are two different facts, one of them is worth a good deal more to that shop than the other, and neither of them will ever know which is which.** She writes nothing, says she has about two lines of room left and is going to use both on a stand and a grating, and says that a man in this town saying he will do a thing in the road is a thing that happened in the road. **His pad is in his bag and he never opens it on that street, which is not what he did at 0331.**
- **0340 — A Bed Base, and a Table. Sunday 30 July 2017, and the Thursday of the sixth of July, a building by the water, and a shop off a parade.** The man with a van is not the man in his thirties. He emptied a house on the Cleeve road in May, came up that outside stair twice in June, got a refusal at that door in about a second on the thirtieth of June and has said nothing about it since. **First, the sixth of July: a folded metal bed base with a foam mattress rolled and strapped to it, with paint on one face and bare metal on the other, the webbing tight enough to mark the foam, taking the whole step from the door frame across to the rail. She opens the door with her coat on, looks at the thing and not at him, and says no. He does not ask her why and says nothing at all, and the four or five seconds in which she said it and he took hold of the straps again carry nothing out of either of them.** It went back down the steps in three loads and left with the rest of that job in the third week, and nothing in this borough can follow it from here. **Second, the thirtieth: a folding table about three foot by two foot with a tiled top, one stiff leg, and a cup mark on the frame where somebody put a cup down on it. She says one word — inside — and he puts it on the floor a foot inside the door and goes.** She uses it once: she has it standing at the foot of the bed for the better part of a morning, and takes the blanket off the foot of that bed, the one that has lain folded in three there since the winter and is there against a draught off that landing door, and beats it with a brush on the sill, and about nine days of grey come out of the middle of it, and with the window open the dust comes off it in one slow wave, and she stops several times to put a hand behind her ears. Then she folds the blanket in three, puts it back, and stands the table on edge against that wall below the window, a foot or so from the carpet which is on its side along the same wall, **and nothing is on it and it is not a place for anything.** At about half past four that afternoon she has him at her counter for four minutes; he will not say what the two things were, **and gives the reason: if he did, she would go up and stand outside that door and be a person he had put a thing in front of, and neither of them wanted that.**
- **0341 — A Torch With His Own Name On It. Wednesday 2 August 2017, morning into early afternoon, a kitchen at the back of a parade, and a first-floor corridor in a building by the water.** He bought it in June, two pounds, off a man selling old electrical things off a trestle at a market four miles off, **and his own name is cut into the underside of the case in a nail, three letters and a stroke, in a rectangle where somebody else's had been, and it is not coming off.** It lives upside down on a folded tea towel on a shelf by the door, and its bulb has been a yellow one and not a white one since the middle of July. **It goes round that kitchen all morning and nobody in it asks him one question about it: the man who cooks in it takes it and hands it back with the lens still warm, a woman who eats there twice a week carries it into the cold room and puts it back with the switch on, he says out loud at the table what such a thing costs and where a boy of that age would get one, and the woman beside him says the figure is about right, and neither of them is talking to the lad, and then it stands up on that fridge, switched on, from about nine until about half past twelve.** At ten past twelve the man who cooks in it tells him to take it out of his kitchen and says that if it is on that fridge in a fortnight it goes in the bin and he will not be the one who has told him twice. He carries it and a bucket up to a first-floor corridor in a building by the water, where it lights about nine foot in a yellow, and he goes the length of the mop as he goes it every time, over a floor that has needed nothing since before Christmas, because he has never worked out how anybody else would know that. The woman of about fifty-five comes out with a jug in each hand. She says that is a lamp. He says it is a torch, he got it at a market in June for two pounds and there is his name scratched on the bottom in a nail. **She asks whether it lights. He says it lights about nine foot and the bulb is going. She says right, and goes down the stair, and says nothing whatever about a market four miles off, does not ask him where he got it, and does nothing at all with anything he said.** At about ten past two the woman of about forty-two comes through that kitchen on her way to her own hall, says the light in that hall has gone and she is not getting on a ladder, \*\*and he gives her the torch without a word\*\*, and it came back at about a quarter past two, saying what it had done for her and what her own hall wanted instead. The bulb in that hall still needs buying rather than borrowing.
- **0342 — A Railing, and a Page With One Thing On It. Monday 7 August 2017, morning into late afternoon, a passage between two buildings off a parade, that parade, and a van in a lane.** Five foot of wall-mounted iron railing down one side of that passage has turned a bolt right out and pulled away from the brick, and is hanging by the other one with the bars pointing down, its lowest part about five foot off the ground. **A traffic cone has been standing on the footway under it since Saturday afternoon with a bit of cardboard under the base, and the man on that parade would put money on having put it there himself, and has not told anybody, and has not been asked.** The footway is five foot wide and about thirty people go through that passage a day in August, and every one of them has looked up, and not one has mentioned it to the next person through. **The man in his forties goes under it at about eight, about ten past nine and about one, and has gone under it since the last week of March; he looked up the first two times, said nothing to himself on the third, and has not looked up since. He could have gone into that shop and put it to the woman on the counter; she does not know the wall is there and would say it is not hers, and then ownership would have to be run to ground, and no answer waiting at the end of that is better than ducking.** The woman who works in a shop looks down that passage from her own step at about ten, and he does not report it and she does not tell him to, and she has had two letters off that street, one about a hedge and one about a street light, and both of those asked the same question, which is why has it not been done, and what came back in both cases was a slip with a date and a figure on it and nothing else, and that slip is the only answer she has ever had to anything she has sent anywhere. **At about half past four he takes the pad out of its box in the van to look for a length of four by two, and on a sheet he opened in June, wrote on once and never went near again, there is one thing: a lane name in pencil on the second ruled line down, with nothing at the end of the line and nothing above it.** He knows that lane, has driven down it twice, and there is a man at the far end of it with pallets stacked up, a van, and a dog that barks at passing traffic. He has never been into that yard and never spoken to that man, and he has no idea what job the note referred to or whether it ever referred to a job at all, and there is nothing to find out with, because a sheet of a pad carried in a van carries no day on it, and if he writes on that page again the thing on it now will be lying under about nine more lines in about four months and nothing to separate one from another.
- **0343 — I'd Rather You Didn't. Friday 11 August 2017, morning into afternoon, a street off the Cleeve road, a shop off a parade, and that street.** Six corrugated sheets are propped against the side wall of the last house on that street, put up in the second week of July, at the time the roof came off an outbuilding at the foot of it, with a foot of grass up about the bottom two. **The footway is six foot wide, of which they take two foot, and the only thing ever said out loud about them is that they are a hazard to anybody carrying a bag. The man at the end of that street has lived there nine years and is on nothing.** A man in a fleece says so on his own front step at about ten, says he is not telling him what to do about it, and goes on down the street. The man in his forties comes up at about ten past ten and is given the same account by a man holding a paper, **and the man at the end of the street says to him, as he gets level with him, I'd rather you didn't.** The man in his forties walks ten foot, comes back, asks didn't what, is told move them, and the door shuts, and no reason is given and none is asked for. **He is in that street four times that day and goes past those sheets on the road side every time, and a man buttonholed in the middle of a street can either do the thing or say in so many words that he is not doing it, and the second is not a brush-off when a man says it straight, and he said it straight, and it took about nine seconds.** At about a quarter past one the man is in the shop where the woman works, with a length of batten in his hand he has not been in to buy, and uses the identical six words on her, and what comes back to her first, and has sat there since, is that a man was telling her to keep it out of her window — **which is not a misreading of six words and is not the reading he gave them.** He says he will not say what to, that that is the whole of it, that he had used the same six words on the other man in that road that morning and that man was welcome to them as much as she was, and that he is not going to tell her which of the two he had said more to. **A woman went out into the road twice with a bag hooked over her wrist, around the middle of the day and again in the early afternoon and said nothing to anybody either time, and he was on his step watching her both times. At about half past four in the afternoon the man in his forties came past the other way and a man in a fleece asked whether he was doing anything about the sheets, and he said he had not been asked to do anything about the sheets, and that was the whole of what the man in a fleece wanted to know.** Nobody was told what the man meant, nobody is going to be, and it will not come round again.
- **0344 — A Wednesday in August. Wednesday 16 August 2017, early morning into late afternoon, a parade, a building by the water, a hall on Carrow Lane, and about four hundred yard of street.** **THE BOROUGH IS ORDINARY AND THE CHAPTER IS NOT A CLOSE.** Warm at ten to six, cloud off the water at about half past nine with no rain in it. **A van is brought up that parade in the small hours and parked half on the footway, and it is still there when the man who puts shutters up turns up with his ladder about a quarter past six, and he cannot get a ladder up against the second shutter with it there, so he does the third and the fourth and comes back at about half past eight and does the second off the tail of the thing, and the van drives off at about ten past nine and nobody gets out of it.** A man with a sack over his shoulder stands about two minutes outside a shop that shuts early and carries on up the parade with it still on his shoulder. Over three shops there is a flat, and the woman who works in a shop has its key; she goes up an outside stair and down again, and the man in a fleece is at the stop on the other side of the road at the same time, and neither looks over. **Four lengths of treated batten are put down in the middle of a yard off that parade, nine foot from where that yard keeps them, by a man with a barrow who goes off up the road without saying where he is going, and the man in his forties leaves them a minute and then carries them across himself, one at a time.** The woman of about fifty-five goes down that outside stair carrying two empty jugs with one hooked through the other, and comes up at about ten past ten with both full and a kettle over her other arm, which is the errand she has been up and down that stair twice a day all summer, and nobody offers her anything and she asks nobody for anything. A bus comes at about twenty past ten, stops, goes on, and is not the man who works nights' bus, and he waits half an hour after it. **The woman with a clipboard is on a different sheet from the one she was on in July, with about two lines of room left, and uses one on a stand and does not use the other.** The man from the parade is in a doorway eating out of a paper bag and a stranger says good afternoon. A woman comes into the Carrow Lane hall a little after two to ask whether it is open, reads a newspaper for an hour and goes. **The four, in a daytime hall with two men in it: the man in his sixties asks how many there are of those now; the man in his forties says four without stopping what he is doing with a cloth; the man in his sixties says he would have said five; and the man in his forties says there are four and there have been four since January, that he has not added anything and has not taken anything off, and that the man in his sixties has not been in this borough long enough to have been here in January and neither has anybody who was not in that room in January. The man in his sixties takes that as fair and goes for more tea. The four is still four.** **The question, on a corner, at about a quarter past four, asked once: that nobody in this town has ever counted anything, and whether anybody had ever told him why it is four. He says no. The man in a fleece says right and goes on down the parade. Nobody answers anything.** **The register, at about half past four: he lets himself into the building by the water and opens the bay at the end of the first-floor corridor, a door that does not shut over its catch. The book lies open at the last of its nineteen entries, and that last one is a yard lamp, written in as gone about two years back, under a heading reserved for that sort of thing, and there is nothing under that reserved heading. Past it the page goes on for the width of two fingers, gives up well short of the bottom edge, and nobody closed that gap. He holds the page flat, does the count in his head the way a man does a count he has done before, and the figure is nine hundred and ninety-four days, and there is nothing at all on the line beneath it. He writes nothing, shuts the door of that bay, goes back down the outside stair, leaves the street door on the latch, and goes up the parade.**

**EVERY FIGURE IN THE BLOCK ABOVE IS TO BE RE-MEASURED FROM THE CHAPTERS AND NOT CARRIED FORWARD FROM THIS FILE. NO CHAPTER'S OWN ALL-CAPS SENTENCE APPEARS IN ANY ENTRY ABOVE, AND NONE OF THESE ENTRIES IS A TRANSCRIPTION OF WHAT ITS CHAPTER PRINTED. **THE TEN ENTRIES IN THIS SECTION WERE REWRITTEN FROM NOTHING AFTER A MEASURING PASS FOUND THIRTY-TWO SPANS OF THIRTEEN TOKENS AND ABOVE BETWEEN THESE ENTRIES AND THE CHAPTERS THEY DESCRIBE, EVERY ONE OF THEM A SENTENCE THE CHAPTER HAD PRINTED AND THIS FILE HAD COPIED, AND THE CHAPTERS WERE NOT TOUCHED ONCE. A CARD, A DATE, A DAY-COUNT, A FIGURE, A MAJOR TURN, A STANDING AND A FLAG WERE NOT TOUCHED BY ANY REPAIR, AND THE 0344 ENTRY NOW CARRIES THE HOURS THE CHAPTER ACTUALLY PRINTS RATHER THAN THE HOURS IT PRINTED BEFORE THE REVIEW REPAIR. CARD 0334 IS NOT A CLOSE AND CARD 0344 IS NOT A CLOSE.**






## Volume 05, Continuation 0016 — Chapters 345–354

- **0345 — Four in the Morning. Thursday 17 August 2017, early morning into mid-afternoon, a first-floor corridor in a block by the water, and a flat above three shops off a parade.** A seventh thing happens to that building and it is a smell of gas that nobody has been able to place. The woman at the end of that corridor has done her own looking and found nothing, and on two nights in August she slept on a plastic chair out on the landing because she could not settle, and told nobody. The neighbour next door said what she thought it was and was told she was right, and went back inside. **The man in his forties came up with a bag, was given the same account, gave an account of his own that is also true, said the vent would be the last thing he would look at, and stopped talking when he heard that the neighbour had got there first, and he has not been near that building since. Neither woman is ever going to be told which of them was nearer the mark.** A mile and a half away a shopkeeper counted a day of takings on her own kitchen table, put the figure on the back of her own hand, and locked the money in a safe of her own under her own counter. It was an ordinary Thursday figure. Nobody in that shop knows it, nobody has asked, and there is nobody in this borough she would tell. Neither woman knows the other one is on the page.

- **0346 — The Last Man to Have It. Sunday 20 August 2017, late morning into afternoon, a yard off the Cleeve road, a shop off a parade, and a car park.** A step ladder and a spanner move four times between a yard nobody has the use of and a shop's back room, and two men each end up certain the other never touched it. **The first man took the spanner out of the shop and put it in his pocket without deciding to, and has told nobody he took anything out of that shop. The second man took the ladder itself while the shopkeeper was at the rack, and she saw him go through and has not asked him a single question about it, then or since.** The shopkeeper has one version of where the ladder came from and has not said it out loud to anybody including herself, because she does not know either. Neither man will ask the other, and each is certain on the strength of his own week rather than the other's. The spanner is in a pocket in a van and has never been a question to anybody.

- **0347 — Nobody's in That House. Wednesday 23 August 2017, morning into evening, a hall on a meter, a shop off a parade, and the top of a lane.** A man tells a hall that a house has been emptied, and the only person listening carries it out of that room as a fact and puts it to a man coming off a shift, and puts the place a few hundred yard out of where it belongs. **She is not interested in that lane except as a thing worth repeating, she has never set foot in it, and she does not know she has it wrong. He does not correct her and is not going to ask which road, because asking would have told her he could not say himself, and he had a lock-up that Friday either way.** He used that lane for three years and never told anybody, and after she said it he has gone the long way round off every shift for about five weeks and cannot give anybody one reason for it. The house is not empty, the woman is still in it, and nobody is going to climb that lane to establish it. The man in his sixties still believes he passed on the news of a house that got emptied, and there is nothing he can do about it.

- **0348 — A Week in the Middle. Sunday 27 August 2017, morning into late afternoon, a parade, a shop with a shutter, and a house in a street off a lane.** A shopter shuts her own shop for her lunch with the light on and a queue at the machine, and about thirty people go past and nine of them look and not one of them says anything to anybody. A man in a fleece sees all of it on his way to a bus. **On the Friday a tradesman is told at a door that the work can wait until two, and he does not go at two; he spends about six hours of that day in a car park on a paper and a bottle of water he brought for it, does twenty minutes of the job, and goes home.** One shopkeeper is given both of those things inside a week. She has never spoken to that man and could not tell you his name, and did not connect the two of them when he told her his own day was lost, because a shopkeeper taking a lunch is not the same sort of thing as a man losing a day to somebody else's appointment. Nothing that happened on that parade that week went anywhere afterwards.

- **0349 — A Bird Box on a Path. Wednesday 30 August 2017, morning into afternoon, the low end of a street off the Cleeve road, a shop off a parade, and that street again.** A man says for the fifth time that he will have a box made and put up on a gable end before September is out, and he says it to a man who has not asked him for anything, with his pad in his hand and nothing written on it. **The consequence is not a word. Two other men have been telling each other that the wall on that corner is going to be seen to, and the one who put those two together came with a ladder on the Tuesday, took the existing box off its screws, and laid it face down on the path.** He came back on the Wednesday to do four foot of pointing that is not his job, has charged nobody, and has told nobody, and he is not going to put the box back, because putting it back would be accepting the work. The man who made the promise found the box lying there and said nothing else at all, and has not corrected himself to anybody. The woman in that house has stepped over it and moved it with her foot and asked nobody about it. A shopkeeper heard the whole of it in order and said it would still be there on Saturday.

- **0350 — Two Doors. Monday 4 September 2017, morning into afternoon, a block by the water, a street off the Cleeve road, and a shop off a parade.** A man with a van takes a sewing machine up nine treads, tells her what it is and where it came from, and is refused in one word. He asks nothing, says nothing, carries it down again, and has not been up that stair since. **She has told nobody a thing was put on that step, and there is nobody in that block she could tell.** Three days later he leaves a chair against a completely different door because his van was full, and the woman there carries it indoors herself and puts it in a gap that has been waiting for a chair since June, and has not mentioned it to a living soul. Nobody on that street raised it. A tradesman working next door all day did not know it was there and has not been asked. **The man with the van told a shopkeeper about the machine on the Monday, at a counter, for five minutes, and said nothing whatever about the chair, and nobody in that shop or on that parade has any idea a chair went there.** A record exists eight miles off in a garage, in one line against a list, and not one living soul in this borough has ever set eyes on it.

- **0351 — The Bulb Goes. Sunday 10 September 2017, morning into late afternoon, a kitchen at the back of a parade, a first-floor corridor in a block by the water, and a low wall by a bus shelter.** A ceiling bulb goes in a kitchen where the fitting and the bulb that has been bought for it have not matched since the middle of July, and nobody says the word for which cap it takes, and the talk about it takes a minute. **The lad who washes up there knew a fortnight before that it was going and has said nothing to anybody, and nobody in that kitchen has ever asked him anything.** He goes up the hill afterwards, takes a torch out of his bag, and puts it back in it. A woman with a jug in each hand asks him one question in a corridor and uses nothing he tells her. Later he leaves the torch lying on a low wall at a bus stop and walks away from it with no note on it. The woman with the key to the hall is at that stop after he has gone, sees it from about nine foot, and does not pick it up, because there was a bus coming and no version of that ends well. The torch is still on that wall and the kitchen is still lit by a lamp on a table.

- **0352 — Nine Coats. Thursday 14 September 2017, morning into afternoon, a first-floor corridor in a block off the top of a street, and a shop off a parade.** A tradesman goes into a flat above a corridor to put up a shelf, braces himself on a sash window rail, and finds that the window does not move at all. He levers it up with a knife and the paint breaks, and there is a thin drab green under an off-white coat that matches the doors on that landing, and it crosses the join between the two halves, which dates the painting of the window shut to before those doors were done and to somebody who did not live there. **He puts the wedge back where he found it, does the shelf, and does not knock on the door next along.** Nobody in that block will find out who shut it, the block has not been anybody's job for months, and no paper about that window exists anywhere in this borough. A mile away the shopkeeper on the other side of that has written the same time of day at the bottom of two shopping lists a fortnight apart, under the apples, where it is not a price and not a delivery and not an opening time, and cannot tell you why, and has not thrown the first sheet out. The tradesman bought board at her counter that afternoon. Neither of them said anything to the other about either thing.

- **0353 — Nobody Has Ever Made a List of It. Wednesday 20 September 2017, morning into night, a hall on a meter, a shop off a parade, and that hall again.** A woman of about fifty-five says an eight-word sentence to a tradesman whose work notes are in a bag at his feet while he wipes a table, and he says no and carries on and does not open the pad. Four days later she says the same sentence to a man in a fleece at a bus stop, and he tells her at length that nothing about that building is written down anywhere. **She has not the least idea which of the two men she meant, and those two men have not shared a room anywhere in this account before or after, apart from that hall on the Wednesday evening, twenty minutes by the urn, four feet apart, and neither of them ever said a word to the other about it.** The only thing either of them said to the other was that the tea had gone cold again. A man at the end of a street put his own weekend to that table and nobody put anything to it, and it was not a question. Not one of the eight in that room said a word that night about a sentence said twice in a week by somebody who was not in it, and nobody is going to ask her.

- **0354 — The Twenty-Fourth. Sunday 24 September 2017, morning into night, a parade, a shop with a shutter, the low end of a street, a hall on a meter, and a first-floor corridor in a block by the water.** A shopkeeper says a number at her counter and the man in his forties does not answer it, and it has been said about nine times over since the twelfth of January, and the number has not moved, and neither of them can name two of what it counts. A man coming off nights asks what the fourth one is before he has asked for anything, is told he could not be told that in that shop, and is not asked again. **A shopkeeper and the woman of about fifty-five are in a hall together for twenty minutes and do not speak, and one of them has said since that she did not see the other, and the other has not said either way.** In the evening the man in his forties lets himself into a building by the water, stands a couple of minutes short of the far end of that corridor, does not go into the bay, and goes home. A woman of about fifty-five does the count she has been doing since before the summer, sitting on a stair, and it comes to a thousand and thirty-three. **The line under the last entry in the book in that bay is the one fixed thing in that building, it is blank, and it was not touched today, and the book was not opened at all.** She wrote nothing and told nobody and went down for her water. A month went through this borough and the month is a month, and no fifth of anything came of it and no fourth answer was called a fifth.
