## Volume 05, Continuation 0017 — Chapters 355–364

- **0355 — Half an Hour Each. Monday 25 September 2017, morning into mid-afternoon, a shop off a parade and the back room of it.** A shopkeeper named a fault in her own stock room to a tradesman in August, in passing, and he looked at it through a doorway for about a second and said nothing back at all, and she took that for an answer, and he was never in there again. She dealt with it herself on a Sunday in August with the shop shut, alone, in about half an hour, with packing she cut herself out of a piece of oak that was standing in that room, and said nothing to anybody. He dealt with a dropping fire door in a yard on a Sunday in September, alone, in about half an hour, and said nothing to anybody. **Nobody knows what the other's half hour was worth and neither of them ever will, and there is a cancellation available in the air between them that would settle it in one sentence, and a settlement would be an arrangement, and there is no arrangement in this borough to make one in.** On the Monday they traded ordinary things across a counter for an hour and got within one exchange of saying both of them out loud, and the exchange went past it.

- **0356 — Four Feet of Stud. Thursday 28 September 2017, morning into late afternoon, a first-floor room at the top of a street.** A man doing half an hour's work in that building stopped on his way out because of something another man had made in June, and put his bag down on a bench and looked at it properly. **He is the sort of man who can find what is wrong with another man's work in about four minutes and has never before failed to, and he went through the whole list twice and had nothing, and what is left on that wall is a gap between the two boards and a set-back at both ends, which is either a working habit or an accident, and he cannot tell from the floor of that room, and it is not a fault, and he kept the question to himself because he is a stranger in that room and has no standing in it to ask a question.** He went downstairs and has not been back. The man whose work it is came up at the end of the afternoon, stood in the middle of the room, and did not look downwards because a man standing in a room does not, and nobody has told him that anyone was ever interested.

- **0357 — The One on the Step. Monday 2 October 2017, early afternoon into evening, a street off the Cleeve road and a passage at the top of a street.** A hammer with its maker's name taped over lay on a doorstep from Saturday to Monday because the man working in that house went out without it and has not thought about it since. **A woman waiting ten doors away picked it up because it was in her way and put it back; the man who came along picked it up, nearly undid the tape with his thumbnail, thought better of it, carried it back down the street, held it out to her, and she looked at it and did not reach for it, and he put it in his bag.** Both of them now believe it is theirs, each for a reason that has nothing to do with the other, and neither will say so, because one of them saying it would be giving it back and the other saying it would be claiming it. A third man watched the entire business from a chair he carried out into his own doorway for the sunshine and would resolve it in a single sentence if anybody asked him, and nobody is going to, and it is on a shelf in a workshop now, handle out, tape still on, not his.

- **0358 — Which Way It Opens. Thursday 5 October 2017, early morning, a parade, a passage and a shop.** A man walked a routine he has walked for years and, at one moment in it, pushed a door that had always gone away from him and had it come towards him instead. **He had been putting his hand on that door about nine times since he was twenty-seven and could have told you which way it went every time, and now he cannot, and there is no way of establishing it from where he was standing at ten past six in the morning with a ladder on his shoulder.** He stood still in the dark looking at the light for a while, went back and finished his round, cut a length of tape off a ledge without slowing down, and has not been to that end of that passage since. He has told nobody, and there is no mark on the door that would tell anybody else.

- **0359 — Somebody Says. Tuesday 10 October 2017 and the Saturday after, a shop off a parade and a market four miles off.** A man coming off nights put a rumour into a shopkeeper's ear and it arrived with a place on it and nothing else, three removes deep and finished by a woman who sells flowers two days a week. **Nobody in the chain had a name or knew what the man was supposed to have been doing, and so nothing could be checked, and she carried it out of that shop in a shorter form and stopped mid-sentence because there was nothing after it, and she has not been right since.** The man she carried it to went up that market on the Saturday, stood about in the middle of it for twenty minutes in a crowd, refused his usual stall twice and bought nothing, and the stallholder has since decided he is not somebody to offer things to. Two lives have been altered by seven words with nothing in them and neither man will ever know the other one is part of the same thing.

- **0360 — Two Screws. Saturday 14 October 2017, late on the Friday night before into afternoon, an outside stair at the back of a house in a street off the Cleeve road.** A handrail in a house cut into four flats had come away from a wall by two inches in August, and that landing has never had a light on it at all and its four residents come up in the dark, and the man whose door is at the end of that landing is the one who put the original screws in and is the one who knew what would hold. **He did it alone, in the dark, at half past ten on a Friday, and there is no book in that house and a landlord nobody believes in, and he told nobody then and has told nobody since.** On the Saturday a woman who has never put a hand on a handrail in her life put one on it because a man was coming the other way, found it solid, and went on up to a door. Going past his own door later she said the rail was sound, and he had about two seconds in which to hand the whole thing over, and he asked her a question about somebody's mother instead. He has begun a sum he did not decide to start, and it is a sum about how long ago a thing is, and it will not come out at zero.

- **0361 — Two Figures on a Slate. Friday 20 October 2017, morning into afternoon, a yard behind two houses and a shop off a parade.** Four hundred and seventy-odd slabs of paving were delivered to a yard in nine loads and sixteen of them came off the truck loose, never banded and carrying no tag, and those sixteen are the whole of the difference between the two numbers. **Two men counted the heap, properly, in two different ways, and got two different numbers, and both of them are right, because that yard's own pallet boards get reused and about a quarter of what is in it is wearing a number that belongs to some other load in some other town.** They compared them once, in the middle of the yard, and got as far as a point and a reply, and then neither of them said the sentence that would have finished it. They went back to work. The two numbers are on a slate on that wall, one above the other, in two hands, and it is the only record of that count in this borough and it expresses no preference.

- **0362 — One Tile. Monday 23 October 2017, morning into afternoon, an archway at the top of a street and a shop off a parade.** A man carried a bag of floor offcuts through a covered way and stopped and put one of them on the stone shelf along the wall, squared it, looked at it and went to work, and nothing else about it was done or said. **The one man in this county who would recognise that tile goes through that archway twice a day, and the man who put it there stood on the far pavement and watched him go through, and did it again four days later and watched again, and has not been near that street since except once to walk past the outside of it.** The tile is still on the shelf with rain on it, and nobody in that street knows it is there, and the man who would know is not going to be asked why he put it there, because that question has only one answer and he is not giving it.

- **0363 — At About Nine. Saturday 28 October 2017, morning into afternoon, a hall at the top of a street and a shop off a parade.** A meeting on Wednesday the twenty-fifth of October let out, one man stayed to stack the chairs, found a door open that should not have been, closed it, chained it, locked up and went home, and there is no clock anywhere on that route and he did not look at one, so the only part of the bookkeeper's sentence that is wrong is the hour. Three days later the man who keeps the hall wrote in his book that the premises had been found open at nine o'clock, which is the hour his round takes and the hour his book always says. **The man who was actually there is the only person alive who could put a different time on that sentence and he is never going to, because a correction goes in the book and a man who puts himself in that book is a man who admits he was somewhere he had no business being.** He has never opened the book, only learned of it three weeks ago from a woman pleased that the place is written down, and has no way of being careful about a thing he does not know exists.

- **0364 — The Chair on the Other Side. Tuesday 31 October 2017, early morning into evening, a parade, a hall on Carrow Lane, a building by the water and the low end of a street.** Fourteen days of ordinary rounds: a shopkeeper with a pad, a number said at a counter and not answered, a man through an archway three times, a man left waiting for a bus that was not his. **The one thing that is different is a chair in a hall that has changed walls, and the man who puts those chairs up has never had to think about a chair in his life and cannot say when it changed and never will.** In the evening a man went into a building by the water with his own key, went up, stopped short of a landing, did not go into a bay he has not entered since the summer, and worked out in his head that the empty line under the last entry of a book in that bay has been empty for one thousand and seventy days, which is the third time on the page and the first time with the door standing open in front of him. He wrote nothing and went home and the line is blank and the book was not opened.

## Volume 05, Continuation 0018 — Chapters 365–374

- **0365 — A Day and a Half. Wednesday 1 November 2017, early morning into early evening, a house at the end of a row off the Cleeve road and the yard behind it.** A man took a small overhead job for a household and gave them a figure out of his own experience, and the room was not as described to him, and the work took four nights instead of one and a half. She lost the use of her only warm room for the week and has never said what the delay cost him. **A floor-layer half a mile off stood waiting for him on the Tuesday until nearly the middle of the morning, then began, and finished the last of it alone on the Thursday, and the whole of those three days was spent in the back room of that house.** The household then went to a man of their own finding, who took the work out and did it again in a day. He came back a fortnight afterwards for a canvas bag of fixings, could see from the gate that the work in that room was not his, and asked about a socket in another room and went out. Nine sacks of his are still under a tarpaulin in that yard.

- **0366 — A Hearth Set. Saturday 4 November 2017, early morning into mid-afternoon, a first-floor room in a building by the water and the landing outside it.** A set of implements for a fire appeared on the floor of a room with no fire in it and no grate, put there at about ten at night by a man who had nowhere else to put it and used a room that was not his without arranging anything. **Three people on that landing have seen it and all three are waiting for one of the other two to raise it, and none of them ever does, and the man who brought it is one of the three and does not know the other two have looked.** She will not move it out of her way, because moving it is an admission, and she has hung a jug on its rail for want of anywhere else in a small room to hang one. Her neighbour, whose door never shuts properly, saw it from her own doorway and said nothing then or since. Nobody has asked where it came from, and the only man who could say is the man who did it.

- **0367 — Nine Words. Tuesday 7 November 2017, mid-afternoon into evening, a room at the back of a shop off a parade.** A woman closing up put a hand on a jug and said nine words that closed a subject about a man who used to come into that shop on that day and stopped coming in the summer. **The man who does that hall heard a man finished with, which is what she meant, and swallowed a half-formed addition. The man in his sixties heard himself finished with, and had been on nothing for six years, and had never in that time been the subject of anything said aloud in a room.** He is not going to ask, because the only route to asking runs through saying he thinks she was talking about him. He had come in that afternoon with a question of his own about a hall on a Wednesday, wanted to ask it since the summer, and had twice got as far as the back room door and turned round. He went home not knowing anything had been said in that room before he was through the door. Nobody was entered anywhere and nobody was asked anything.

- **0368 — What It Was For. Sunday 12 November 2017, morning into late afternoon, a block of flats at the top of a street and a shop off a parade.** A man laid a hard surface along one side of a block of flats over twelve weekends, in three passes, out of his own wages, without telling anybody he was starting. **Nobody stopped him and nobody asked him, and it is finished, and the whole of that building can see what he laid there, and none of the eight of them has ever been asked what he meant it for.** It has put water under one woman's back step twice a week, which she wipes up and has never once gone out into that yard about it, and it has taken a planted bed out of another woman's sight line, which she asked him to move once. She told the man who does floors about the water with tea in her front room, and he knew who had laid it, and could have given her a name at about the fourth minute, and did not, and will not. **What stopped him was not loyalty: naming the man would make him something he has never been, and he is on nothing at all.**

- **0369 — No Ice. Friday 17 November 2017, mid-morning into early evening, a shop off a parade and a yard about a mile off.** A weekly errand of five months failed on one morning because a loaded lorry blocked a yard and its driver went for his lunch, and the man who had done that errand every week did not divert for another sack, because that is not how it goes. **A man who works nights found the chest down, asked the shopkeeper for an ice, was told there was none, and has not asked her since, and buys half a mile further on where the shop shuts sooner.** The man who was bringing it found out at ten past six in the back way, with a bag of plugs, with the man who works nights still at the other end of the counter, and about ten seconds passed in which one of the other two could have said something, and neither did. She shut the chest and put a cloth on the outside of it and told nobody. On the Saturday he came back with two sacks because a load had come in, and she took one, and the other is in a passage at the back of that shop.

- **0370 — The Barrow. Wednesday 22 November 2017, mid-morning into mid-afternoon, a shop off a parade.** A builder's barrow with a squared front and a tyre new in the summer stood at the back of a shop for twelve days with a price on a card, and the shop had no use for it. **The man in his thirties came into that shop four times in those twelve days, stopped at it properly twice, said nothing to anybody on any of them, and on two other mornings went round the back of that parade rather than go in.** The man in his forties asked the price, tipped it to look at the underneath, said the front end was squared, paid, and then tied it onto a pickup on the pavement in front of the first man walking the length of that parade, who did not turn round and was not looked at. Fourteen days later, on the Wednesday of the sixth of December, the shopkeeper said the barrow had gone on the Wednesday and asked, in a gap, whether he had wanted it. He said no and bought his screws and left. **She does not know he had paused, and is not going to ask, because asking would say out loud that she had been watching him.** They worked the same yard for two hours on the Tuesday of the first week of December and neither mentioned it.

- **0371 — A Hundredweight. Sunday 26 November 2017, early morning into mid-afternoon, a yard off the Cleeve road.** A man has stated the weight of a sack of sand wrongly for nine years and it has cost nobody anything, because he has never lifted one and the material is weighed where it is loaded and priced there. **A bag split on a nail on the Friday a third of the way along and about thirty pounds of that sand went across the apron of a yard and set, and it went back on the stack inside five minutes, and that is the only consequence in the chapter and it is unrelated to the figure.** The woman of about fifty-five came through that gate on the Sunday with two jugs and stopped while a man was on a stack, and heard him say the weight to somebody else, and worked out on the spot that it was wrong, because she bought the same material herself in the summer for a bay of her own front and stood in her own window and could not see how deep it went. She went on to her stop. She said nothing then and has said nothing since, and there is nothing in it worth saying to a man who would answer that sand is sand and go on shovelling it.

- **0372 — A Stone on the Landing. Thursday 30 November 2017, late morning into late evening, a stair in a block of flats and a landing on it.** Two men were moving a piece of an old hearth up a stair for a flat whose tenant had not been in for days, could not turn it on the half-landing, and asked a man in his own doorway with his bag in his hand to take the other end. **He took the weight in both hands, worked it round with them, and was then told the tenant was not in and that they would fetch it back on the Monday, and they went down the stair and did not come back, and he carried the stone back down one flight and left it against the wall of that half-landing opposite his own door.** He cannot return it. There is nothing on it, nothing on either man, and the only address he has is the flat at the top of that block with a door nobody answers, so returning it would mean standing up there holding something he cannot account for, and a man who gives a thing back has admitted it was never his. It is a foot and a half square on a landing four foot three across, it leaves about two foot nine to get past, and it is in the way of his own front door. The woman who works in a shop lives across that landing from him and has gone past it sideways every evening since, and neither of them has raised it. He could have taken it inside and closed his own door on it and did not.

- **0373 — An Ordinary Day. Monday 4 December 2017, early morning into evening, a street at the top of the town, a shop off a parade, and a low wall by a yard gate.** A man lost part of his working day because a house was shut, waited in the cold, and went and did something else instead. **Three people saw him go past that Monday, and none of the three was watching him.** A shopkeeper noticed a purchase made at her counter for years and not made, and thought about her order. A man in his thirties, standing on a pavement with nothing to do, saw a man he does not know take a short flight of steps in two halves and stop, and told nobody and would not. A man in his sixties on a low wall read nothing into a man stopping in a road, and went home and could not have described him. None of the three knew the other two were out. He was paid in cash, ate standing up, bought screws, spent the afternoon in a yard and came home. Nothing happened to him and he has no idea any of it was seen.

- **0374 — What Came in on the Air. Thursday 7 December 2017, early morning into evening, a parade, a shop off it, a hall on a meter and a building by the water.** Fourteen days of ordinary rounds, and the one thing different is a sweet smell that comes into that parade in the mornings and is gone by ten, and a hall on a meter that opens at ten and has not smelled of it once, because by then it was already gone. **Two people can date it closely because they began noticing it later than it arrived, and the one man who has walked that street several times a day for months cannot date it at all, and has stood in the middle of it twice on purpose since the start of the month trying to find out whether it was there earlier, and cannot, because he was there every morning before it and every morning after it.** Three explanations are available in that borough and none of them fits, and nobody has gone to the door. Four answers to the same question were given at one counter in about ten minutes by three people who each had a point, and the four are not comparable, and nobody answered anything. A man went up to a building by the water for about an hour's work and, coming down, stood in a corridor and looked into a recess with an open door in it, and did not go in. **A line under the last of nineteen entries in the book on that shelf has been blank for one thousand one hundred and seven days, and nobody counted anything on that stair.** A fortnight is a fortnight.

## Volume 05, Continuation 0019 — Chapters 375–384 (Friday 8 December 2017 to Saturday 20 January 2018)

- **0375 — A Day's Work, Unasked For.** A tradesman came to a kitchen off the Cleeve road for a joint under a sink and found the front edge of the worktop had gone soft where it sat on the frame. Nobody had asked him to look at it and nobody in the house knew it was like that. The woman of the house was on a shift and the man of the house said one word and left for his own work, and the tradesman did the extra piece on his own with a saw on a table in the yard. He put two tiles back with filler in the joints and did not go over the lines again. Nobody in that house has mentioned the front edge since, and the man who cut it has told nobody he did it, and no one who works alongside him knows. The man of that house still does not know that the front edge of that worktop is not the piece that came with the kitchen.

- **0376 — Something Put Into His Arms.** A man going to a van with a chest under his arm set it down in the crook of a builder's arm on a footway and kept walking at the same pace, and said nothing at all. The builder had one arm full of wire and a box of clips and the other full of coin, and could not have stopped him and did not try. He carried it a hundred yard, put it against a wall, tipped the grit out of one bottom corner, and read what was left of four letters stencilled on the lid without getting far enough to make anything of them. It is in his front room with a lamp on it and a bowl on it, and he has not asked anybody about it and is not going to, because asking would mean standing in a street and saying that somebody handed him something he never asked for. The man who set it down was clearing a house for a woman who is not named here, put it in the space there was, and has not given it a thought since.

- **0377 — An Hour Neither of Them Will Ask About.** Two men in this borough want the same small fact about one shop, which is what time it opens its door, and there are two routes to that answer and neither has been taken. The man in his forties could put it to the woman who works in a shop; the man who works nights could put it to the man in his forties, who answers a question that is not asked directly. She answered it in that room on a Monday, out loud, to a man with a van and to nobody else. One of them took it as a fact about a person and the other took it as a woman being annoyed at the end of a long day, and the hour itself went past both of them. Neither heard the hour, and she has not asked either of them what they took from it, and the answer is still in the room and still available to both of them.

- **0378 — A Landing, Early.** A light on a landing in a block of seven began coming on an hour and a half before it had any business coming on, and three people in that building formed three different accounts of it inside a week. The woman who lives in the first flat put it down to the clock and has not been in the cupboard to look. The man in his thirties, who was up and down that stair all week putting a bath in, put it down to the lamp and has kept his opinion to himself because it is not his building. The man in his sixties, who came up into the light and had it come on under him, put it down to somebody standing on that switch and went up for his tea. The man who had the keys was under that landing four days later with his hand on the wall and looked up at the fitting and went on. Four evenings of that stair have been dark since and the man with the keys has not been back.

- **0379 — One Word at the Kerb.** A man in his thirties had a chest freezer in the back of his pickup that he had bought in October for a job that fell through, and on a morning in late December he offered it once, at the kerb of a shop, to a man in his forties. The man in his forties had come along that street for a roll of tape and did not stop and did not help, and the answer was one word with nothing behind it, and the freezer went back into the pickup and the tailgate came up. Neither of them gave a reason and neither has since. The woman behind that counter kept her back to her own window until the pickup had gone up the street and then found nothing out there to look at, and she has not put it to either of them. He has not put it to a second person either, and that was not a decision he took on the day: after one refusal there is a price on going round a town asking other men.

- **0380 — A Morning and a Counter, an Hour and a Bit Apart.** Two small things failed on one man on one day and he straightened both of them himself and told nobody. His van would not start in a cold street and he turned it over five times in a minute and a bit while a man in his thirties watched from a kerb thirty foot away with a bin, and the man at the kerb did not move and did not offer and did not go and tell anybody. An hour and a bit later, at a counter, a machine would not take a man's card and did the two buzzes three times, and the man in his thirties was eight foot from it facing it and stood through the whole of it, and the man paid in money and the woman at the till said nothing about either failure. The man in his thirties has told neither of them anything and has not put the two together in his own head, and would say that things break.

- **0381 — Six Days on a Landing.** Two men needed the floor of an empty flat and a chest was in the way, so they put it out on the landing and left it there for six days without a word. The two men were there to lift a floor and were paid for that, and not one of the four people on that landing opened a door or asked about a box somebody had shifted out of a flat. It went out in a pickup on the Friday, the sixth day, with nobody asked. The next morning the woman who lives on that landing and the man who works nights stood at opposite ends of it within a few minutes of each other, both of them looking at the mark on the paper, and neither said a word, and neither knows the other was there. The man who took it away has it under a sheet of roofing felt in a yard at the top of the town that a man he used to work for lets him keep things in, does not know whose chest it was, and was in that building ten minutes without knocking on any of the four doors.

- **0382 — Five Words on a Stair.** A man in his sixties said five words in a passage to nobody while a man in his thirties went past him, and he went on thinking about a man he had been with that morning, four streets away. The man in his thirties went up the stair and took the words as being about a man on the floor above him who had told him in December that there would be no more work coming his way, and he took them correctly. The man in his sixties went home that day believing the other one had understood, because somebody answering with nothing is somebody who has understood. He was never told otherwise and is not going to be, and if the two of them had stood in that passage for four seconds the whole thing would have come apart and neither of them would have been the wiser about the other. Both of them have said nothing about it since and both of them will not.

- **0383 — A Wall by the Railway Arch.** A man who has traded out of that yard for longer than the younger man has been in it says a class of wall will not take a screw, and has said it for decades, and the younger man has carried a resin gun up ladders on his account for about a year. On a January afternoon the younger man went down on his knees at that wall to take out a batten he had fixed the hard way, and the screw would not come, and he scraped the resin off and knocked the block and found it is the hardest thing in that yard with a furring batten on it that is what he was fixing into in the first place. The older man was out at the time and the younger man did not say a word to anybody, and there is nothing standing for both of them to stand over, and nobody in that yard could be asked where the belief came from. Everything the older man has fixed on the strength of it is still exactly where it should be, and he will say the same thing next month.

- **0384 — An Ordinary Fortnight.** The same people did the same rounds at the same hours and nothing in the fortnight was different, and nine of them went through it carrying nothing for anybody else. Four answers given at that counter in December are still going round and two men who gave one of them said in a shop that it was still not settled, and neither said which of the four he holds. A hall on a meter was open on the Saturday morning with the urn on and about sixteen people through it, and a man behind the counter that nobody put anything to. A man in his forties did an hour's work on a Thursday, came back down a warm stair, and came back down a warm stair and stopped at the end of a corridor with a door at the end of it that he did not open, and nobody has put a figure against the last line in that book. Nobody put a mark on that page and nobody worked out what it would add up to, and the one man who could have sat down with a pencil and done it did not, and there is nobody in that borough who could tell you what the rule underneath it is for. **CARD 0384 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.**

## VOLUME 05 — CHAPTERS 385–394

- **0385 — What Was Not There.** A man in his forties went back to a yard off a side turning for a tin of grease that had been left on a concrete bench, and it was not there. The man who keeps that yard was thirty foot away with a broom and was not asked and will not be told. What was on the bench instead was a crate of apples, and he carried it across thirty foot of concrete and out of the gate in front of the man who keeps the place, who watched him go and said nothing. He put it in his own van, ate some of them, and left the crate on a kerb of his own street, where it was gone by two o'clock on the fifth of February. He has mentioned neither half of that morning to anybody since, does not mean to, and nobody has gone looking for the tin.

- **0386 — One Question.** A woman who runs a shop off a parade asked a man in his forties, once, whether there is anybody in this town who can look at a bell that has not rung since the middle of December. He thought about it for about three seconds and answered her in one sentence — that he has never had one done — which was true and gave her nothing at all. She did not ask him a second time, including on the Saturday with his name in her ear, and she tore the number off the card in her kitchen and put the rest of the card in the bin. A man in his thirties was at the far end of that counter and heard both halves of it and has put it to neither of them. The man who answered does not know the question was ever asked.

- **0387 — On the Ledge.** A galvanised churn has stood on a brick ledge in a shared back passage since a Saturday in November, put out by a man in his sixties to be painted and left there because of the rain. A man in his thirties wheeled a bicycle as far as that ledge on the twenty-seventh of January and could not get past, with a man in his sixties coming out of a gate about ten foot off at that moment. Both of them looked at it. Neither of them said a word. The man in his thirties went back up the passage and round by the parade and lost a quarter of an hour getting to where he was going; the man in his sixties drank his tea and went in. He has been down that passage about six times since and gone round it every time, and the man in his sixties has walked past it on his own account every time, and neither of them is going to be the one to start it.

- **0388 — The Room at the Top.** A man in his forties laid hardboard and a length of sheet vinyl down over a floor at the top of a landing in that block where he has no address, with a man in his thirties holding the other end of two of the sheets. There was nothing wrong with the floor. He has the use of that room because a woman who lets that block asked him in a corridor in November to keep it shut, and there is no money in it and nothing in writing. A woman who has the flat below went up for a parcel on the Sunday at about twenty to one, saw him on his knees in there, and has said nothing to him and to nobody else, including the woman who lets the block. He came through that passage again on the Thursday for half a day's work in one of the flats and was not spoken to differently by anybody, and he is not told that anybody knows.

- **0389 — Two Rails.** A man in his forties put a length of rail on two brackets that go over a course of brick and hook into nothing at all, at the back of an outbuilding in the middle of January, about five foot off the floor, with three hooks in it and his own things on them. A man in his thirties put a second length of rail on his own brackets into the same four foot of brick about three weeks later, at about six foot two, because a bench he is building wants it out of the way of four sheets of material. The two rails are thirteen inches apart and the lower one is behind that stack. A woman with the letting of the shop alongside went into that building for a box, stood in it for four minutes, saw one rail and has not been back. Neither man knows the other has been, and neither would call the other's a mistake, and the bench has not been built.

- **0390 — The Chair.** A man in his forties went into a front room off a side street at about half past ten on the tenth of February to look at a floor that turned out to be all right, and carried a chair into the middle of the room to get at the boards behind it. He walked it back inside the hour, and while it was out he found a leg working in its joint and short, folded a piece of the rug's stiff backing under it and knocked the joint down twice with the heel of his hand, and put the leg back into the mark in the dust on the brick. The man it belongs to came in at about ten past one, sat in it and noticed nothing at all, and has noticed nothing since. The man in his forties told nobody he touched it, and the woman who works in a shop, who watched him go up that street and come back down it, has not told the man in his sixties either.

- **0391 — A Minute and a Half.** A patch of plaster came out of a corner of a ceiling in a first-floor flat on the Sunday before the fourteenth of February and went across a table and broke a mug. The man who plastered that corner in October and the man who had put his thumb into the same corner in December and told the woman there it would come down talked for about a minute and a half where they stood, in that shop. Each of them gave one thing that was true, neither gave the other what the other one needed, neither conceded anything, and it stopped when somebody else came up to be served. They stood about two foot apart at that counter twice in the week after and raised nothing. Two foot of that ceiling is still open under a plastic sheet hooked over a rail, and the man who did the October work does not hold that he is at fault.

- **0392 — Where It Came From.** A man in his sixties put a tin into a man in his forties' hand on a street off the parade on the afternoon of the seventeenth of February, in the middle of a sentence about work at the Cleeve road, and said nothing about the tin at all. It had come off the top of a wardrobe in his own front bedroom and had been there since about 2014 with about nine other things nobody has moved. The man in his forties carried it in his van for four days, did not open it and used it for nothing, and asked one question about it on the Monday; the answer he got was about where it had been and not about why it was handed over. He set it down on that ledge again on the Tuesday, when the giver was not there, said nothing to anybody, and the giver took it off on the Wednesday and put it back on the wardrobe. Neither has mentioned it, and the man in his forties has not worked out why he was given it.

- **0393 — On the Table.** A man in his forties had a boxed electric fire in the back of his van from the fifteenth of January and carried it about with him for a fortnight, using it for nothing, because in fourteen days there was not one moment when he was standing at the back of that van with his hands free and somewhere to put it. On that Friday afternoon he set it on the table in that small room off the shop, said nothing to the three people sitting there, and went at about five o'clock. The man who works nights moved his bag of ice out of the way, the woman who works in a shop put her elbow nearer it and later put a cup on it, and the man in his sixties did not look at it once. The man who put it there has been in that shop three times since and has not been through that hatch, and none of the three has asked anybody anything about it.

- **0394 — An Hour Late.** On the third of March a gate off a side turning kept a man in his forties waiting for about ten minutes because the man who keeps that yard was out on a lorry, and he had gone the other way first and turned up fifty-five minutes after the hour he had had in his own head. Neither of the two of them said anything about the hour, and nobody in this borough knows it happened. Two small things on that parade stayed wrong: a shutter that has been stopping about a foot above the pavement since the twelfth of February, and a paving slab that has stood an inch and a half out of its bed across the whole footway. About nine people used that parade and not one of them had a thing in their hands meant for any of the others. A line under the last of nineteen entries in a book in a block by the water had stood open across one thousand one hundred and ninety-three days, the four answers are still going round and cannot be laid side by side, a box is still sitting on a table in a small room off that parade with nobody claiming it, and the man who carried it in was not there that afternoon. **CARD 0394 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.**

## Volume 05, Continuation 0021 — Chapters 395–404

- **0395 — Hinges.** A door on the common stair of a building of four flats would not shut, and the man on the ground floor said so once, in about fifteen seconds, to the woman who lets the building, and then never again. She took it to the man in his forties, who came on the twentieth of February, took the leaf off its three hinges, packed the two dropping knuckles with torn brown paper, eased the hinge edge, and touched up two patches with the paint that was standing on the landing, which was a shade off. It started again in the cold snap and she asked the man in his thirties. He came on the fourth of March, took the top hinge off, found somebody else's torn paper packed in the knuckle and somebody else's touch-up on the frame, and worked out in under a minute who had been there and how they had done it. He put the paper back, moved both hinges the other way instead, and went down the stair. The door shuts. The man on the ground floor does not know it was touched twice, the woman who lets the building has not looked at it, and the two tradesmen have not mentioned it to one another.

- **0396 — Behind the Batten.** The man in his forties was given a key to a cellar in March and spent three days in it chasing out a length of stack pipe, which meant taking a length of batten off a wall. Behind the batten there was plaster of two dates with about thirty pencil crosses up it in a column, four inches apart, drawn with a pencil sharpened on a knife; six showed through a coat of distemper and four were days old. He finished the work and then went back twice for nothing else at all, once on the last Thursday of March and once on the second of April, stood in front of that wall, and saw four more and then five more. He has never found the sentence for what they are and has not written it down anywhere. He has not asked the man in his sixties who goes down there most days, has not told anybody else, and has not been down again.

- **0397 — Twenty Feet.** A shop off that parade had a plywood door on it since the week before Christmas. The man in his thirties made a new hardwood door and frame himself in the second week of March and put it in on the morning of the fourteenth, in and out of the doorway all day, and was in the yard behind that shop six times for tools. The man in his forties was in that same yard from eight until half past one rebuilding nine feet of the top of the boundary wall at the back, on an errand the woman who works in a shop had asked of him, and was about twenty feet from the other man for ninety seconds at about twenty past ten and neither looked up. At half past three the man in his thirties came back for a bar he had left, saw nine foot of new brickwork with every arris chamfered along the top, and knew in about two seconds whose it was. He did not go closer, he did not touch it, and he told nobody.

- **0398 — Stair Rods.** The man in his forties has had a room at the end of a passage for most of three years and has a bench in it. On a ledge left over from a chimney breast that came out of that building in 1968 there is a bag of four brass stair rods, and he put them there in May 2015 when he took up a hall floor in a house off the parade and the rods came off the stair with the boards, and he said nothing to the woman of that house and she said nothing to him. That house has stood empty since November and a woman with its keys is emptying it. She saw the bag on a visit in February and said nothing, and thought about it for three weeks in a car park. On the seventeenth of March she came down the passage with a man who had a job in that yard and asked him for the rods in one sentence. He put down a chisel, took the bag off the ledge, and put them in her hand in about ten seconds without a word about where they had been. She wrote nothing down. The man at the door did not turn round.

- **0399 — Raked Out.** In February the man in his forties spent a Saturday repointing nine foot of a frost-blasted garden wall in a narrow strip behind the last house of a terrace, because the water off a gutter above it was running down that face. He mixed his own mortar, kept the old in a sack, wetted the face in March weather, and finished in the dark. He told nobody. In March the man in his sixties who owns the land behind that wall told the man in his thirties it is coming down in June for a garage. The man in his thirties went into that yard for a downpipe, saw nine foot of new pointing, and thought nothing of it. He came back twice, on the Tuesday for a downpipe and on the Wednesday after it, and on the Wednesday raked the whole of it out and packed the rubble back in loose. A bolster went through the face of a brick and took a thumbnail off it. Fifteen days later the man in his forties went into that yard for something else, stood at that wall for half a minute, worked out in four seconds what had been done and by whom, and shut the gate again behind him.

- **0400 — On the Wheel.** The man in his forties had four of his own chisels he had wanted to grind for a week and no room to do it in, so he took his roll up a turning of lock-ups and into an empty one he has a key to and was not asked to be in, where a pedestal grinder stood from a workshop that shut in 2009. The owner is away that week. He got water in the tray, held the wheel still, and ground the half-inch, the quarter, the half and a quarter and the one-inch properly over four and a quarter hours, then wiped the tray, sponged the bench and the floor and put the cover and the brick back. The woman who works in a shop has her car in the ninth of those garages and came out of hers with a paper bag in each hand and stood at the mouth of his for about a minute, and then drove off. He never found out. The owner came back on the Saturday, saw a wiped bench and a covered wheel, and said nothing about it either.

- **0401 — Under the Iron.** The man in his forties bought two dozen slates on a Friday and could not get a van into the merchant's yard, so the man in his thirties said he would collect them on the Sunday and bring them to a yard at the end of a lane. He drove to the top of the lane, carried both bands half a mile on foot, and found that gate standing open on its own dropped hinge with the bar leaning against the brick beside it and nobody in that yard. He waited about twenty minutes, rang once, and would not ring twice. He put the bands on a ledge along the bottom of the workshop wall under a length of corrugated iron that was leaning against the wall above them, and put the iron back leaning the way it had been. The man who works nights came past the gate at half past six that morning, fifteen foot off, and did not stop. The man in his forties came on the Wednesday, saw the iron leaning the other way, lifted it, and did not ask anybody where the slates had been. He carried them home in two loads and was on his own roof on the Friday.

- **0402 — Out of Square.** A hardware shop off that parade has a locked store with about a hundred bundles of laths on a steel rack, and three people go into that store most weeks. The woman who works at the counter has held the keys since the February before last; the man in his forties has had a key of his own about two years; the man in his thirties has none and has not been offered one. On the fourth of April the man in his forties went in for a size and saw that the top bundle on the third stack was two inches forward of the nine under it with its band turned a quarter of a turn, and she moved that same bundle while he was in the store with her. On the fifth the man in his thirties went in for a bag of cement, saw the same thing, and turned the band back the right way. Each of them did about three seconds of arithmetic and each of them was wrong, because the one who cannot be in that store without somebody letting her in is the one who had been in it twice in four days, getting at a box of hinges, and putting each bundle down where her hand could reach it. Neither man will raise it, because raising it means admitting to standing at a rack with nothing in his hands.

- **0403 — Two Things.** The man in his forties had a first-floor flat to himself for a day in April, rewiring the front room. On the sill inside the front window there was a comb in a ring of dust with two teeth gone out of it, and it belonged to the man in his thirties, who left it there on a saucer in February and has not been back. He put it back in the ring. Behind the door of the back room there was a coil of about thirty foot of cable on a nail, and it belonged to the man in his sixties, who coiled it there in June of the year before last and has never been in that room. He took it because there was a job on the Monday and he had not bought cable for it, and because he needed somewhere to put a lamp, and he shut the door and left the nail. The man in his thirties was in the passage thirty foot away and has not been back. The man in his sixties has not opened that door and is not going to before the summer.

- **0404 — The Awning.** A wind came up the river on the afternoon of the eighteenth of April for about half an hour and dropped the front of a canvas awning over a shop two thirds of the way up that parade, with a noise two doors away. The woman who works in a shop heard it, put her head out, and stood in the doorway about half a minute without going out into it. The man who puts shutters up was at the top of the parade and came down off it with his steps, put the chain back over its cleat, wound the awning down, and tied the front bar to the frame with a piece of cord out of his pocket, because he has done that about four times a year since 1991. She came out and stood at the foot of his steps and looked up for about ten seconds while he was already at his van. Neither of them said anything and neither has said anything since. The shutter at the top of that parade still does not shut, a slab in the middle of it still stands an inch and a half proud, and on the way out she put a hand on a door frame she did not need to touch. Behind a door in a block by the water there is a book at nineteen entries, and the space under the last of them was at one thousand two hundred and thirty-nine days on the eighteenth of April and nobody went into that room, and the four answers were still going round with no two of them able to be set beside one another.

**0405 — The End Wall — Thursday the nineteenth of April 2018.** A man in his thirties spends a morning putting a window in a first-floor room on Ketley Street and finds a shovel standing in the middle of it holding itself up against a stack of boards. He stands it back against the end wall where it has not been since November, at about ten past nine, and goes down his outside stair at about a quarter to ten and does not come back. Twenty-five minutes later a man in his forties goes up that stair with a sheet of plasterboard under his arm at about ten past ten, finds the shovel in the way of the door, and lays it on the stack about ten foot away because both his hands are full, and clears his tools out of that room and never goes near the building again. No knowledge either way, and neither of them will raise it. A woman who works in a shop is at the same builder's merchant at about five to ten and stands ten foot from the man in his forties across a counter; neither says anything and neither knows about the room.

**0406 — Nobody's Lid — Tuesday the twenty-fourth of April 2018.** A man in his forties is told at a counter on that parade, in about fifteen seconds, by a man who sells pipe and owns nothing, that nobody has had the lid off a certain tank since before Christmas. He does not check where it came from, opens that lid the same morning, finds the valve stuck wide and the tank running to waste, and cleans it out over two days in May and charges the man at the end of that terrace one hundred and ten pounds for it. The sentence was true. The teller has said nothing since and would not remember saying it. A man in his thirties is at that gate for about a minute while the tank is open and goes and does his own work.

**0407 — Four Posts — Friday the twenty-seventh of April 2018.** A man in his thirties digs four post holes in a back yard and concrets in four galvanised posts for a washing line, and knocks the third one out at about twenty to twelve because that ground is made and a wet mix leans on it, and sets it again at about twenty past one. A woman who lives in that house asks him whether the line will take a wet sheet and gets a straight answer, and asks him for nothing else. On the Monday before, the man in his forties saw a man and a bar and a shovel from the corner of that street and said so in a shop in about four seconds. On the Friday the woman who works in a shop puts that back to him at her counter, and he says neither yes nor no, and asks her nothing, and goes and puts a proper line up on those four posts.

**0408 — A Dark Patch — Tuesday the first of May 2018.** An unnamed man is in a first-floor flat for about ninety minutes on the morning of that first of May, doing a length of pipe and a new stopcock, and moves a canvas toolbag off a shelf to get at a roll of lino, and puts his thumb into a hard dark place in the bottom of it, and says nothing to the man in his sixties who is about four foot away in the room. That afternoon the man in his forties is in the same flat and asks to borrow a screwdriver, and the man in his sixties opens that bag for the first time since about 2014, sees the same place from the inside, decides in about four seconds that it is grease and a wet rag and a stove, does not touch it, and puts the bag back with that place against the wall. Neither man is labelled by his age in that chapter and this summary does not label him. The two never mention a bag to each other. What is in the bottom of it is not found out by anybody in this borough.

**0409 — The Brass Sole — Monday the seventh of May 2018.** A man in his forties is let into a block at a quarter past eight by a man in his thirties while the man in his sixties is out, and goes into that man's back room at about twenty past nine for a stop tap, and comes out with a thirteen-inch dovetail level off the shelf by the window because he has a stair carriage the next morning and his own is in a van in another town. He takes nothing else. At about half past four in the afternoon the man in his sixties comes into his own room, stands in the doorway, goes out, comes back, stands in it again, looks at a pale rectangle on the plaster where the level had stood for about twenty-five years, and goes downstairs. He does not ask and has not asked since.

**0410 — Wired Glass — Thursday the tenth of May 2018, on two days.** Two men strip seventy foot of heating pipe out of a workshop and start at opposite ends, because that is how a run that length is done. On the second morning they meet at a cast-iron column in the middle of it and talk for about six minutes; one of them wanted the pipe over the top of it, the other had measured and the only way past is the far face and a bend. The second way is done, and at about twenty past one the man who wanted the first way takes his own length out again and they do the last nine foot together in an hour and a quarter without a word about it. A woman who works in a shop sits at a desk in a brick office behind a square of wired glass in that door for the mornings of both days and sees the whole of it, says nothing to either man then or since, and is not asked how the job went.

**0411 — The Cage — Tuesday the fifteenth of May 2018.** With no bags left on the counter and six feet of conduit in front of her, a woman who works in a shop puts a green and white wire birdcage into a man's hands so that he will hold it while she measures. It cannot be shut, its door does not work, and it weighs about four pounds. He puts it in his van and it rides on the floor behind the passenger seat for ten days and moves about four times a day. **0412 — Four Foot of Marble — Saturday the nineteenth of May 2018.** Two men go into a store at the bottom of a turning and both see four foot of Victorian marble on a slate base against the north wall, there since about 1990 and worth about three hundred and twenty pounds to a man who knows. One of them has a key to that store and goes about four times a month, and keeps a rule he has never put into words for anybody, and what that rule is about is a locked room and his own van, and under it is a house, and he could only act on it by saying all of it in a street to get two men he needs, and he has nobody to say it to. They pass each other twice that afternoon, once about a bag of cement and once about a heavy door, and neither of them will ever know the other's reason.

**0413 — The Hot Cupboard — Tuesday the twenty-second of May 2018.** A man in his forties spends about eight hours on a third-floor bathroom and the isolation valve is in a hot cupboard off a dark half-landing, the size of a man, with an unlagged cylinder head in it and a door hanging off one hinge screw. He goes in twice with his head and his shoulder in. The first time he comes out wrong for about a minute, goes back and finishes the valve. The second time, at about twenty past one, he comes out at about ten to two, gets four steps down, and sits on the bottom step of the upper flight in the dark for about six minutes, and then finishes the bathroom and comes out of that flat at half past four. At twenty to six, a woman who works in a shop sees him keep his hand flat on a counter for two seconds while she gives him his change.

**0414 — Under One Leg — Monday the twenty-eighth of May 2018.** About nine people are out on that parade in that morning and none of them is carrying anything for any of the other eight. In a room at the back of one of those shops a deal table that has rocked since before Christmas stops rocking, because the woman who works in a shop put it to him across her counter that morning while he was buying washers, he gave it about three quarters of an hour, and then, at about a quarter to nine and on his way out, he put a three-foot length of batten under the short leg and cut it off square and told nobody. The woman who works in a shop comes in for a sheet of paper at about ten, finds it in about two seconds, and does not go four doors up the street. Four answers to one question are still going round and none of them can be put next to any of the others, a birdcage has been standing under a gate hood since the Friday before and the man that yard belongs to has not been down it since the middle of May, a clock switches the light off in the hall at the bottom of that parade at four, and a line under the last entry in a book stood empty that day for one thousand two hundred and seventy-nine days with nobody in the room.

## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0023 — CHAPTERS 415–424

**0415 — The Lime.** A woman who works in a shop, on a delivery to a street off that parade, finds that a gale has put a limb across a fence in a garden she can see from the pavement, and she asks the man whose garden it is in about seven words. He is the man in his thirties, and the limb is his to have cut or not, and he declines. She does not ask again and he does not explain, and a woman who lives in the same house has asked him the same question earlier in the morning and got the same one word. Two days later the man in his forties, who is in the neighbouring garden for a job to do with a chimney, looks at the same limb for about a minute and decides the same thing, without ever learning that the other man was asked anything. Nobody in either house is told anything and the limb is still there.

**0416 — A Pair of Glasses.** A man in his thirties needs to read something for an afternoon and asks the man in his forties for a lend of the glasses he once saw him use. The man in his forties refuses him in one short sentence without explanation. He has them; they are in his own van and will stay there. Nobody in the borough is owed the truth about what a man keeps in his van, and nobody asks him for them again, including the woman who works in a shop, who heard the whole of it and is not the sort of person to raise it. The reason for the refusal is his own and is about an optician in another town in 2016 and not about the man who asked. The cost of it is invisible and is borne by a customer whose shopfront was set out from a drawing the man in his thirties could not read properly.

**0417 — The High End.** A woman who works in a shop uses a service yard behind her own shop every day and on a Monday in June finds that rain has got into a man's stock under a lean-to, and that the top of that lean-to has been made sound that morning by somebody who was not asked and said nothing. She works out who it was at a glance and does nothing about it. The man who built the lean-to in April does not know anything was done to it and will not find out. The man in his forties does not know that the far end of the roof he has just made sound is still letting water into a wall that was already damp, and nobody in this borough ever finds that out, including the woman who saw both and has kept them apart.

**0418 — Taped Over.** A man in his thirties and a man in his forties each see a cracked pane of glass on a landing in a block of flats and each leaves it alone, and neither of them ever finds out that the other one saw it. Some weeks afterwards the woman who works in a shop, who has never been in that block for any reason except carrying a bolt, decides that the window is hers to do, and takes it out, pays for another, puts it in, and tells nobody. She is not thanked, does not expect to be, was not asked to do anything and is not on anything. A man from the top of that block looks at the finished window in the summer and goes back upstairs without a thought, and that is the whole of what anybody in that building knows.

**0419 — The End of the Lane.** A man in his forties has a window out of an empty house and no van to put it in for two hours, and instead of waiting he walks it the length of a lane and puts it down on grass at the end of it, against a wall, for a reason that has nothing to do with the window: he wants to know whether the ground there will take a lorry. The man in his thirties sees him pass with it, offers to help, is told no, and forgets the whole thing inside a minute. Nobody in the borough is going to that end of that lane, there is no made road to it, and a window is standing there in July with no writing on it and nothing under it but the ground.

**0420 — The Same Hour.** In the same hour of one Saturday morning, a man behind a counter and a woman who works in a shop each tell one of two men a true thing about the other man, neither knowing they are telling the other anything. Both men do arithmetic and neither of them does anything at all about it, and neither ever mentions either fact to a living soul. In between, the two men carry the same length of board across a shop between them and put it down, and neither says a word. They then leave the shop by different roads. It is the only time in this account that two men each learn something true about the other and both of them keep it.

**0421 — A Gate.** A man in his forties finds a gate at the back of a yard has dropped out of its hooks and is dragging, and he puts it right in about three quarters of an hour without being asked, without taking money, and without saying one word about it to anybody, and he will not say why. A man in his thirties is in the house all day, sees the job afterwards, and tells the man who lives there that it is done, and is told that the man he means is not in the house. The man who lives there sees that it works, says nothing, and never asks. The man in his forties was there in January clearing that house for a man who died, hung that gate back on the same hook in four minutes because it was in the way, and has not been near it since.

**0422 — Coming Back.** The front door of a shop off that parade is heavy and has nothing stopping it, and on one windy Monday in June it catches the man in his forties as he leaves and, four hours later, catches the woman who works in that shop as she carries something out. She stands still against the front of the building for a couple of minutes and nobody in that borough stops, because that is what this borough does. The man in his thirties is inside and sees the second of those from four foot away, and he had already seen the first, and he tells nobody either time. The man in his forties comes back that evening for something small and neither of them says anything, and a fortnight later neither has raised it.

**0423 — The Front Room.** A man in his sixties starts a wall in his own front room in June and gets nine foot of it done before a corner beats him, and leaves it. A man in his thirties comes across that wall weeks later, finds the fill has failed, and comes back on three separate evenings to do the whole thing properly in his own time, taking his own equipment away with him every night. A man in his forties walks through that building in the middle of the second evening with a ladder, sees him at work, and leaves without speaking. On the Sunday the man in his sixties finds the wall finished, looks at it, and makes his tea. He never asks, he has never said a word about it to anybody, and the tools the other man did not use are still where he left them.

**0424 — Ordinary.** On a Friday in July, early, a man doing that parade's shutters stops on his way back up, moves a bicycle out of a footway against a wall, and goes on without a word to anybody, and nobody on the parade sees him. The woman who works in a shop is in a room at the back of her own shop at that moment and misses all of it, and spends the rest of the day on her feet. About nine people pass through that parade and none of them is doing anything for any of the others, a hall at the bottom of it is shut and does its own lighting at four to an empty building, and everything else about the day is what that day is. The four answers are still going round, they still cannot be set beside one another, nobody has said what they are answers to, and the question is still a question.

- **0433** — A man in his forties went into a store room to price a range and priced it at about four times what the room was worth. The line under the last entry of that book stood open since the middle of March three years before that. ## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0028 — CHAPTERS 465–474

- **0465** — A man who has crossed a cut between two rows twice a day for nine years found that something which had always been on a wall inside it was not there, and without deciding to, he began taking the long way round. - **0472** — A man had known for four years that a boundary wall in the back of a row carries the side of the house next door, and he is right, and the only thing that makes him certain of it is two occasions in 2013 and 2016 when he was inside that wall and no one in either house knew. ## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0029 — CHAPTERS 475–484

- **0475** — A woman who has done nine years of other people's gardening at the bottom of a hundred-yard way and a man who has used it for nine years and never once been the person to do anything about it both worked out, separately, that the other of them ought to cut four yard of privet back. ## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0031 — CHAPTERS 495–504

He has told nobody. On 30 June the second came, went up, and put up his own table without a word, and the first came back at ten past six, stood thirty paces off for twenty minutes, and went home.
- **0503** — A woman began washing a man's clothes in a back alley in the summer of 2016 after a Sunday when the rain came down, and has done his Mondays and Thursdays ever since without being asked once. In March he opened the subject himself, wanting to know whether anybody was putting anything in her hand for it, and what came back was whether she would go on doing it if he never raised it again, and he said she could have asked him, and she said nothing. He has carried that for four months as a debt he cannot pay. In July he washed his own for the first time, badly, and left it in a bag, and there was a cloth in the bag with no business in a fortnight of one man's washing. She washed it, folded it, put it at the bottom, and said she had never intended to stop. Neither of them has put it right.
- **0504** — An ordinary Wednesday afternoon in a lane at the bottom of a row. A length of shop shuttering about seven foot long stood in the only turning place for three days and about nine people a day went round it, one woman stood and looked at it twice, and on the Wednesday a man who comes round with a barrow said out loud to nobody that it had been in the way all week, lifted it in, and took it away. Nobody was asked, because there was nobody to ask, and nobody believes anybody put it there. The concrete it stood on is now just concrete. In the same hour the four accounts of one thing are still in circulation and still cannot be put beside one another, the line under the last entry of a working book off a passage by the water is still empty at 1,687 days, and the one thing this borough cannot name has not shifted since the middle of August last year.

## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0032 — CHAPTERS 505–514

- **0505** — A man had gone out of his own front door at half past six every morning for four years and been back by nine. He put it back on the Saturday a week later and told her it had gone down with the water, and she said right. She has not asked him why and will not, because the question would be her own admission. What she worked out in a doorway a few days ago is that he had already stopped going before his back went, and that she cannot put both halves of that to him either. She was away for a week in July and did not go on the Sunday she came back, and has not managed a reason. On the Wednesday he came early and moved one bench two feet out of place to see whether anybody was watching. She came round the wall, stopped dead at the fifth, put the seventh back, wiped the paint where her hand had been, and walked on. Neither spoke. He has decided she knew and has been carrying that. She has decided he has been counting and has been carrying that, and neither one is wrong about what the other did not say.
- **0507** — Two brothers agreed in a yard in 2009 that one would go to their mother on a Sunday afternoon and the other in the evening, and neither would ever say the other gave it up. The older read it as giving something away and took the evening; the younger read it as a share and took the afternoon. Each believed the other was taking the earlier hour, so both have gone at seven every Sunday for ten years and their mother has had nobody in the afternoon. She told the younger in June, when she was tired of a question he had not accepted the first answer to, and he has said nothing to anybody since. On the Monday he went to her house at twenty past twelve, which is not when he goes, having decided on the Saturday not to fix the tap that has been dripping since May and not being able to name a reason, and stayed three hours in her front room with his father's flask and nothing to do, and saw a flask and a used cup on a chest in the back room that come out at half past six on a Sunday and go back at nine. He washed his cup, told his mother the tea was his father's, and left. He has decided nothing and has been through it four times.
- **0508** — A man took a small painted bell off a plate in a porch in March 1998 and put it on a ledge at nine foot in his own back room, and it is still there. He told one man, in a parked car in 2003, in about ninety seconds, and did not say why. He is the only person alive who knows, and he has had nobody to tell since 2011. On the Sunday in July a woman at number nineteen came to his door about a wall, and looked up at the back of the house on the way out and asked whether something up there was a bell, and he said yes without a pause. She thought it was a shop bell and apologised and left. He shut the door and stood where she had been standing. What he has been carrying since is not that she found anything out but how fast the answer came, and what he has worked out about that is that saying no would have meant explaining, and explaining would have put a stranger in that porch in his own head. He went into the back room later that afternoon, looked at the ledge, touched nothing and shut a door he does not usually shut.
- **0509** — A woman has carried a two-gallon can from a tap in a yard round the side and up three floors every morning at a quarter past seven for six years, because there is no water on that floor. She went on carrying her own anyway for a fortnight, so two cans went up every morning, and nobody on that floor said anything about it. On the sixteenth she asked him why and he let go of the handle and said the can was heavy and shut his door. On the second of August she was four minutes and ten seconds up, against closer to six before anybody touched it, and she has worked out that the last ten steps are quicker because there is nobody behind her. - **0511** — A man and a woman were both in a house in June 1994 and each went away certain the other had carried off a blue umbrella from the entrance and told somebody else about it. In May this year he put the question to somebody who had been in that house in 1994 and was told that there had been a blue one of hers, that it went missing at her sister's, and that neither woman in that house ever mentioned it again. He has said nothing since and has reached the point of wishing the question had never come out of his mouth. She has worked out that her whole conduct for twenty-five years was protecting him from being told, and has not been able to finish the thought. On the thirteenth of August they met on a parade at a quarter to twelve, stood about a yard apart for nine seconds, said good morning, and went on, and neither said one word about 1994.
- **0512** — Two men in the same trade keep opposite stories about a noise on a May night, and neither has any way of putting them to the other. The first puts it at the top of the steps of the building over the parade, where he was on a wall with his back to it, and where a man with a torch and a bucket came out of the side door. The second puts four foot of lath off a corridor ceiling on the ground floor of a building four streets off, and says he put his hand in it, and that there is no lath in the first building. He gave that version once in June to a man who talks, and that man has passed it on twice. On the Saturday in August that man came up to the first one's step to ask about something else, said it as he was leaving, and was told there was no lath in that building, and said he had not been in it at all. He apologised at the step and meant it and has not mentioned being taken back. The first man has said nothing to anybody, including the man who was there with the torch, and is now carrying two noises in different buildings at the same hour of the same night with no way of putting them together.
- **0513** — A woman has been on a sea wall at six o'clock on a Tuesday evening twelve times since the middle of March and has never fished and never looked at the water. A man who goes there every Tuesday asked her twice why she was there and she gave him a true reason each time, and on the second occasion he believed it. The evening is the thing she is after and not the view, and she has no wording for that which would survive being said out loud. On the twentieth of August he told her he was not going the Tuesday after and then asked whether she would be all right up there on her own, which is the wrong question. She had about four seconds, and gave him the truth, which is that she does not fish, and he said right and went along the wall and put his line out into nine feet of water. She has decided nothing about what comes next. In June, in the rain, she wrote something on the back of her hand and rubbed it out at the foot of the wall, and it was not about him.
- **0514** — An ordinary Sunday. A woman went over on the same one of eight steps for the third time since May, in front of a man with a broom who had swept them for nine years and who did not turn round until she said she was all right. A man who is not a tradesman and not a relation goes to a house at number twenty-five on a Saturday morning and knocks, and has done for about four years, and the woman there made him a cup of tea the first time and has not made him one since and has never said she will not, and he has never asked and has never stopped coming. A man went into a side room off a way down by that water for a coil of cable, put his hand flat on the desk to shift a working book out of the way of the door, read the ruled gap under the last line of writing in it, turned it over in his hands, set it back down with the spine the same way round, and went out and shut the door, and told the man he works with the cable was not in there. Two men who each carry one of four accounts of a single thing put them side by side outside a place on a street, said *different, though* to each other and went in. ## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0033 — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 515–524
