**0515.** A woman at the far end of a street kept a six-minute walk to the end of the street and back at the same hour every morning for sixteen years, and did it differently once in June and told nobody. The woman across from her had been watching from her own front for five years and worked out that something in the round had changed, and could not ask, because asking would be the admission. On the last Tuesday of August she was out early without having decided to be, the other woman came back past her, and neither said anything about why. She has started standing at the end of her own garden on the mornings the other is coming back, and has never been in the street on the mornings she is going out, and the two of them have exchanged one whole sentence in sixteen years, about trees.

**0516.** A man carried another man's shopping across a row of bays on Saturday mornings for three years and stopped in August without a word. He had already seen, in June, a younger man do the same carrying for the same man, and had taken from it something the other man would not endorse. The man he carried for found out four days late from a man who sells in the row, and has since worked out for himself a reason that is not the first man's reason. On the first of September the first man went back and stood in his bay for four minutes while a younger man was told he was not needed, and said nothing, and drove out the other way. He has decided not to start again, on a ground that is about being seen rather than about pride, and he has not told anybody.

**0517.** Two women settled something quickly while standing in a queue in a town in 1997 and have never referred to it since. In August a man who cuts their grass told the older one that the younger had been into hospital and had told two people she does everything. The older one has decided not to say so, on a reason that is about not handing the other woman her own complaint back through a third person, and about not being the first to ask for anything in twenty-two years. On the Thursday the younger one told her on the pavement that she had been told something too, and neither of them mentioned any of it, and the older one went home and did not take her coat off.

**0518.** A man said three words to a brother in a kitchen in 1996 and never repeated them in the family. His brother's wife heard the same three words said to a third man in a different kitchen in September, in the same voice and with the same hand on the worktop, and went and sat in another room. On the twelfth she put one plate down and said the sentence she had been carrying for eight days, and he said ay, filled two cups, and did not deny it. She is not going to put it to him again, because an apology would tell her it was a judgement and she would have to begin again, and she has not said that reason out loud to anybody.

**0519.** A woman carried a felt hat off a wall in a lane to a hook in her own porch every Wednesday for seven years without the man who wears it ever knowing. In May a neighbour moved the hat four yards and never moved it back, and she carried it back down every Wednesday for fifteen weeks, and then on the fourth of September she stopped waiting and said nothing to anybody. On the seventeenth it rained and she put the hat on the hook on a Tuesday evening, which it has never been, and a man walked past at seven and stopped and looked at it and went on and in. She stood at her own front and believed it would be back on the wall by the Wednesday, and that Wednesday is not on the page and is not to be put there by anybody.

**0520.** Two people who have known each other since 1988 agree about every part of the eighth of May except the one thing said down a telephone that morning, and neither of them has ever turned out to be the one who was wrong. In September the woman asked a third person which of them was right and was told she already knew, and was told, and declined, to be given a name for it. On the twenty-fourth the man said he was through with it by June and she said she was not, and he told her the thing was not a grievance and that she might have said it on the Monday, and she said she did not want to be somebody who had said it on the Monday. They have talked about a boundary and a man came on the Friday and charged her for a washer.

**0521.** Two men have described a third man neither has met to each other, once a month or better, for eight years, and the two descriptions do not fit. In August one of them was handed a picture of the man on somebody's telephone and said it was him twice, and the picture does not match either description, and he has said nothing to the other for six weeks. On the last Sunday of September he gave his own description aloud in the order he always gives it, and the other man went quiet and gave an account of his jaw. He has put no question to the other about any subject at all for six weeks, and the first has worked out from that silence that something has been said to him somewhere and is not being repeated.

**0522.** A woman and a man who work in the same building carry two accounts of a Wednesday in March, when a girl of fifteen on a placement was crying at the end of an office. She has told it once and he has told it four times and they disagree about what she was carrying, and there is no copy of it anywhere, and the girl is in another town. On the sixth of October they were in a room together for nine minutes because two other people had booked it and had not turned up, and she said a sentence that ran to more than one, and he said all right. She has not learned whether he told it four times, he has not told her that he worked out the length of the nine minutes, and neither of them has any way of finding out.

**0523.** A woman has written something down every day since the fourteenth of June and showed it to nobody, on the inside back cover of a hardback with a pencil. On the twenty-second of September the man she lives with said she had been quiet, and she gave her reason, and he read a hundred and twenty days of it in about four minutes and told her he was not going to put a single question to her about any of it, and gave her a reason for that which she accepted. He has since started writing the things he needs to say to her on a piece of paper on the side, and has asked her nothing, and has read it four times on his own. She wrote one line about him on the hundred and fifth day and has not said it, and on the twelfth of October he shifted the low thing it lies on out of her way by a foot, and she sat in front of it and did not reach over for the pencil.

**0524.** An ordinary Thursday in this borough with four things in it, none of which is about any of the others. A heather behind number thirty-four has been spreading out of its border since June and the edging that would have held it has gone at two places. A swing at the end of a row has been making a noise since the summer and the oil that would stop it is in an outbuilding with a rusted lid on it. Down by the water a working book has a line ruled under its last entry and the space under it is still empty, and nobody has been into that room for three Thursdays. The man in his sixties who was in that line went out that afternoon the way he does four or five times a year, and got as far as the corner and came home earlier than he goes, and the woman he used to go with has not been out since the summer. He did not ask her and he is not going to. He cannot say why she stopped and believes she has worked it out, and he looked for a mile on the way home for somebody she would tell and did not find one.

## Volume 05, CONTINUATION 0034, FIRST HALF — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 525–529

**0525.** Two sisters have done the same short walk together every morning for thirty years and a scarf has gone one way in the cold and come back the other, and one of them stopped on a Thursday in September 2019 without saying a word to anybody about it. The other has gone on going to the corner, and is not waiting for anything, and has lost the use of one arm for the scarf and has not considered stopping. On the twenty-fourth of October the one who stopped came out and walked the walk anyway, with her hands shut and nothing in them, and they were on the same pavement for sixty yards without either of them lifting a hand, and at the corner four words were said about the wind. The scarf went home in a coat pocket instead of over a chair, which is where it has been kept since the September and where it had not been in thirty years.

**0526.** Two men who met by accident at the end of a row every Tuesday for some years and never arranged it, and one of them stopped walking slowly past that end in March 2019 and told nobody why. On the Sunday of the twenty-fourth of March he drove to a yard to look at a lorry that had already been fixed on the Friday, and was told, accurately, that he had not needed to come, and he went home. On the twenty-ninth of October he slowed down for the first time in seven months and the other man was coming out of a building, and handed the same sentence back to him word for word. He had a question ready and did not ask it, walked the five minutes home without slowing once, and has not rung the flat.

**0527.** A dozen and a half people have sung on Monday mornings in a room at the back of a building since March 2000 with nobody running it and nothing written down. A woman of about seventy-one has counted them in the first few minutes every Monday since then with a hand down the side of her leg, and has never said the number or written it anywhere. A man who started coming at the end of July said one sentence about it on the second of September and she gave him one back, and he has not asked since. On the fourth of November there was a woman in a green coat standing at the front who had not been before, and the counter counted her in without asking, and spent the whole interval deciding not to go over, and did not go over, and the new one sang, and nobody asked her anything.

**0528.** Two sisters have disagreed since 1999 about whether their mother, then eighty-one, was to be moved, and the disagreement is not about what anything costs, and both of their reasons are good, and neither has yielded in twenty years. The mother died in the house in 2011 and neither sister has been inside it since. On the Tuesday of the fifth of November a woman who used to live next door and heard the younger sister say something in that house in 1999 in a room they did not know she was in told the older one what it was, and the older one has not said a word about it to anybody. On the Friday the eighth she went up the row at half past two and stood at the front of the house for about twenty minutes and did not go in, and a boy on a bicycle stopped and looked at her, and a woman she has never met spoke to her for four minutes, and she went home by the other way.

**0529.** A man and a woman have been in two rooms at the end of a row on a Wednesday for fourteen years, and he has said one word at the entrance every time, and she has come at half past four every time. On the thirtieth of October 2019 the word was not said, and on the way out at the archway she asked him for the first time in fourteen years whether it was the same time next week, and he said right. On the sixth of November she knocked and nothing happened. On the thirteenth she decided on a bus not to knock, stood at the end of the row in the rain for the best part of an hour, and a man who shuts those rooms came out and told her twice that there was nobody in, and she said she knew. He spent both of those evenings in his own front and told nobody, and did not put the heating on until about half past five.

**0530.** A woman in her early forties has been putting a single word down in chalk on a bathroom mirror every night since the March of 2008, and nobody in her house has cleaned that mirror in the whole of that time, and she reads the year back once, in the last week of November. Her partner told a woman he works with a wrong year in October and has not been able to put it behind him since. On the Friday of the eighth of November he asked whether he could see what she writes, and she said she would think about it, and on the fifteenth she put it where he would find it and went out to the shops and told nobody why. On the Wednesday he went into that bathroom at ten past seven, put a thumb on one word in the middle of the field, found that it came off, wiped his finger and put the chalk down squared to the edge, and came out without having read anything. He said one sentence about it in the kitchen and she gave him one back, and there were two of them in the world who knew that had happened, and the bare patch his own thumb made is the first thing either of them has ever altered on that mirror.

**0531.** Two men have played croquet on a green whose club is shut until the spring, every Sunday since the March of 2013, and the whole of what passes between the two of them amounts to about nine sentences in six years, which the chapter sets out. On the Sunday of the twenty-fourth of November the younger one arrived with a third man he has known since the middle of 2017 and said nothing about it to anybody, and the older one worked out inside about four seconds that he had been brought to be looked at. The third man is no good, apologised twice, won a game, and asked one question about how long the two of them had been at it, and he does not know that anybody in this borough has an opinion about his being there. At about twenty-five to four, an hour and a quarter after the three of them were standing together, the man of about sixty-one put his mallet in the grass and said he had to be going, and gave one reason and no other. Neither of the two men who have been at that green since 2013 has put it to the other, and the man who brought the third man stayed on the green afterwards for twenty minutes with his hands in his pockets.

**0532.** A woman of about sixty-two has been putting a pair of spectacles back where she finds them since 2016, and the one thing either of them has ever said about it is a single sentence she uses when she cannot find them, said once, in a voice her husband of about sixty-five could describe to a stranger, and neither of them has ever discussed that either. On the twentieth of November she could not find them for ten minutes and found them folded on the bathroom sill, which she has never once done herself, and she said the sentence. He heard it through the floor. By the following Friday she was going along the three places early on purpose and they were there folded, and by the Sunday she had stopped being able to put that down to her own hands. He has been getting up at half past five for a fortnight and putting them back before she is down, and the reason, which he has told nobody, is about the sound of that house before six in the morning and not about the spectacles. On the twenty-eighth she came down at twenty to six on purpose to catch him at it and he had already been down and gone back up, and at ten to seven he came down the way he does and said good morning, and she said good morning, and neither of them said anything else, and each of them knows the other knows.

**0533.** A woman of about fifty asked a man of about fifty-two, a long time ago, for three hours of an evening in a house in the town, and he said yes, and then he was not there for any of it and sent no word of any kind, and she has spent twenty-five years assuming that he did not want to, and he has known that since the week after. On the second of August 2019 a third man, who works with him and has known him since 2008, said in front of both of them that he would have said it was the first man all along, and the first man said nothing at all and has said nothing to anybody for four months. The three of them are again together on the steps of a building on the evening of the third of December, outside a house in the row where a woman is moving on Sunday, and the third man says the same thing again in the same voice, meaning the drive, and the man says nothing at all. The woman says that nine is fine, and then tells him she will not be any trouble, and the man repeats it back to her, because that is what he said to her on the first Sunday in September and again on the second. Nobody has said one word about 1994 and the man has not moved from the top step.

**0534.** An ordinary Saturday in December in four streets and a piece of ground between them, with two small things in it that have nothing to do with one another. A man who has put grit in the dip at the bottom of a ramp in a block of nine flats every morning for nine years has been at his daughter's since the middle of November, and there was ice in the dip on the Saturday morning, and a woman of about eighty-one who uses a frame went up, stopped, and came back down and went round the whole of the block to reach the other end. At about half past ten a man in the third flat came out with a shovel of his own, did the whole width twice over, banked the grit to the sides of the dip rather than the middle of it, and went back in without turning round. A little before midday she went up again and found it done, and did not knock. A woman in her forties, on the other side of that open ground, put her washing out before eight, it came through for six minutes, and she brought it in wetter than it went out, told her husband one sentence about it, and then went through the whole of it separately and put it away the way she would have if it had been dry.

## Volume 05, CONTINUATION 0035 — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 535–544

**0535.** Two households at the top of one street have been using it at the same hour every morning since November and have only ever exchanged two words doing it. In December the shop began shutting before he arrived and he came back up on the side he has never come back up on, and she was coming back down that side. They passed each other. **0536.** A weekly telephone appointment that had run for years came apart in June when the man on the other end went away without giving her the new address. She wrote none of it down. A few days afterwards she put it in from memory and reached a stranger, and having got it right she has not used it, and she has said nothing to anybody about any of that.

**0537.** A woman in her early seventies has walked down to a shop at the bottom of her street every December since she was a child and handed the keeper the same article, and has never once been given it free. In November the keeper told her that her brother's daughter has been buying the same article for three years so that it would be waiting when she arrived, and asked her not to say anything. She has said nothing and has been in that shop twelve times in the six weeks since without raising it. In December she paid for a second one herself, carried it home in both hands and put it where there was no room. Her brother rang that afternoon about something else and she has never mentioned any of it to anybody.

**0538.** Two sisters have walked to a burying ground and back into a town every Saturday for eight years and nine months since their mother died, and neither has ever said her name. In December the older brought a woman she has known for two years, because she had promised somebody who could not come. The younger came at the hour she always comes and did everything she always does and gave the woman seven sentences across a whole morning, and not one of them had anything to do with the morning itself. She left at noon after saying one thing to her sister that was not about any of it. In the car the older tried to explain her to the visitor.

**0539.** A woman has carried a sack up two flights to a flat she rents by the week and does not sleep in, every morning since 2010. In November a man who lives at the bottom of that building offered to carry it, was refused, stood waiting for about a month, stood waiting again after she had refused him, and then gave up of his own accord. She carried it up every morning after that. On New Year's Day the water was off in the building and in the afternoon she found the sack on the landing, having been brought down. She sent it back up herself.

**0540.** A man has put the same fixed sentence into his wife's house once a year since 2009 and she has never given him a word back that answers it, and he has never once asked for one. In January 2020 he said it and stayed on his feet and said something he had never said to her before, and she answered the first and said nothing to the second. Five days later, on a day that is not the one either of them fixed, he came and said the first again. Six days after the second sentence was said, neither of them has raised it.

**0541.** A woman who does not live in that building has gone to a ground-floor front part every Monday evening for eight years because she cannot bear her own flat on that night. A man in his eighties has been in that front part most Mondays for a decade and has never asked her why. Since November two people who do live there have started arriving an hour before her and neither has given a reason. She went early twice to see for herself and found an empty cold place both times and walked out. In January all three of them were there together for the first time and she stayed the hour, gave two sentences into it, and left at her own hour. She is not going to ask.

**0542.** A man went down a street and back up it twice a weekday past a barrow at the turn for nine years, and in December 2019 he began going round the other way and has told nobody why and nobody anything else about it. He walks a quarter of an hour further each way now and has a back that is not good. A woman in her early eighties has a window that looks at that turn and worked out what he was doing in the second week of December and has not gone down since. In January she watched him stop beside the barrow, look at it and walk on, and what she has done about it is move her seat so that she has to stand up to see it.

**0543.** Two brothers in their mid sixties inherited a workshop in 1979 and have paid half of one annual figure between them every January since, with nothing in writing anywhere and no arrangement either of them would admit to. In January 2020 the older went and settled the whole of it in one visit out of his own money and told nobody. The younger was told later the same month by a man who sells firewood, in the middle of a sale, and the man realised too late that he should not have. The younger did not go in that afternoon for the first time in his life, told his wife the stove was out, and will still pay his half in three or four days. Neither brother will ever mention the January.

**0544.** An ordinary Friday in January in five streets of this borough, with three small things in it that have nothing to do with one another. A woman missed a train because she had gone to the far end of the platform to read a board that gives different times from the other one. A woman in her late seventies asked a man behind the front of a shop for what his predecessor used to do with something, and he did not know who she meant, and she has not told him and has not told anybody. On the other side of the borough a man has been ordering a cooked breakfast by a name that was taken off the board in November and has been getting it every week. Down by the water, in a place none of those streets reaches, there is a working book with a line ruled under the last entry in a column since September 2015 and nothing under it. Nobody went in this week and nobody counted.
## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0036 — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 545–554

**WRITTEN AS DESCRIPTIONS OF WHAT HAPPENED TO A PERSON AND NOT AS TRANSCRIPTIONS OF WHAT A CHAPTER PRINTED, AT A LOWER ALTITUDE, AND NO ALL-CAPS SENTENCE FROM ANY OF THE TEN APPEARS IN ANY OF THESE TEN ENTRIES, AND NO ENTRY WALKS ITS CHAPTER IN THAT CHAPTER'S OWN ORDER. FOUR OR FIVE SENTENCES AN ENTRY.**

**0545.** A young man he had never formally taken on spent a whole day beside him and watched him take a chest apart, and he answered a question about a place at the end of the road by saying only that he had been there, and by refusing, flatly, when asked whether he would go again. He gave the young man the one job that matters and the young man put a joint back the way the last one had failed, and he took the clamps off and did it again himself without a word, and then did it a second time to be certain. What he said at the door that evening was about the cold, the time and the glue, and the visit he has not mentioned to anybody since November stayed where it was.

**0546.** Two people who have both spent two years letting each other go first at a road neither of them wants to be at, both said the same sentence about it on the Wednesday and both meant different things by it, and neither of them went while the other was standing there. A woman with a basket came the whole way across between them and neither had to stop for her. She has carried an answer about traffic for her own household since the November, he has carried a sentence to a man in the post about going in later, and this month she went out eleven minutes earlier than she ever has and gave no reason, and he came out at his own time, found the road empty and stood at it for a minute anyway. Neither of them will mention any of it.

**0547.** A parcel arrived for a place she had been given as a temporary in the autumn and it carried her own name over another woman's name. She asked one person one question in a corridor and was given a name and nothing that a name could be sent to, which is not enough and which she knew would not be enough before she asked. She took it home and opened it on her kitchen surface and found about a third of somebody else's work, with marks on the pattern in two colours, and she tried to carry on from the wrong side of it and had to take two inches off. She put it down twice in one evening, left the needles in it on the surface, and has not told anybody that she ever lifted it again.

**0548.** Nine days were worked on the outside of a building in a fortnight and three of them are not in the book the man keeps the hours in, and he has known since the first week and has written them down nowhere. A young man came out of a vehicle three times and told nine men to go home, and did not think about it again after the third day. The man who worked those three days came in on a Saturday he did not have to and named them, once, and the other went on filling in a week with nothing in it. The woman in the office on the ground floor worked out what had happened by herself from the book and from a man who had stopped saying good morning, and she has not put it to either of them and does not intend to.

**0549.** She had been paying for a twelfth above her own since the June, when the last person in it left, and a mild week in which nothing in that block was heated at all is what made her ask about a reading that had not moved since the December. She was given one true sentence by a woman who is right about every part of it, and she asked no second question, and she went back up and shut her door. She did the sum on a page out of a book, got the same answer twice, put the torn half of that page through the cooker door, and told the woman on the ground floor on the Monday that she would not be paying the upper part from the first of March. She will be colder for it from the last week of that month and nobody is coming to see her, and she has not asked for anybody.

**0550.** She went out with a bucket and salt on the first morning after the snow because her own door was the one you could not get through, and four other people were out before eight the next day and nine of them were doing it inside three weeks. A man who had lived on that street since about 1979 and had never once been out before nine started coming at half past seven on the twenty-fourth of February and has come at that hour ever since. She came at eight as she comes, they worked the same stripe within thirty yards of each other for about an hour, she said one sentence to him about the morning after and he gave her no answer at all. Nobody counted anybody on that street and nobody is going to, and if you had asked four people they would have given you three close numbers.

**0551.** He wrote one line down every week for two years after the water went off on a Tuesday morning, and a man came in February and opened something under a window and left without asking him a question or writing anything or turning a tap. He has not written a line since the twelfth of February and there have been three of those mornings since, and he did not decide to stop and would not know how to explain it if he were asked. The woman on the floor above heard him up at an hour she is not used to on all three, worked out four ways of asking him about it and put all four away. On the Thursday she knocked and said it was about the weather, and he said he knew, and she went back down without asking him anything, which is what she has done for six years.

**0552.** He has sold four things out of a small place since 2018 and took less than the written figure on three of them and has never once said so. In the March a bench with a vice on it came in and was priced at two hundred and ten pounds, and he went four miles home, counted out the sum the first of the four actually brought him, and came back with it. He told him that was the first price, and then said a second thing about a very good week, which he wishes he had not said. The other man has asked him nothing about the other three and is not going to, and there is nothing in the world obliging him to hand back what he has already had, and he will not.

**0553.** He said out loud in September that a path would be shut in the new year and two people carried it for six months without asking him where he heard it. In the March he went up and read a notice for himself and found the date on it was the fourth of June, which is five months after the January he had meant, and he took no photograph and wrote nothing down because there is nobody he would send either to. He told both of them the date anyway at the end of the week, and the two of them walked the path once the long way together without saying why, and one of them made a remark about mud and the other one offered no reply. Nothing has been sent to anybody and that path closes on the fourth of June and not before.

**0554.** Three small things went wrong in three places on an ordinary Monday and none of them has a person to take it to. A woman who hands out six small wages every week has been one whole figure short every week since the middle of February and has not noticed and will put it straight without mentioning it to any of the six. A woman who has had the same delivery on the same morning for nine years had it come out a day early once and was not opened by the following Tuesday, opened her door on four mornings, and has settled that she will not put a note on it. A man opened a place he had never once opened in six years and found that what had been behind it was not there, shut the door, did his day, told nobody, and has been coming in a few minutes earlier every morning since.

## Volume 05, CONTINUATION 0037 — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 555–564

**0555.** She has cooked the one thing she is responsible for the same way for four years and no week has ever contained a moment when she decided it. He watched her do it for two years and learned the rest from her, and in the first week of March he sat down with everybody else for the first time and understood what he had been eating. He let three weeks go by without raising it and then said one short thing in a corridor at ten past one, and she gave him the reason and went back downstairs. One woman agreed with him and said nothing further. He asked her nothing afterwards and the batch that went in that morning went in exactly where the one before it had gone and he ate all of it.

**0556.** She lived under a noise every night for nine years and never once let anybody know she heard it, including the nine people she does talk to in that building. It stopped inside the first week of March and nothing was done and no reason exists on the page. He was about two hours off for a month and came home on the eighteenth and stood in the shared passage waiting, without knowing that he was waiting. They have come out into that passage at the same hour four times since he got back, and each of them has worked out alone that the knocking is finished, and neither has said so to the other, and neither knows what the other has worked out. She raised it once, got as far as two words, and let a shopkeeper answer her instead. On her own date she came out and asked him why they were both standing there, and he gave her a word about goosebumps that neither of them has taken further.

**0557.** He brought the same load on the same morning every week for six years and paid the same small figure every time, and then one month there was nothing, and he told nobody. She is the only person who writes down what goes into that pit, and she found the gap only because somebody asked her a question about that month. She asked him one thing on the Friday and he gave her a reason which was accurate and which did not touch the thing she had asked about. She wrote his load down at the usual figure anyway, has not questioned him again, has not mentioned it to either of the two who come in on a Tuesday, and has gone back to the empty month twice standing up rather than sit down.

**0558.** Two people have split one job for two years and their money for it has never matched, and there is no document anywhere that says it should or should not. He arrived at the difference in the first half of March and she arrived at it four days later by accident, and neither has mentioned it since, including to the nine other people who work where they work. He sat down on the Friday, wrote a single number in a hand everybody there recognises, left it where signing happens, and left the building at two. She picked it up at four without reading it twice, folded it once, and it is still inside a jacket at home. She has not gone upstairs to see the sheet and has not asked him whether he wrote it, and she takes her days off the list in the order they arrive.

**0559.** She has swept the floor outside a flat with nobody in it since the spring it was shut, at the same hour every morning, because she was asked once by the woman who had it and nobody ever took the job back off her. A man three floors above her comes down on the mornings he has not slept and stops on her floor on the way back up, and she has known about it for two months without ever going to look. On her own date she finished later than usual and then stood still rather than go in, and she left the brush on the floor and shut the door behind her. He stepped over it on his way out and has not knocked and has not stopped coming on the mornings he has not slept.

**0560.** Three people have kept the same March Sunday in a town half an hour away for seven years and paid their own way. The middle one of them stopped going in March and let her two brothers find out at the table rather than telling them, and she did not explain it to them afterwards either. The two brothers did not ask that night, or since, and the youngest of them has not sent another photograph. She went to the youngest brother's door on the nineteenth of April with shopping and told him one thing about his path, which was not what she had come to say, and then went home. Nobody in that household has asked her why and she has not offered.

**0561.** He is the only person alive who can describe a set of buildings he built out of somebody else's rubble, and he has not been back inside the one he built since about 2011. Somebody is selling that ground and he has been given no date and no paper. A woman he had spoken to twice was asked to take him round it once with the only spare key, and she did so in April, and he gave her one sentence about each part of it and nothing else. She asked him something about himself by the tap and he answered in one word. He went back alone three weeks later and found the gate standing open with the padlock off its catch and somebody else's work in his place, stood at his own door for an hour in the sun, put a spade back without touching anything that was not his, and drove home. He has told neither the woman nor his sister and he has not been back.

**0562.** She has done one thing at the same hour every evening since 2014 in a room cold enough to need the fire on, and the man in her home has never once asked her about it, and the sound of it has gone straight through four inches of concrete every night for six years. He came down for the first time on the second of May and stood on her step for barely a moment before going back up, and the two words he said going up were not asked for by anybody. She let him go without asking him in and has not been up to his door and has not told her husband. He has not been down since, and she is aware of every sound on that way up until well past midnight, and there has been nothing since the second of May.

**0563.** They have shared two jobs in a garden every Saturday for four years and the younger one stopped turning up in January without giving a reason, and the father did the whole of it alone nine times and asked nothing. He came back in March, stood at the far end without speaking, took the handles off the machine when the father stopped it, and neither of them has said a word since. He has been there every Saturday since, which is eight of them, and on the second one the father handed him a drink without comment, which is also all that was said. On the fifth of May he rang to say he would miss the next Saturday and gave no reason, and the father gave him one syllable and nothing further, and has not said to the woman he lives with what he will be doing on the Saturday.

**0564.** Three small faults in three buildings in this borough have been going on for months and none of them has anybody attached to it. A woman on a ground floor has given up on one window that will not open and has told nobody. A man cutting grass has walked over a failing length of path edging twice a week since March without looking at it. A woman on a row of houses has swept around a wet patch every fortnight since the New Year and has never looked up to see where the water comes from. A fourth thing happened in a building by the water, where a woman who has come in on Sundays for six years found the line under the last entry still empty and left it empty, with the count beneath it now standing at a figure nobody in that room has ever read out.

## Volume 05, CONTINUATION 0038 — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 565–574

**0565.** A man on the top floor of a block of four has taken a container of water up those stairs every morning and evening since 2009 and nobody in that building has ever asked him about it. In the first week of May he had it in one hand and something else in the other and left it on the turn, and he went down early and did not go back for it. It stayed there nine days and no one said anything, and then it was gone, and there were seven of those containers in the building before and six now. He has not counted, has not asked, and is not going to. She asked him once at six in the evening and he gave her something that was not an answer, and she walked away, and that is the whole of what has passed between the two of them about it.

**0566.** Two sisters have put the same sum into the same account on the same day of the month since 2017 and have never had anything to say about the money. The younger one left one month empty and put two months' worth into the month after it, so as not to have a month standing open. The older one found it out on the twentieth of May by going through two years of her own records and adding them up against what she already knew was hers, and she came to the missing part exactly. She has told nobody, has not raised it with the other one, has not said it out loud in her own kitchen, and has not looked at those two months again. They were at the plot on three Sundays afterwards and she stayed longer than she used to and did the two ends of one length, and neither of them let it go near the conversation.

**0567.** He has opened a building at the back of a parade every morning since 2013 and has always set three boxes out in one order, for a reason that is not a good one. A woman who came to work there in the February began opening it on the mornings she was in first and put the boxes down the other way round, and she never asked him whether she should. He noticed and said nothing for ninety days. On a Monday in March she was not there and he set them out her way, and he has not said where he got it from and nobody has put it to him. He went back to his own order the next morning and has been going in later since, so most mornings are now hers, and she has not found out that he ever did it.

**0568.** He put four slates on a roof over his own back door on a Saturday in the February and told nobody, and the two he took off are still in a heap against his garage. In the wind on the twenty-ninth of May something came off that roof and went over into the garden behind the house next door, so that a piece of it landed there and a piece of it landed in his own. She found hers just before midday and his wife found his at about one, moved them out of the way and mentioned it once. She took hers round at ten that night and told him where it had come from, and he looked at it and said it was all right and shut the door. He has not been up on that roof since, and she has never asked about what else of it is still where it fell.

**0569.** She has paid her share of that household's running costs since 2015 and nobody in the building has ever asked her for anything about it. For nine days now a man on the floor below has been putting something folded down outside his own door on his way out, and she has had a week to work out what it is and has never mentioned it. She took two of them inside her own door and said nothing, and then she left the third where it lay, and it lay in that corridor for three days in front of everybody who came in. On the third of June he put another one down and she folded one of her own the way he folds his, put it by his door and went out. He found it at nine that night and put it in his own flat and said nothing, and he put another one down before he left in the morning.

**0570.** Three of them have gone at a hill about fifty minutes off in the first week of June every year since 2014 and nobody has ever known who started it or what for. In April one of them told the other two in her own kitchen that this was the end of it, said it once, said there was no need to ask, and nobody asked. All three met at the road at the bottom, walked up, stood at the top for about half an hour and came back down. Two of them went into a place and had something on plates and she sat in her car outside for twenty minutes and then drove home, and nobody has rung anybody since, and one of them said something about September that was not about any of it.

**0571.** He has carried a bundle up to her door every Monday for eight years, in two carries, and has put it inside against the side of the room and gone back down, and neither of them has ever given a reason. There has been more of it in that flat for two years than the thing it goes in can ever consume, and she has not said so. On the thirteenth of April he went up as usual and did not knock, left it against her door and went back down, and he has not been up that run since. She waited for the knock for about four seconds, heard him go, and then took it in. It is still against the side of that room, unbroken, and none of it has been used, and they meet at the front door about twice a week and talk about the day and the weather.

**0572.** She has spent one evening a week away from that canteen since 2013 and the man at the seat facing hers has never once put a question to her about it, in eleven years of eating there. On the sixteenth of June he did not get up when he normally finishes, and when she left he sat on until about twenty to ten and then went out and round to the front and got the service. He came back twelve minutes late, which is what that journey costs, and she had her tea in both hands and did not look up. He has not sat on after his own time since, neither of them has raised the twelve minutes, and he has four things he worked out about that evening in eleven years and has never gone a step past them.

**0573.** He has let his own front door stand open for about a minute at seven every morning since the year he came into that house, and it is not done for anybody else at all and he has never tried to say what it is for. A woman nine feet away has been up since ten to six for longer than she can remember and has watched that door every morning without once counting it. On the twentieth of June it did not open at seven, and she waited without knowing what for, finished her tea and did not go out to anything. He did it an hour later the same morning. Neither of them has said anything about either half of it, neither of them is going to, and the door opened at seven the next morning as it had every morning for eight years.

**0574.** Three faults in three places in this borough are going to keep going wrong and none of them has anybody attached to it. One end of a flag on a footpath has lifted and rocks under a heel, and a man who walks over it thirty times a day has not looked down at it. A front door in one block needs a hand under its bottom edge before it will shut, and three people lift it every morning and every evening without thinking about it. The same fault is on a door in a block about a mile off, of the same make and hanging the same way, and the man who lives there has been there since 2004 and has never decided whether that is the door or his hands. Nobody who lives in one of those blocks knows anybody in the other, nobody has reported any of it, and and the thing in this borough that nobody has ever got into words is still here, and not one person here would have the least idea what to do with it.

## Volume 05, CONTINUATION 0039 — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 575–584

**0575 — Monday the twenty-ninth of June 2020.** A woman in a launderette told a man she has spoken to about six times in two years that her husband has been going since March, and because of where she was sitting and what is behind the back of her head and a dryer that has been running hot since before the middle of April, that sentence went into that room as a report on the dryer. He got up, went along the far side, crouched down at the end of the hot one, said it was in there and that he would have a proper look at it after his tea, and she said *right* and drank her tea. She heard him take it that way and she let him. She took it back to the dryer on the way home and twice more that afternoon, and worked out by about three that it was not that he had it wrong, it was that he got up, and that if she had said *I meant my husband* it would have been a different sentence with nothing in it and he would not have got up. A woman in her early sixties heard every word of it and turned a page of a newspaper she was not reading and turned it back again, which she has never once done, and has not told anybody and is not going to. A man in his early thirties was not listening and has no version of it at all.

**0576 — Friday the third of July 2020.** In a second-floor kitchen a man in his late sixties reads his wife's mouth, and has done so long enough that a sentence said over a kettle or a radio at any volume does not arrive, and he has never once said so. She said *I've had enough of it* quietly at about seven with the kettle going and he got two words of it. She said it again louder and it still did not arrive. Their daughter, who has been in that kitchen on Friday evenings for two years, heard all three. Their mother then said *Then you can do it yourself* at a volume she had not used in that kitchen before and it went straight across, because nothing was under it and he was not reading anybody's mouth. He said *right*, filled the kettle, sat down, did not ask what the first sentence had been, and about ten minutes later asked whether it was a Thursday week for the collection. The daughter had her own sentence about a fortnight and a bannister and a thing she has been doing on her own since before the February, and she could have said it after the second one and would have got somebody to go at it, and she did not, and she knows exactly why and has never once asked herself.

**0577 — Tuesday the seventh of July 2020.** A woman in her early fifties has been going in and out of a small workshop since about 2009 without a key and has said *that's no trouble* to everybody in it about everything for years. On the Friday before she said it with her hands under one end of a length of stock. On the Tuesday morning at about nine, while she stood on the other side of a partition with her back to him, a man who has been in that building six days a week since before she started coming in said the same four words to another woman, out loud, without looking round, and then said he would go and get a part. She stopped for about four seconds and carried on with it. He had never once used those words in the time she has been coming. She put the bar down at about half past nine and said *you never used to say that*, and he said *I might have been saying it before you ever came in here*, which is a fair thing for him to have said. She has gone back through the whole of it and there is not one morning she could put her hand on, and she cannot say that he took it off her and she cannot say that he did not.

**0578 — Sunday the twelfth of July 2020.** In April a man asked a woman outside a shop to do a thing at the end of that month and said why do you have to think about it, you have never asked me for anything, and she said *I'd rather not* and nothing came of it. A third woman was in the back of that car, had asked for the lift herself, heard both halves, and said nothing because it was not hers. That conversation was over on the Wednesday of that week and she watched it end and nobody in it has ever said out loud that it ended. On the Sunday evening, in a hired club with twelve people in it, he turned round and asked her to do the same thing again and she gave him the same four words back before he had finished. The third woman said out loud, across four rows, *You asked me that in April. Outside the shop.* He said *You did, yes*, and did not ask which April, and turned back round. The woman in her late twenties went outside for about a minute and a half and came back in and sat down. The third woman did not get up and did not go out and could not see any way of getting it back out that would not make it worse, and had known that before she opened her mouth.

**0579 — Wednesday the fifteenth of July 2020.** Under a shelter a man in his mid sixties said five words to a woman in his early thirties and meant his brother, whom he has not seen since the middle of the February and who is at home on Saturdays only. She took it as being about the truck that stands across the gate of number fifty-one on Saturdays, which is what anybody on that row would have taken it as, and said *right*. Later that morning he came out and told her and a woman in her late fifties that he had not seen his brother since the February, twice, in slightly different words, and both versions had a Saturday in them and neither had the truck in it. At about half past three the woman in her late fifties went up to number fifty-one and told the other one what he had meant. She stood in her own open door for about three seconds and said nothing at all — not a word, not a shake of the head, not the face she would have made if she had been about to disagree — and shut the door the way anybody shuts a door when somebody else is walking up the row behind them. The woman who told her went back down the row and did not knock again. At about six he came out for his tea and said the shop was shut and that it was three days off Saturday and he had plenty of time, and she said *right* and went in.

**0580 — Saturday the eighteenth of July 2020.** A man in his late fifties has driven nine boys seventeen miles each way for six seasons in his own car, told nobody including his own wife, and decided at the end of June to stop, and carried it about for a fortnight. At about ten, with the second half about to start, he put the crate down on the touchline and said, flatly, *That's me finished.* He meant the driving. A man in his late thirties who has been coming since the February heard that he was finished with him, said *right*, and then did not move the crate. He stood on the halfway line with his hands behind his back and did not go down the row once, let a ball go past that would have gone two yards, called nothing, and did not take the spare ball up. When the boys came off the man in his late fifties picked up the crate and the other man watched him do it from about fifteen feet away. The man who said it noticed at about quarter past ten, because the crate was the wrong way round before the February and is right way round now and nobody picked it up. He could have said *I meant the driving*, and saying it would have taken half a second and cost him the fortnight he spent deciding it, and he did not.

**0581 — Thursday the twenty-third of July 2020.** At the railings of a playing field a woman of seventy-one asked a man in his early forties whether she would do again in the August what she has done since the February — twice a week, always the same two days, to the hospital, paid in cash into her hand every single time so that there was no occasion to write anything down — and she said no. He said *right*, and then she said *You knew when you asked me in the February. You knew I'd say no*, and he said *I did* without taking a moment. He did not apologise and she did not ask him why he had asked, and neither has brought the February up since. What the two sentences did to the rest of the evening was not visible from outside: for about a minute the two of them were the only people in the borough who knew what they were talking about. They walked the length of the street at the speed of two people with nowhere in particular to be, went into the shop, stood where the buses stop for two buses, and he went off up the road at about ten to nine. She has not rung him and did not think of ringing him.

**0582 — Monday the twenty-seventh of July 2020.** A man in his late forties has been asking one question since the February and had four answers before these two. At ten on the twenty-seventh he asked a woman in her mid forties on a towpath whether it got any easier, and she thought about it properly and said it turned for her from about the May. At about half past four he knocked at number nine and asked a woman of seventy-two the same question exactly, and she said no, not one bit of it, that you get to know what to do and then it is not any lighter, it is just that you know what to do. He then told her that somebody on her street said it turned for them after the May. That was not a lie, and it was not even much of a shape, and the woman of seventy-two took it to mean she was the one who had not managed it and went back inside with it. He had decided on the walk back at about half past one not to go and tell the first one, because he has no account of it that is both complete and something either of them could carry.

**0583 — Friday the thirty-first of July 2020.** A man in his early fifties came into the back of a pub on his own and, at about half past nine, put his face about a foot from a woman of sixty-two and said into the noise: *You can tell her it was you that asked and she was never told.* Then he put two pound notes down and went back to the bar. The woman of sixty-two reads mouths and had him for about the whole of it. The woman of sixty-five listens past the noise and had the whole of it. Both wrote it down — the first on the back of a fiver in biro, the second on the left-hand half of a pad she keeps inside a jumper — and the two writings came out four words apart, and the four words are *could* and *at the time*. They went out into the road because it had got cooler and worked through it word by word. The three words and the modal are the whole of the disagreement, and what the sentence does is entirely in the four words at the end of it, and those four words are in both writings, in the same order, with a full stop after them. Both were certain and neither mentioned it. The woman of sixty-five wrote out the wording she was going to use on the Sunday, tore it away along the fold, folded it twice and put it away.

**0584 — Wednesday the fifth of August 2020.** At about half past nine a woman in her late seventies, standing in the door of a shop with a jar in her hand, said six words to a man in his mid thirties: *I won't say anything to him.* There was no third person. He thought about it at about twenty to twelve standing at the till and worked out that the somebody was the man two doors along who has been digging at the front of her garden since about the June, and at about twenty past two he put a note through her door saying he would ring the council and let her know either way. He did not expect to hear anything and did not particularly want to. She found it at about half past three and carried it through to the kitchen and put it face down in the box she keeps the things she means to deal with in, and there is a great deal in that box. At six in the evening the six words were still true and nobody had to do a single thing about them. A fountain in a square has run brown for its first half minute since before the middle of July and nobody has reported it. The fourth space in an alley has had a broken catch since the June and holds the best-kept thing in that alley. A barometer above a bar has not moved since the June and the man behind that bar does not know what the weather is doing. The three have nothing to do with each other and none of them has anything to do with the six words.

**0590 — Monday the thirty-first of August 2020.** A man in his mid forties and a woman in his mid forties, thirteen years married, are emptying a two-up two-down at number sixteen the night before a van neither of them can move. At about twenty to seven she says the first sentence anybody has said about that house in thirty-one years that was true: *It was a good house and we were no good in it, and I'm only sorry we took this long to work that out.* He says *that's about the size of it*, and drives the length of the county to his brother's. **0591 — Thursday the third of September 2020.** A man in his early fifties is paid four hundred pounds to talk for two hours in a municipal hall about how to fill your days when you have retired. ## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0042 — CHAPTERS 605–614

- **0605 — The Wood Up Three Flights.** Friday the twentieth of November 2020. A man in his late thirties carries firewood up three flights of stairs to a flat on the top floor of a block, has done since before the summer, and has never asked why. A woman in her early fifties has a boiler that has not worked since June. He buys wood green and stands it in his own yard until the weight has gone out of it, which he finds by breaking a piece across his knee. Today the man who owns the block tells him the fire is finished with and that a flue will be looked at on the Tuesday after a gas man comes. He tells the woman he will see her Saturday, carries the bag up again the same morning, and afterwards stands on a landing with his hand on the tape and works out four things, of which the fourth is that he cannot tell which of the first three is a reason and which is not. Going back up he realises she has never asked him anything once, and reads the silence as being about the wood. At a quarter to five he puts the bag on the board by her mat and knocks on a shut door. On the way down he understands that the reason he will give her on Saturday involves a nurse who does not exist.
- **0606 — The Number in Pencil.** Wednesday the twenty-fifth of November 2020. A woman in her early fifties wrote a mobile number on the back of a mattress envelope in July with the word *ask* beside it, and has not rung it. She moved it out of the kitchen drawer and up onto the hall shelf on the Saturday, and that shelf is where everything she has meant to do goes. Her husband in his early fifties comes in from the supermarket and the two of them have the entire conversation in a few seconds: she asks whether she has decided, says she decided in the summer not to, then says she has not decided, and he says she has decided and then undecided. She goes into the hall, takes a chair up onto the floor because the shelf is over a cupboard, and puts a folder of two hundred photographs out beside the envelope. She has worked out that this shelf is not a hiding place, because nobody goes and looks in a hiding place, and that she arranged it from before the summer without knowing she was arranging it. He later notices the chair and says there is a lot on that shelf now. At six she leaves the chair standing in front of it and goes to the bus stop.
- **0607 — The Steps He Does Not Take.** Tuesday the first of December 2020. A man in his mid thirties teaches in a school on the other side of town and drives there, and his route has grown a spur past a church that leads to an estate and back, and it costs him time and saves him nothing. He has measured the long way twice by the clock in his car and has decided he would rather not know the figure than know it badly. He worked it out once, properly, over a stretch of driving in the summer, that the gap in the middle of his morning does not exist, and he has told nobody. Sitting in his car at ten past four on the Tuesday he works out that he would have to be able to say out loud what the turn is, and does not get further. On the drive home he finds the turn is harder to come out of than to go into and has never tested that. The woman in the passenger seat has noticed his windscreen wipers and has asked him once whether he is going the long way.
- **0608 — The Tables.** Saturday the fifth of December 2020. A man in his late twenties has his mother's key and it no longer turns, because a woman in his late sixties who has the care of it and does not live in it changed the cylinder. He has been to the door about seven times since before the summer and gets in by knocking. Today he carried a chair out of the front room to the garage, because that is where the work happens, and put it in the garage, and came back. While he was in the front room with her he took the sill off the window, carried it round into the garage on his shoulder, and worked on it there on the bench, because that is where the work is done so that nobody is shown anything: cut the old paint off, cut new bead to length off the offcut, got it level, two screws in. He stopped with the third screw in his fingers, because he drilled in June and found the stud behind the frame is not there any more and moving the bead along an inch would fix it for good on that same bench in ten minutes, and because finishing it would leave him no reason to come back and no reason to knock. He came round the side and saw her standing in a lit front window and understood that she was standing in the light so that anybody on the road would see somebody in. The screw is on a table under a stack of post at home.
- **0609 — The Set of Twelve.** Thursday the tenth of December 2020. A man in his mid forties did not go to his mother's funeral and there are twelve people who did, and he has their names, and he has had the list since before the summer and gone over it nine times since before the summer in a kitchen, in a car park and in bed. He cannot get to nine of the twelve, the fifth among them, and of the three he can get to two or three live right by the ones he cannot. He has decided not to write, been pleased with the decision, then worked out that a decision ought to have a shape and his does not. He drives past four doors in this borough in order to check that the count is still twelve and could draw you the four, and it is not about the houses. His wife asks him three times whether he has decided. Late at night he runs through the list aloud by himself in his own kitchen and puts the envelope back with the post, and the chapter closes on the reason he cannot let the twelfth name arrive in the form that would give him something to do.
- **0610 — The Bag on the Wall.** Wednesday the sixteenth of December 2020. A woman in her early sixties, a nurse until 2014, makes a carrier bag every Wednesday morning and puts it on a low wall by a door and stands next to it. There is a list of twelve items in a plastic wallet with three of them ringed, and the list is what the whole arrangement rests on. The woman it is for is in her mid twenties, lives a couple of hundred yards up the road, and has not been asked one single question about any of it. Today, for the first time, the list is not in the bag, and she cannot account for that. The woman comes out of her front door at a quarter to twelve, puts her hand in the bag and finds nothing where the list should be. The nurse works out, standing in her own hall at half past twelve, that the list is not for her and is the reason she is still wanted, and that both of them have known that since before the summer. - **0611 — Twenty-Eight Names In A Canteen At Seven.** Monday the twenty-first of December 2020. A man in his mid fifties copies a waiting list into a sheet of A4 in a canteen before the building is full and puts a line under every name, and has done since before the summer. He started because a sequence of weeks will not stay in his head. A man in his early twenties comes in, says he is in early, notes that he is there before the lights come on, gets a tea and leaves a sheet of paper face down under his cup. He does not think about it for a while. Then he thinks: nothing happened. At ten past seven he puts the sheet in a lever-arch file behind a dead folder, which is what a document goes into when it is finished, and takes it out again at ten, and puts it in his coat. - **0612 — The Lamp and the Armchair.** Friday the twenty-fifth of December 2020. A woman who is thirty-one was asked in a kitchen, before this summer, to go and see whether a house was all right, went, found it all right, and went the next Friday, and has never been able to account for the second visit or any since. She has gone up a terrace every Friday since the June to sit on a wing chair for a few minutes and plug in a lamp. She was given keys in a car park at the end of that road on the way to signing the paperwork and has never once used them and has not given them back. The front door is on the latch and she has never worked out whether somebody in that house leaves it on the latch for her or whether it has been on the latch since long before she had a key. Today she goes up with the keys in her hand, does not use them, and goes in anyway. Inside, she finds the sister-in-law of the woman who is away living there, who has known about the lamp and the chair throughout. She works out that she has been coming for something to be needed, that she is not needed, and that there is nobody in the house at all while she does it. The keys go back into the cloth bag on the passenger seat, and she tells the woman in her own kitchen that she has not been since before, which is untrue and is let stand.
- **0613 — The Bench He Took Off a Wall.** Thursday the thirty-first of December 2020. A man in his late fifties builds things and cut a welded iron gate off the side of a garage he had no business on in September, at seven in the morning, and carried a lump of somebody's slab away with it. It has been in his boot and in his van and on a trailer and, once, in a scrapyard office where he put it down and took it home. He paid a man ninety pounds to cut the slab off the foot. He has been to four other gates with a tape measure and has not asked the price of anything at any of them. On the Saturday he meets the man in his early forties who now rents the garage and finds the wall was re-clad two summers ago and stands proud of the post by about an inch. He writes the inch on the back of his hand and stops. He tells the man he will not charge, will not put his name on it, and will ring a fitter for him. He sets the gate down on the soil at the back of his own garden, where his own wall would take it exactly, and does not open the paint tin he bought in September.
- **0614 — Three Drawings and a Tape.** Tuesday the fifth of January 2021. A woman in her mid forties has had a bathroom drawn three times since the summer before last by a man in his mid sixties who is very good at it, and has paid for two of them. Each drawing alters a single detail, so there is always one new and good reason not to make the call. He asks her, for the first time, whether she is going anywhere with it at all, and she says she will ring him. She drives to a retail park and turns down nine bathrooms on reasons that are all real and none of which is the reason. In her car she works out four things, and the fourth of them is that producing another drawing would be easier than either of the other two options. She draws one this afternoon with a credit card and a shoe, gets the window in the wrong place and knows within a second, puts two doors in and crosses one out. Sitting in the front room she sees that this is not a set of drawings but a way of not deciding, done properly, and that nobody knows she does it. She measures the room for the first time in her life and finds the cistern end of the floor is where it always dips, which she learned about at mid-morning, and which she is now going to have to tell somebody.
