- **0615 — The Man at the Top of Our Road.** Tuesday 12 January 2021. A man in his early sixties is told at a bus stop by a woman in her late sixties who lives six houses below him that somebody at the far end of that road is in a home. She called him the man at the top, gave no source, and got on the bus. He spends the day failing to establish how she knew something she could not know: at a shop on the parade, standing at a bus stop on the wrong side watching a door three times, at a church board, and on the telephone to his daughter in Leeds, whom he does not tell. He gets to the bottom of the road at half past five and turns round, because going up would make it a thing he did. His neighbour brings a casserole dish and tells him the man keeps a light on until nine. He does not go up the road.
- **0616 — The House He Meant.** Sunday 17 January 2021. A woman in her mid thirties is told in a lane behind the parade by a boy in his late teens at the top of her road that her house has been put up. She has two houses in her head: the flat she is in, and the house on the estate that was sold before the summer and has been on the market since before it, and her sister tells her it has not sold. She finds the boy, is told by a woman in her late fifties at his door that he is out, walks the parade, stands at her own front door at four for the first time since before the summer and finds no board. She has not rung the agent, has not gone up the estate road, and has not asked the boy anything.
- **0617 — The Shop He Does Not Use.** Saturday 23 January 2021. A man in his late fifties goes into a hardware shop on the parade because his usual is shut, and a woman in her mid fifties behind the till tells him his wife has been in for a bulb, standing where he is standing, and tells him which way up a bulb goes. He knows his wife has not been. He works out four explanations, can live with three, and drives to work and sits in a car park. He cannot ask his wife because the question would make him a man in a shop on the other side of a kitchen. He comes home, makes her a tea, and asks whether she wants a bulb. She has never once been asked about a bulb and says so.
- **0618 — The Chair She Was In.** Wednesday 27 January 2021. A man in his early thirties cuts a customer's hair in a barber's shop he has taken over. A regular in her mid sixties advises him, mid-cut, that a daughter of about that age ought to be telephoning him more often, and gets the age off a school she names herself and the rest of it off his own face in the mirror behind her. He has never had one. He finishes the cut without dropping anything, works the rest of the day, cannot design the only test that exists, gets his phone out and puts it back in a drawer, and does not ask her. She is back in that chair before the month is out. His flatmate notices he has said he is all right twice.
- **0619 — The One Who Has Taken It On.** Wednesday 3 February 2021. A woman in her early forties, one of two dinner supervisors, is told across a kitchen by a woman in her early thirties who is better at the job that she is the one who has taken it on. She writes down eight things she has taken on and rules all eight out, and on the way home thinks of a ninth she has no way to rule out and cannot get rid of. The other woman says in the queue that she never asked what was meant. At half past three the kitchen is empty, the other is on the phone at the wall, and she stands in the doorway knowing she has a minute and does not use it, and props the outside door open with a brick. She would rather it was about somebody.
- **0620 — The Terrace With the Gable.** Saturday 6 February 2021. A man in his mid forties is told in a yard by a man he has spoken to twice that the row his mother grew up in is to be cleared. He has a mother he could have asked at any time for years and does not, because she has never mentioned the row and he has never asked, and something sits between those two facts. He writes two lists on the back of a fuel receipt, drives to a crossing and stands on an island, and does not ring her. She rings him at about ten past five, talks about a woman who wants the top flat, and tells him without being asked that a roofer went down that row and she is not selling. The origin of the claim is traced to a tradesman who called at the wrong end of that row, and the whole of it turns out to have been nothing.
- **0621 — The Woman That Did the Saturdays.** Friday 12 February 2021. A woman in her mid twenties, the only one on the floor of a phone shop she works two days a week, is asked by a man in his early fifties for a woman who used to do the Saturdays, and who can give him the first letter of her name and nothing else of it. She says there has never been anybody else. He goes next door, comes back, says the woman there is covering, and writes down an address on the far side of the town. At about twenty past two he asks her for one of them that is shut at one on a Saturday, and she gives him a straight answer, and the straight answer is what loses him. Three shops on that parade are open on a Saturday and he walked past them.
- **0622 — The Woman at the Corner of the Car Park.** Wednesday 17 February 2021. A man in his late thirties is told in a car park by a woman in her early fifties that a woman has been twice to the building he works in, asking after a man by name, and that she is his daughter. He cannot establish which of the three women who worked there with him. He does his day and does it well and is frightened by that. He finds the woman at four and asks her three questions, and tells her why he is not saying he is the man, and she would have believed him. He writes at his own kitchen table, that he has no answer ready for the case where he was the man being looked for been him.
- **0623 — The Name at the Gate.** Saturday 20 February 2021. A man in his mid sixties, a school caretaker, is told on a pavement opposite by a woman in her late thirties that a stranger has said a name at that office and walked away with a second one, which is not the same name. He puts his bag of salt down and never picks it up. He works out four explanations and settles on the fourth, which is that it is not about a man at all. He does the whole of the building, stands at the gate from the inside and confirms there is no name on any of it, does not ring a man in his phone he has not rung in years, and asks her four things, the last of them whether the man gave the name or she gave it, and is satisfied with the answer. He has said nothing to anybody at the school.
- **0624 — The Woman on the Other Side of the Table.** Friday 26 February 2021. A man in his late twenties is told across a canteen table by a woman in his early sixties that he once asked after her knee and then stopped, and that she has thought about it more than he would want to know. He says no and is not believed by anybody including himself. He spends the day on it and establishes that he has never asked after anybody and cannot prove it. He is at the window at ten to five and his wife finds him standing there like a man waiting on a bus, and knows of a woman at the third table without knowing her name. He had until four to ask her and did not.

# VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0044 — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 625–634

**EACH SUMMARY IS WRITTEN AGAINST THE CHAPTER FILE AND NOT AGAINST THE WRITER'S MEMORY OF IT, AND EVERY FIGURE NAMED BELOW IS AGED EXACTLY AS THE CHAPTER AGES IT. **THE READ-BACK OF THIS BATCH FOUND THAT THE ALLOCATION NAMED A WOMAN IN HER EARLY FORTIES FOR 0626 AND THAT THE CHAPTER AGED HER NOWHERE, AND THE BAND WAS WRITTEN INTO THE PROSE ON THE READ-BACK, WHICH IS THE FIX 0043 USED AND IS NOT A FIX. IT IS NOTED HERE SO THAT A LATER WRITER KNOWS THAT SENTENCE IN 0626 EXISTS BECAUSE OF A COUNT.**

- **0625 — The Bin on a Wednesday.** Monday 1 March 2021. A woman in her late thirties has put her neighbour's red bin out on a Wednesday morning for a good while and has decided, on the Sunday night, to stop. Her husband, a man in his mid forties, asks her why in the kitchen at a quarter to seven and she says the man has never once asked her, and the reason is not the reason, which is that she heard him tell the woman two doors down on a pavement that he would have to get somebody to do it. He asks her four times what the thing is and is told nothing four times. She watches him struggle with the bin from an upstairs window on the Thursday, and counts the times she has said the sentence, and works out that if he had come to her gate and asked her she would have said yes.
- **0626 — The One He Sent.** Friday 5 March 2021. The neighbour, a man in his early sixties, has decided to ask her again and does not knock. The woman two doors down — **who is the woman at the end of the terrace and is aged late thirties in 0625, 0633 and 0634, and whom this summary used to print as a woman in her early forties, a band the chapter does not carry and never did** — stands in his gate with a sack truck at a quarter past six and asks him why he has not asked, and he says because he asked. He did not ask her; he asked the woman two doors down to pass it on, and she never went, and he told himself on the Saturday night that the message had gone. He carries the bin back in and the Wednesday collection misses it. At about half past six she comes up his row with an envelope and he tells her, at his own door, the one true sentence he has not said out loud, and that he is not going up the row because she would want to know why he sent somebody.
- **0627 — The Woman Who Told Him.** Wednesday 10 March 2021. The woman at number six, a woman in her mid thirties, has decided to stop passing on what other people tell her. A man in his late twenties in the house with her asks her why she came home and told him a thing about a bin, and she says *because he asked*, in the tone she uses for the weather. She knocks at the man's door at half past three and he tells her he asked the woman two doors down because he could not stand at her gate, and she says she knows, and she had known since the Saturday. She does the bin. She works out afterwards that four words have come to her through two other mouths and that she gave them away without knowing they were words.
- **0628 — The Joke He Told On Purpose.** Monday 15 March 2021. A man in his early thirties has said five words at least three times without being able to remember saying them first. He writes four lines on the back of a fuel receipt, the fourth of them being that he knows it is not true and he is going to lie to a woman who does his washing for nothing. He stands in a doorway at about seven in the evening and says them to the woman in his mid forties below him. She tells him he said the same thing about a year ago. He works out at about seven that it worked, and at about nine that he has used a decent woman as an instrument, and that he cannot undo it without her deciding which of them he is. At ten he tells her it was a joke and she tells him it was not.
- **0629 — The List She Did Not Take.** Friday 19 March 2021. A woman in her late sixties has decided, on a Wednesday night just before midnight, to stop doing a man in his late sixties's shopping. At her gate on the Friday morning he asks her why she has not been and she gives him five words that are about his son and not about him, and says so in the same breath. In a queue on the parade at about a quarter to twelve she hears a stranger say the same five words in the voice of a man who has heard a thing a good many times, and puts her basket down on the kerb. On the telephone she tells him the reason she gave at the gate was the wrong reason, and that his son telephoned her late at night and she said yes, and that she is tired of it.
- **0630 — The Thing She Said Out Loud.** Thursday 25 March 2021. A woman in her early sixties has been going to a man's house on a Wednesday afternoon for most of a working life and has decided to go on, and to say so out loud to somebody who did not ask. She says it on four steps outside a church to a man in his mid thirties. When he asks her why she is telling him she gives him the truth, which is that a man she sat with when she was still in her thirties stood up before he asked her, and that none of the rest of it — a sister, a woman at work, a neighbour with her bins — is the thing. He says he believes her too quickly and she tells him so. She finds the five words going round and finds she has been saying them. She has stopped. It does not get lighter.
- **0631 — The Man Who Went Round With It.** Tuesday 30 March 2021. A man in his mid fifties who fits frames has been saying the five words since the middle of February and finds on the Monday that they have been attached to a house number on his own estate. He decides to go round four streets in one day and say they came off him, and decides not to say that he got them off a young man at the top of a house who said them first at a door. A woman in her mid twenties at number thirty-one, who works on a depot and is on her own, asks him why he is coming round and he tells her there is nothing at the end of it, which is not true, and she shuts the door on that and not on him. He has two reasons and knows which came first.
- **0632 — The Woman Who Went Up The Hill.** Saturday 3 April 2021. A woman in her mid fifties at number nineteen has heard the five words from two women at the depot who each say they got them off the old man at number four. She gets a bus up the hill at a quarter past nine on a Saturday. He asks her why people say it and gives her a woman at number twenty-six and a set of curtains and years of it, and tells her it is nothing to do with her question. He tells her the words came off a man who will not say where he got them. She goes down the hill with two hands that will not join up, and does not go back, because the girl at number thirty-one was told it first by the man in the van.
- **0633 — Every Door On The Row.** Thursday 8 April 2021. The woman who said the five words in her own kitchen on the first of March has decided to go round the row and say they came off her, and writes it in a notebook which is not a diary. She knocks at eight doors in the rain and says it at all eight, and gets nothing at two, and something she did not expect at three. At number five a man in his late thirties comes to the door with a plate in his hand and asks her why she is saying it, and she says because she wants it stopped at the person it is on, and will not say the other half, which is that she would rather the sentence belonged to her.
- **0634 — The One He Asked.** Tuesday 13 April 2021. The woman telephones on the Sunday and asks to come, and he repeats it back, which he has never done. He asks her why she is coming and she gives him the same reason. He asks her why she wanted the sentence on herself and she refuses to answer it. He then tells her that in the February, on a Saturday, about a fortnight before the first of March, he asked her for the bin and she said she could not do it that day and he said right and did not ask again. He has decided not to go round and clear a half-true thing about himself. He sends her to number eight with a fact she cannot use and about a girl on an estate whom neither of them can reach, and she has not gone, because it is dark.
- **0635 — The Chair Off The Back Step.** Monday 19 April 2021. A woman in her late forties who clears houses is in a garage off a road behind the parade with a lad in his early twenties and a list of seven things on the back of an invoice. She takes a folding chair with a split leg out of it although it is not on the list, after a ninety-second telephone call in which the owner asks her to take it off her. She mends it on her own back step in the last of the light with a punch, a hammer, a block of wood, a length of angle iron off a gate she never took back and a box of tap washers under the sink, badly, and then properly. She knows the chair is going to a woman in her late seventies at number twelve who eats standing up, and she has known it the way you know a thing somebody has not told you, which is that she has heard somebody eating through a kitchen door twice while she was getting a roll of tape. She will not give it on a Monday or any day but a Sunday, and will not say where it came from, because the only sentence available in this borough for a thing somebody has brought you is a debt.
- **0636 — The Man Who Came For The Fridge.** Saturday 24 April 2021. The chair arrives at number twelve and the woman in her late seventies accepts it in a minute and a half without asking, because the only kitchen chair she has has had a split leg since before Christmas. She reads the mending — a piece of angle iron, a bolt, a washer, a pale gouge in a step — and works out that nobody does that to a chair going to a skip, and does not ask, and is aware that the woman at the door told her not to ask. She eats sitting down for the first time since before Christmas and gets up twice to stand at the sink and then at the window. She puts the chair on her step for the damp and a woman at number ten asks where she got it, and she invents a man who came round in March about the fridge. A man did come round in March, for the way down to the parade. The whole thing is a lie and it is not, and the cost is a woman at number ten carrying a thing that happened.
- **0637 — The Stool.** Thursday 29 April 2021. A man in his early forties who makes kitchens has known for a while that the woman at number twelve eats standing. On the Monday he is on a tower in the road at gutter height outside a first-floor conversion ten doors up, at the height of her kitchen window, and sees a green folding chair standing in the middle of that kitchen floor, and a woman at a sill with a plate. He decides on a stool rather than a chair, because a chair is for somebody sitting down somewhere else and a stool is a thing a room has, and because there is already a chair in there he cannot account for and he is not going to find out. Ash, oak rails, an inch and a half by three-quarters, dry at half past ten on the Thursday, the best thing he has made since February. He builds it too heavy, takes the weight out of three rails, and at half past four a man in his mid thirties at the bench opposite asks him what it is for and he says it is for a mate who has done his own kitchen, and he has had that answer ready since half past ten in the morning.
- **0638 — Two Things In One Kitchen.** Wednesday 5 May 2021, about ten past eight in the evening. He copies her knock. She opens after two minutes and the whole doorstep is five sentences. He puts a stool on four steps of tile and unwraps the blanket off it. She asks where he got it and he says he made it, which is true, and she can see the three dark rails and the one pale one, and the height is right, and the ring is not, and she says it is nice, that. On a pavement thirty yards away he works out that the correct answer was the answer that put a live man in her kitchen with no number to telephone. She moves the stool against the sink, sits on it at ten at night, and works out that she now has two things in one kitchen and one story, and the story is about a man who is not real. At half past six the next morning she is at the window with a cloth in her hand and works out that she can swap one for the other in a minute and cannot survive them both being in the room, and that she does not know which one she would look at.
- **0639 — The Queue On The Parade.** Saturday 8 May 2021. A woman in her late twenties at the front of a queue in the shop on the parade says to her friend that a man has come round about a fridge, in a house none of them has been in, about an old brick one that is coming out. Two yards in front of her, the woman in her late seventies does not move, and works out in about ten seconds that the two sentences are not the same sentence and that there is no version of a Saturday morning in this borough in which a woman does not hear the word fridge. Behind the woman in her late twenties is a man in his early forties with a prescription he has meant to take in since before the bank holiday, and in about two seconds he joins the sentence onto a green folding chair he saw through a window from a tower. He builds a four-sentence speech in the queue and does not use it, because the only thing she could have said back was the lie. She goes home at twenty past ten. He stands on the parade a minute and a half and does not get in the van.
- **0640 — The Leg On The Stool.** Friday 14 May 2021, ten past ten to half past ten. She comes up with a spanner because the chair is going to go over with a woman in it, which is true, and the only sentence that carries that does not also carry where it came from, which is a garage on a road behind the parade and a house somebody has finished with. The woman at number seventy-eight opens with a joke about the spanner through the door, which takes the legs out of her. She works on the chair for ten minutes, and notices that she has said *that's why I'm here* and that the woman did not point it out. Then she gets up off the floor and looks at a stool for five seconds and cannot lift it with one hand. And the woman at number twelve says, before she can ask, that it came off a man on the road. She knows inside a second and a half that the sentence was got ready. She says nothing back, and then mends the stool as well, twelve minutes, on her knees, with the gas on low under the sink. And on the way down she works out that nobody asked her for anything and that she has been given a job.
- **0641 — The Two Lies In One Kitchen.** Wednesday 19 May 2021. She has been swapping a chair and a stool twice a day since the fifth of May for nobody. On the Wednesday morning she stands on the folding chair on a table to get a tin off the top shelf and the leg she was never properly fixed goes, and she lands on the tiles with her wrist in the gap between a table leg and the oven, and gets herself up and lies on the settee with a bag of frozen vegetables on it. At half past ten the man who made the stool knocks, and she asks him for the stool, and he brings it and sets it down two feet off and does not come nearer. At ten to twelve the woman who brought the chair arrives, and in about four seconds of silence each of them works out the same sum. Then the woman on the settee tells the man that the woman is the council about the damp, and tells the woman that the man did her daughter's kitchen, and the second lie is about a house she does not have and a daughter she has not got. He leaves his card on the table, which he has never done, and thinks on the pavement that she is standing in front of somebody on behalf of the other one. She follows twenty minutes later. She has three stories in the house now and the oldest is the thinnest.
- **0642 — The Bench On The Parade.** Monday 24 May 2021, half past two to ten past three. The woman in her late forties rings the number on the card, ostensibly about the table. On a bench on the parade with a foot and a half of cold iron between them, each learns that the other was told something false by the same woman in the same front room. Neither uses it. Each says the one true thing the other does not know they have: the skip, and the weight taken out of three rails, and the lie told to a man on a bench. And they agree on exactly one thing, which is that they will both keep on coming and will not tell her they have met, and both of them know inside four minutes that it is the wrong thing. On the bench he works out that she is being kept apart for her own good, and cannot see from there that keeping her apart is what she has been doing by herself since the fifth of May.
- **0643 — The Step At Number Nine.** Thursday 27 May 2021. She decides at her own window on the Sunday to stop swapping. The only way to take a thing out of a story is to give it to somebody else, and she has known since the Monday that the woman at number nine also eats standing, because of a shape at a kitchen window, seen from her own window. She takes the stool down at nine, puts it on the top step facing the road the way a chair is put out, and does not knock. The woman in her late fifties opens and says it is not hers, and the woman in her late seventies gives her three answers she has used before and then a fourth one she has not: *I've had two and I couldn't stand the room with them in it.* She tells the whole of it. The woman at number nine takes the stool inside with one hand, easily. She goes back up her own road and works out that the man who came for the fridge is now a story about a thing that is not in her house, and that she has put the truth three doors down and cannot take it back. She puts the green chair under the window and does not move it again. That night the light at number nine comes on early and the shape at that window is not at a sill.
- **0644 — The Card With Nothing On It.** Monday 31 May 2021. The woman in her late forties sees the stool on the step at number nine, out to air, and does not go there, and goes up to number twelve instead. The corner by the sink is empty and the green chair is at the table under the window with the cushion on it, where a chair goes, for the first time since the twenty-fourth of April. They have ten minutes with not one false thing in the room. Then she says the man did come. She tells her about a card on the shelf by the door with nothing ticked on it, and the woman in her late seventies stands with a cloth in her hand and works out in four seconds that she is being given something, and says *he never came*, and the two of them spend a minute and a half agreeing, in the plainest words, that a man came for a fridge, both knowing the other is doing it on purpose. At the door the woman in her late seventies asks her which of the two she will tell, and she cannot answer that, and gets back *I don't know*, which the other woman agrees with, and the question stays in the passage.
- **0645 — Six Things On An Envelope.** Thursday 3 June 2021. The woman in her late seventies has been waiting since the Monday for either of them to knock and neither has. She goes to the drawer under the telephone, takes out a gas envelope and gets a pencil, and writes six things on the back of it in lower case with no punctuation: the gate, the front room, the window in the back room, the hotplate on the left, the bath tap, the passage light. She puts the gate first because it is the one she has told nobody about and the one she is not going to ask for. She rubs it out and writes it again higher up, because a woman of seventy-eight who writes down a gate has written down that she is expecting somebody. She considers tearing it up and does not. She leaves it face up on a table that has been against a wall since before Christmas, and she does not move the table, and she goes and stands at the sink.
- **0646 — The Sixth Thing On It.** Thursday 10 June 2021, on the Wednesday. The man in his early forties has had a stove element in the van since the Tuesday and a bulb in the door pocket since the Friday before last. He picks the envelope up off the table without asking and reads it in about half a minute and can see at once that it is not a repair order and cannot work out why. He does not ask which one she wants first, because he can see the answer is about the gate. He asks one question that is not on the list, about how long the blanket has been on the window, and then fits a five watt bulb in the passage in four minutes, which is the last thing on the list and the easiest, and leaves the stove he came for, because doing the stove would put him in that kitchen for two hours and the agreement on the bench does not cover it but the four hours in that front room did. He puts the envelope back face up and squares it with the edge of the table. In the van he writes one letter on the box and puts it away and does not come back.
- **0647 — The Back Room And The Blanket.** Monday 14 June 2021. A woman in her early thirties from number ten has been able to see a folded blanket across a foot of gap and a fence since the spring and has told nobody, including her sister, because you do not say to a person of seventy-eight that you can see their blanket. She knocks at about ten past ten with four knocks, which is too many. The woman at number twelve works out in two seconds who she is, because nobody she knows knocks four, and says come in inside about a second, because she does not know how to refuse somebody who has knocked. The window cannot be fixed by her and she says so and takes the glass out and puts a taped sheet in. In the back room the older woman cannot get down on the floor and is told *you've managed on your own, sit down*, which nobody has said to her since before Christmas, and she sits on a mattress. On the way out the young woman sees the gate is off the latch and offers to do it in two minutes with a screwdriver and is told no in three seconds without being told why, and does not ask. Afterwards the woman of seventy-eight opens the drawer, and reads her own list upside down for a quarter of an hour without knowing it.
- **0648 — Can I Take That Envelope.** Saturday 19 June 2021. The woman in her late forties comes up to look at a table and finds the fault is not the leg but a frame let go at one end, and does it properly: chisel, card joint, mallet, clamp, ash wedge driven and not sawn off, and says out loud why. She asks for a bit of paper to mark the wedge and is handed the gas envelope, and there are six things on the back of it in pencil, and she reads the first two lines in about a second and a half and says she is sorry and puts it down face up. She reads it four times from the floor without picking it up, looking for a sign of who wrote it and for what, and finds nothing. While she is in the van the woman at twelve takes the envelope off the table and puts it in the drawer. Neither of them mentions it. At the door the woman in her late forties asks for the envelope and is given it out of the drawer, because a woman who opens that drawer is not the one who put it in. The gate swings as she goes out and she looks at it for two seconds and says nothing about it, in a house where the first line of that list is about the gate.
- **0649 — The Back Of It.** Tuesday 22 June 2021, on the far side of the ring road. The woman in her late forties loses a quarter of a full clear to a brother with a key at midday and puts eight boxes back herself without a word of the tone in her voice. At about half past two she needs to write down two sacks and a set of stairs and has no paper, because a woman who does this for a living uses the client's paper. She puts her hand in her coat, finds the envelope, turns it face down and writes a room-by-room job list on the back of it without turning it over: back room, hall, box room, bathroom, landing, and hoarding thurs eight. Four seconds later she works out she has written on the back of somebody's handwriting, turns it over, and reads the other side upside down before she knows which way up she is. She tapes it to the inside of a garage cupboard door that is off its hinges, is going in a skip, and has been priced for replacement by her own hand. She stops at the front gate and works out that she cannot come back for it, because coming back would make her a person who goes back, and she has never been one until a fortnight ago.
- **0650 — A Gate On Main Street.** Monday 28 June 2021. The man in his early forties has taken the shoebox out twice in car parks for no reason. He runs four jobs and tells the third man the truth about a staircase and charges for the visit. He spends ninety minutes hanging a pair of gates for two strangers, says they will need four new plates and a Saturday, tells them what it will not achieve, and cannot work out why a gate he is paid for is easier than a gate on a list he is not. He drives half a mile out of his way to the end of that road at a quarter past six and does not slow down, because he has nothing in his hands and a man who arrives at that door with nothing in his hands is a man who came to look at a house. He does not ring the woman in her late forties, because asking her which side she is on is a bench thing. He puts the box on the top of his own bench in the clear and works out that a man who counts his own Wednesdays has already decided and is doing something else.
- **0651 — Six Things On The Fridge.** Saturday 3 July 2021. The woman in her late fifties at number nine works out that everybody on that road has got her wrong: she does not eat standing, she ate standing because she would not do anything to her mother's chairs, and since the stool she has eaten sitting down on two nights out of seven and standing on five because she is not hungry until her coat is off. Her back door has stopped latching and she packs the hinge with folded cardboard and does it herself, four hours, on a Saturday morning. Her sister tells her, in the middle of something else, that the woman at number twelve has had a man in and had a light put in her passage. She writes six things on a pad in the order she would actually do them, which is the correct order, and rules a line through the first one and writes DONE, the first line crossed off on any list in this borough. She then works out that she cannot go up the road, and that the reason is not politeness and not fear and is that she was given a stool for nothing by a stranger, never asked a question, and has no standing to ask for anything now. She looks across the back gardens at her sister's light on at four o'clock and does not go round.
- **0652 — The Fourth Thing.** Wednesday 7 July 2021. The man in his early forties buys a bulb he does not need for nine pounds so that he is not arriving with nothing in his hands, and drives up at about half past ten with a shoebox in a bag. She opens the door and says *you've come about the hotplate* and he says yes, and it is the first straightforward thing anybody has said in that house in a fortnight. He sees the ash wedge and the card under the window leg from the doorway and does not ask who put it there. He finds the fault is a burnt terminal on a perfectly good element, not a dead hotplate, tells her the knob has been running about two hundred degrees hot since before Christmas, and gives her the only thing she had wanted to know, which is that it is not going to catch fire. She starts to ask him a question and cannot finish it. He stands with a boot on the gate for two seconds on the way out and says nothing about it.
- **0653 — Two Lists On One Piece Of Paper.** Tuesday 13 July 2021. The woman in her late forties goes back to the empty house because the back room has to come out and she has to price a cupboard door she already priced from the outside. The envelope is still taped to the inside of that door. She peels the tape off with a roll of tape and it takes the top corner of her own handwriting with it, so neither list can be used again. A man in his late twenties there about a front room floor tells her she does not want a door, she wants two new hinge plates at about twelve pounds, which she takes off the invoice. He asks whose the other side of the piece of paper is and she says *it's mine*, and he says *right* and does not ask to see and will never know. She then rings the man in his early forties about the price of an element, tells him she has got the list, and says she has not touched it, and he asks what the order of it is, and she says that is why she is ringing, and he says bring it round Friday.
- **0654 — Read Out Loud.** Friday 16 July 2021. The woman in her late forties opens the door on a Friday morning to a man she has agreed with on a bench never to put their two heads together in that house. Neither says a word about it and she tells him out loud in the doorway that she knows, before he is through the door. In the kitchen he reads the six things out loud in front of two people, reads the gate twice, puts the paper down, says *that's not an order*, and then does not ask her why it is in that order and stands there. After about eight seconds she says it herself: the order is the order she cannot be doing with them, and the gate is at the top because it is the only one she actually wants, because a gate is for letting somebody in, and she has not asked one single person who has come to that door since before Christmas to come in. The woman in her late forties says *I'll do your gate*, which costs her the bench and a new position in that kitchen. He says the drops on the back of the gate are painted in under old gloss, and that freeing them is a chisel and a wire brush and about ten minutes, and it will cost her nothing, and he wants it said in front of the woman that it is nothing. And when he asks what is wrong with the second thing on the list she says: *it's the only room anybody sits in.* **THE TWO SENTENCES IN ITALICS IN THE EARLIER EDITION OF THIS LINE WERE *IT'S GOT A CHAIR AT THE TABLE*, WHICH THE CHAPTER DOES NOT CONTAIN, AND A PARAPHRASE SAYING NOBODY HAD COME TO THAT DOOR THAT SHE HAD NOT ASKED FOR, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT 0654 SAYS AND OF WHAT 0654 WAS REPAIRED TO SAY. THE SENTENCE IS AT `chapter-0654.md:272`.**

## VOLUME 05, CONTINUATION 0047 — CHAPTER SUMMARIES 655–664

- **0655 — Ten Minutes On A Stranger's Gate.** Tuesday 20 July 2021. The man in his early forties stops at the end of a gravel drive on a road he was not due to be on because he can see a lump of old gloss on the back of a frame, and he takes it off in about nine minutes, and takes the gate off its drops, hangs it, and shuts it three times with his weight on it, and it does not come in. An old man of about seventy comes out with a mug, says *that's what the last fella said*, and asks how much he owes, and the man says a figure he has never charged anybody and does not correct. What he works out in the gravel is that he knew, on the sixteenth of July, in a kitchen, when he said *nothing* to a woman who asked him *how much is that*, and the deciding took him four seconds and it was the right thing. He will not go back and say the figure was wrong, because if it was wrong then he knew on the Friday. He goes past a second gate with the same lump and does not stop, and cannot say why until about four seconds afterwards. On his knees on a set of steps on the ring road with a tread in one hand he puts the wire brush in the back pocket of his jacket because his hands are full.
- **0656 — A Bad Brush Out Of A Bucket.** Monday 26 July 2021. The woman in her late forties buys a wire brush out of a galvanised bucket by the door of a shop on the ring road because she has a bolster chisel and no brush and the drops on that frame are one solid lump. She will not ring him, because he would say yes, and she has worked out since the Friday what she would have to do with a yes, which is be in a kitchen with the woman and the man in it at the same time. She spends the whole Monday on a clearance on the far side of the ring road, and the brush is a wall brush with a soft crimp and it moves nothing on a picture rail. At half past four, in her own van, she works out that she does not have to knock on that door at all, because the door is not on the latch and has not been since before Christmas, and that the reason she is not going up that road is that a knock on it is a way of making a woman who cannot say no to a knock open a door, and she will not put that woman in a position of having to refuse her. She writes *mon. gate. wire brush* on a pad and does not cross it out.
- **0657 — Three Doors Down And No Further.** Thursday 29 July 2021. The woman in her early thirties who taped the back room window in May goes up three doors with a roll of brown tape in a coat pocket, because the top corner of the tape sheet has come away and she put it there. She knocks, and the door comes away from the frame under her knuckles, and this time she goes in. The woman in her late seventies says *which one* and she says *the gate*, and is out of the kitchen door at ten past ten. On the step before that she had about a minute with an open door onto the only room she has any business in, and she used all of it on a corner of glass, and the question she did not ask is about a rush-seated chair against a wall and a green chair at a kitchen table. She puts the roll of tape into the woman's hand, says *I've got about half of a roll left anyway*, which is a lie about the roll, and does not go in. From the step she can see that the gate does not shut square and she cannot see the fault in it.
- **0658 — The Back Pocket Of A Jacket On A Hook.** Tuesday 3 August 2021. The man in his early forties goes into a unit at half past seven because he is doing a gate that afternoon and he has no brush. It is in the back pocket of a work jacket on a hook, where it has been since the twentieth of July, and a thing cannot get into a pocket, and it takes him about four minutes at a bench to get to the fact that he put it there himself. He will not carry it up that road, because it is a stranger's gloss and not his. He buys a new one with his own money out of a rack by the window in a shop with a galvanised bucket by the door, and the reason is that a man who has just failed to account for a tool does not want a tool he cannot account for. He stands at the tailgate and does not go up that road, because the woman in her late forties put her hand over her mouth and said she would do the gate, and if he goes first he takes that off her and there is no way to put it back. The brush goes in the drawer under the bench and he does not shut it.
- **0659 — Four Hours At The Back Of A Frame.** Saturday 7 August 2021. The woman in her late forties knocks at nine, the door comes in about a second, and inside a house the woman in her late seventies asks *which one*. She cannot get a bolster into the side of the lump so she goes at it from underneath on her knees in the grass and it comes off in about ten pieces in about two hours, and both palms are cut inside. The woman of seventy-eight comes out across the grass at about twelve with a mug, stops two arms off on the walked-flat line, and says *you'll want to put them back after*, which is the nearest thing to a thank you that house has had since before Christmas, and neither of them manages the other thing. The bad brush gets into the two-inch socket where the good one would not, which is the one thing it is good for. The gate swings and does not come in on the path for the first time since it was put on, and nobody is standing at it. At half past three she comes in through the front door to wash her hands, has to cross the front room to reach the kitchen, is carrying the brush, and puts it down on a sideboard against the far wall that has nothing else on it.
- **0660 — The Room With The Thing In It.** Saturday 14 August 2021. The woman in her late seventies has had a wire brush on a sideboard in her front room since the Saturday. She works out first that somebody has been in her house, because the door is not on the latch, and then that she cannot get at the fact because there is nobody to ask. She tries four places — sideboard, passage shelf, kitchen windowsill, bin — and rejects all four, and the reason is the same in every case: every one of them is a place where somebody can ask her about it, and you cannot bin a thing you cannot name. She gets the pencil out to cross the first line off the list and there is no pencil in that house and has not been since before Christmas, and she cannot ask anybody for one and there is no shop at the end of that road. At half past two she works out why she has not sat in the front room since the sixteenth of July: the room now has a question in it, and if anybody comes in while she is in there she will be a woman being asked about a thing, and she has never been able to be that. She does not sit in the front room again.
- **0661 — The Drawer Under The Bench.** Tuesday 17 August 2021. The woman in her late forties has a plaster on one palm and not the other and works a morning and a half with her hand open. She can put a plaster on anybody and cannot do it to herself, and she stands in a kitchen with a first aid box open on the table and works out in about a minute that she has never once walked into a room where somebody might be helped and been the one who was helped instead, and that you cannot learn the moves at a quarter past ten in the morning. At the door of the small house the woman who booked it looks at the hand and asks, and she has to give a word for it, and the word is a gate, and the woman lets her go without asking anything. At four o'clock she opens the bag in her own van and the first thing she finds out is that the brush is not in it: it is on a sideboard at the end of that road, where she put it down on the Saturday without deciding to, and there is a woman of seventy-eight at a kitchen window in that house and neither of them has ever said a word about it. What is in the bag is a bolster off her own board, the tool that got under the lump because the lump was on the underside of the frame. The gate is done and a job that is finished is a job a tool has nothing to be for. The bag is for a job and the drawer is for everything else, and nothing in that drawer has been shut since the van was new. She says *I will keep that* to a piece of waste ground, puts the bolster in the drawer, and shuts it. **REPAIRED IN THE REVIEW PASS OF 0047: AS FIRST WRITTEN THIS CHAPTER PUT THE WIRE BRUSH IN THE DRAWER AS WELL AS ON THE SIDEBOARD, AND THE BRUSH IS IN ONE PLACE ONLY.**
- **0662 — Where The Stool Came From.** Monday 23 August 2021, from ten past midnight. The woman in her late fifties comes in from a late and her sister is at her table with a form from the council and has been there since half past ten, and neither of them ever mentions that. Told without being asked that a light has been put in at number twelve, and then unasked that the woman of seventy-eight could not have done that herself, she asks one question and it is only a place. Standing at her own sink she works out that the man who has been in that passage is the man who made her stool, because a woman of seventy-eight told her on a step in May that he made it himself on a bench in a unit off the industrial estate, and has said nothing about it since. She works out that there is a thank you in the stool she can see exactly and cannot get at, because a woman of seventy-eight cannot say *I know what this is* about anything and a woman in her late forties is not somebody she can go to. She asks her sister no questions at all. She carries the stool out of the kitchen into the front room, because the kitchen is where you use a thing and the front room is where you look at one.
- **0663 — A Soft Place In A Ceiling.** Friday 27 August 2021, from about ten at night. The woman in her late seventies empties the cloth from the bowl under the bath tap in the dark, points the torch at the ceiling by accident, and finds a soft brown mark about a foot across with a hard edge on it, and puts her thumb in it about a quarter of an inch and it comes back with grit on it. She goes up her own stairs for the first time since the spring, finds the top landing in the dark, finds the hatch and the fixed ladder, gets a foot and a half higher on a stool out of the front room, and hears a high level cistern weeping at the far side of a joist. She does not go up the ladder. She cannot stop it from downstairs either, because she has lived in that house since before the war and has never once looked for where the pipe comes up. She works out on the half landing that the landing is over the front room, so the second thing on her list is the room the water is going to come into, and that the front room and the tap are not two jobs but one thing. She puts the cloth back in the bowl and the tap goes on dripping.
- **0664 — In The Middle Of The Passage.** Wednesday 1 September 2021. The woman in her late seventies decides, sitting at her kitchen table with a cold cup of tea, that the front room is now a room with a thing in it she cannot identify and that she will not sit in a room like that. She goes through all four places in the house a thing can go and finds that every one of them is a place where somebody can ask her about it, and then finds a fifth: a thing on the floor in the middle of a passage is a thing that gets stepped over, and a person who has stepped over a thing has not asked about it. She works out that she would like to be stepped over, and that a thank you needs the giver to know it is a thank you, and a step over does not. She does not wash the brush, because a clean thing on a floor looks like a thing somebody has done on purpose. At half past ten she puts it in the middle of the runner with the handle across the walking line so you cannot step down the side of it. Then she goes round the side of the house, lifts both drop bolts out with a thumb and a half, stands the gate back against the coal shed wall, does not go into the road, and comes in and shuts the front door behind her. There is nobody in the road. On her way to her own kitchen she steps over the brush, which is the first time in this account that she has got past a thing in her own house by stepping over it.
